title: Enrolling on an evening course

script_json.title: Enrolling on an evening course
script_json.scenario: A man telephones the enrolments office of a community college to join an evening course; the officer takes his details and explains the practical arrangements.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man and an enrolments officer at a community college. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good afternoon, Northgate Community College, enrolments. Rachel speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'm ringing about the evening classes — the autumn ones. Is it too late to sign up?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Not at all. We've still got places on most of them. Have you studied with us before?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No, this'd be my first time.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, then I'll need to put you on the system. Could I take your surname first?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's Okafor.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sorry, would you mind spelling that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Of course. O. K. A. F. O. R. Okafor.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Lovely, thank you. And your first name?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Daniel.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thanks, Daniel. And could I have an address?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Yes, it's twenty-seven Bellfield Road. Bellfield — that's B. E. L. L. F. I. E. L. D. — Road, Northgate.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twenty-seven Bellfield Road. Got it. And are you working at the moment? I only ask because a few of our courses have a daytime group as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Yes, I'm an electrician, so honestly the evening is the only thing that works for me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's no problem at all — nearly all the craft courses run in the evening. Can I also ask how you heard about us? We have to report it for our funding.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Erm, I think I saw something on your website first. No — actually, that's not right. I picked up one of your brochures in the library.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The library, perfect. They're very good to us. So, did you have a particular course in mind?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Well, I was hoping to do Introduction to Photography, but a mate of mine said it's already full.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'm afraid he's right — photography filled up in about a week. There's still room on Introduction to Bookbinding, though, and it's the same tutor.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Bookbinding. Do you know, that actually sounds better. Put me down for that one, please.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Introduction to Bookbinding. Now, that course runs twice a week — there's a Tuesday group and a Thursday group.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Tuesday would be — hmm, no, sorry, I've got five-a-side on Tuesdays. Thursday, please.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thursday it is. I'll email a confirmation across once we're finished.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, Daniel, just a few practical things. The Thursday group meets in the Beech Building, on the first floor.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And what time does it start? I don't finish work until six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You'll be fine. We used to begin at half past six, but we pushed it back — classes now start at 6.45 and run through until nine.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: 6.45. That gives me time to get across town. And what about the fee?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the full fee for a ten-week term is 96 pounds.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ah. Right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But there's a reduced rate for anyone living in the borough, and Bellfield Road is well inside it, so you'll pay 86 pounds a term.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. Can I pay it in instalments?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can — two payments. One when you enrol, and one at half term.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Great. And is there anything I need to buy beforehand? Tools, or a kit of some sort?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No, all the tools stay in the workshop. People often turn up with their own scissors and a bone folder, but we supply all of that. The one thing I would say is bring an apron, because the glue does splash.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: An apron. I'll dig one out of the van.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And do bring your enrolment reference to the first session. It'll be at the bottom of the email.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Will do. Can I ask what happens if I have to miss a week? We sometimes get called out at short notice.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine — just let the tutor know. She puts a short summary of each session on the course page, so you can catch up before the next one. As long as you make eight of the ten, you'll get your certificate.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, there's a certificate? I wasn't expecting that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, and there's a little exhibition on the last Thursday of term — families are welcome. Most people bring whatever they've made.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That sounds lovely. Right — oh, one last thing: parking. Is there anywhere to leave the van?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, yes. The main car park is reserved for staff during the day, and at weekends it's closed for the market — but from six in the evening it's free for anyone on a course.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Perfect. That's everything, I think. Thanks very much for your help, Rachel.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're welcome, Daniel. We'll see you on the fifth of October.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one.

groups.instruction: Complete the enrolment form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: The form is filled top to bottom in the order she asks for it. Hear the course and the address has gone.
teaching.strategy: This is a form being filled in live, so the officer's questions are your headings. Slot-type all six boxes in the pause: two are names you must spell, one is a job, one a place, one a course, one a day.
teaching.preview_focus: Mark the two boxes that will be spelled out, Surname and the street name. Those are transcription, not comprehension, and they need your pen ready.
teaching.watch_out: Half these boxes are given wrongly first, then corrected. Writing early is what loses them, not failing to hear.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Time first, then money. If she has reached the fee, question seven has already gone past.
teaching.strategy: Two figures four lines apart, and both are announced by a change of value rather than by a keyword. Fix the shape of each answer first, a clock time and then a price, and write only the figure.
teaching.preview_focus: Notice what is already printed: 'until 9 p.m.' and the pound sign. Both tell you the answer is a bare figure and repeating the unit costs the mark.
teaching.watch_out: Form, not hearing, loses these two. '6.45 p.m.' and 'eighty-six pounds a term' are heard correctly and written wrongly.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Ten's answer comes after nine's. Once she is talking about parking, the workshop question is finished.
teaching.strategy: Both of these name all three options out loud, so option-spotting is worthless by construction. Listen instead for the small cancelling clauses, 'we supply all of that' and 'reserved for staff', and keep the one thing nobody cancels.
teaching.preview_focus: Read all six options now, because there is no time later. Underline the verb in each stem: 'bring' in nine, 'can park' in ten.
teaching.watch_out: Attribution, not vocabulary. Every wrong option is spoken in its own words, attached to somebody else or to another time of day.

questions.instruction: Complete the enrolment form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
NORTHGATE COMMUNITY COLLEGE — ENROLMENT FORM
Surname: ______
questions.explanation: The printed word 'Surname' tells you before the audio that this is transcription, not comprehension. 'Would you mind spelling that for me' is the cue to stop listening for meaning. He says the name, then gives six letters. No trap: the whole mark is orthography. Write the letters as they land.

prediction.note: A name you cannot guess. Put your pen on the box and get ready to write single letters.

signpost.phrase: would you mind spelling that for me

teaching.answer_quote: O. K. A. F. O. R. Okafor.

form.note: Take the letters, not the sound of the word. Case is not marked, so lower case scores.

questions.instruction: Complete the enrolment form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Address: 27 ______ Road, Northgate
questions.explanation: '27' and 'Road' are already printed, so predict one word: a street name, spelled. 'Could I have an address' announces it a turn early. He says the whole address, then spells the middle word only. No trap. Write the nine letters and leave 'Road' alone.

prediction.note: House number and 'Road' are printed. One word only, and it will be spelled out.

teaching.answer_quote: Bellfield — that's B. E. L. L. F. I. E. L. D.

form.note: Two L's in the middle, one at the end. Write each letter as it lands; do not wait for the end.

questions.instruction: Complete the enrolment form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Occupation: ______
questions.explanation: 'Occupation' wants a job noun, singular, no article. She never says the word: she asks whether he is working. He answers with the trade in his first clause. Clean item. Write the noun, not the verb, and not the employer.

prediction.note: A job title, one word, no article. Expect a trade rather than a company name.

signpost.phrase: are you working at the moment

teaching.answer_quote: Yes, I'm an electrician, so honestly the evening is the only thing that works for me.

form.note: A job noun ending in -ian. 'Electric', 'electrical' and 'electrician's' all score zero.

questions.instruction: Complete the enrolment form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Heard about the college from: a brochure in the ______
questions.explanation: 'a brochure in the' wants a singular place, and 'the' is already printed. He answers, then withdraws it: 'No — actually, that's not right.' The website is the value he takes back; the library is the one he leaves standing. One word, no article.

prediction.note: 'in the' wants a place, singular. A building, not a website and not a person.

teaching.answer_quote: I picked up one of your brochures in the library

distraction.signal: No — actually, that's not right
distraction.note: He answers, then withdraws it in the same breath. Do not write on the first place named; wait for the sentence after the correction.

form.note: One word: library. The article is already printed, so 'the library' is two and scores zero.

questions.instruction: Complete the enrolment form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Course chosen: Introduction to ______
questions.explanation: 'Introduction to' is printed, so predict one word: a craft. 'There's still room on' is the offer, one turn before he accepts. He asks for photography and is refused; the course he says yes to is the one that goes on the form. Write it as one word.

prediction.note: The second half of a course title. One word, a practical craft, and it will be said twice.

teaching.answer_quote: Bookbinding. Do you know, that actually sounds better.

paraphrase_link.audio: Put me down for that one

distraction.signal: photography filled up in about a week
distraction.note: He asks for photography and is refused. What goes on the form is the course he says yes to, not the one he wanted.

form.note: 'Bookbinding' and 'book-binding' both score. Write it as one word and you cannot go wrong.

teaching.recovery: If the correction in six cost you, drop it. She names the course, and Daniel repeats it as the first word of his reply.

questions.instruction: Complete the enrolment form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Class day: ______ evenings
questions.explanation: 'evenings' is printed, so predict a weekday. 'hmm, no, sorry' is the repair marker and it lands mid-sentence. He starts on Tuesday, gives his reason for refusing it, then names the day he wants. The last day stated for the slot is the answer. Singular.

prediction.note: A weekday name. Two are offered a line apart; only one survives the sentence.

teaching.answer_quote: hmm, no, sorry, I've got five-a-side on Tuesdays. Thursday, please.

distraction.signal: hmm, no, sorry
distraction.note: He abandons Tuesday mid-word and gives his reason before naming the day he wants. The day after the reason is the answer.

form.note: Write 'Thursday'. The printed 'evenings' already carries the plural, and 'Thursdays' is not the keyed form.

teaching.recovery: If the day blurred, guess a weekday in the check step. The narrator's pause for questions seven to ten comes next and resets you.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Practical details
Classes start at ______ (until 9 p.m.)
questions.explanation: 'until 9 p.m.' is printed, so predict a start time only. 'we pushed it back' is the repair marker. Half past six is given in the past tense and replaced in the same sentence. A time in the past tense never answers a present-tense timetable. Write the figure alone.

prediction.note: A clock time, evening. The finish is printed, so only the start is wanted.

teaching.answer_quote: classes now start at 6.45 and run through until nine

distraction.signal: We used to begin at half past six
distraction.note: 'Used to' is the whole item. A time in the past tense is never the answer to a present-tense timetable.

form.note: Write the figure alone: 6.45 or 6:45. 'p.m.' and 'quarter to seven' are not keyed forms.

teaching.recovery: If the correction beat you, let it go. The fee is next and she opens it with the words 'the full fee'.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Fee Daniel will pay per term: £______
questions.explanation: The pound sign is printed, so predict a bare figure in the tens. 'But there's a reduced rate' is the contrast that carries the answer. Two prices arrive seconds apart; the stem asks what Daniel pays, not what the course costs. Write the second figure only.

prediction.note: The pound sign is printed. Expect two prices and take the one attached to Daniel.

teaching.answer_quote: so you'll pay 86 pounds a term

paraphrase_link.printed: Fee Daniel will pay per term

distraction.signal: the full fee for a ten-week term is 96 pounds
distraction.note: Two prices, one gap. The stem says what Daniel will pay, so the figure attached to him beats the one attached to the course.

form.note: The pound sign is printed, so write 86 and stop. The bare figure is always the safest form.

teaching.recovery: If the figures blurred, take the second one. Question nine follows Daniel's own question about what to buy, so you will hear it coming.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Rachel tell Daniel to bring to the workshop?

options.A: an apron
options.B: a pair of scissors
options.C: a bone folder

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three items to be spoken. 'The one thing I would say is' marks the endorsed one. Scissors and a bone folder are named as things people bring, then cancelled by 'we supply all of that'. Only the apron survives. Write A, not the word.

prediction.note: All three will be named. Listen for which one is his to bring, not which one is mentioned.

signpost.phrase: The one thing I would say is

teaching.answer_quote: The one thing I would say is bring an apron, because the glue does splash
teaching.recovery: If you hesitated, let it go. Question ten is about parking and Daniel asks that question himself, so it is audibly announced.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Scissors are named in the option's own word one clause before the answer, and a learner scanning for equipment stops at the first familiar thing.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: 'We supply all of that' cancels the scissors and the bone folder together, in five words.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is the only specialist term in the list, and an unfamiliar word feels like the technical thing an item writer would ask about.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It sits inside the same cancelled clause: people bring their own, but the college supplies them.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Course members can park in the main car park

options.A: at any time of day
options.B: from six in the evening
options.C: only at weekends

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect every time of day to be named. 'one last thing: parking' announces the topic a turn early. Daytime is for staff and weekends are closed for the market, so both wrong options are stated as true facts about other times. Only the evening is open to members.

prediction.note: The stem asks when course members can park. Expect three times of day, two of them attached to somebody else.

teaching.answer_quote: but from six in the evening it's free for anyone on a course

distraction.signal: at weekends it's closed for the market
distraction.note: Three times of day in one sentence. Attach each one to whoever it belongs to before you commit to a letter.

teaching.recovery: This is the last item in the part. Fill any blank box in the thirty-second check; an empty box is a guaranteed zero.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Her answer opens 'There is, yes', and a learner who hears the car park confirmed marks the least restrictive of the three options.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The daytime is reserved for staff, so 'at any time of day' is directly contradicted.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Weekends are named out loud in the option's own word, and a learner listening for a time window takes the one they recognise.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: At weekends the car park is closed altogether for the market, so it is the one time nobody can park.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Nothing here is hard to understand. Six of the ten answers are offered wrongly first and then replaced, so the mark turns on when you write, not on whether you heard.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: Two fees seconds apart, and the printed frame asks what Daniel pays, not what the course costs. The wrong figure is the loud one.

title: Welcome talk at the Fairhaven Leisure Centre

script_json.title: Welcome talk at the Fairhaven Leisure Centre
script_json.scenario: A duty manager gives an introductory talk to a group of new members of a leisure centre: the history of the building, the practical arrangements, and which part of the centre suits which kind of member.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a duty manager giving a welcome talk to a group of new members at a leisure centre. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to Fairhaven. My name's Marissa, I'm one of the duty managers here, and this little talk is what we do instead of a guided tour — mainly because the tour takes forty minutes and the coffee is free for the next twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, a bit of history first, because somebody always asks what this building used to be. Most people guess it was already a swimming pool. It wasn't. And it wasn't the old cinema either — that was two streets over, where the car showroom is now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: This was the town's bus depot, right up until 2019.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can still see it, actually. That high curved roof over the main pool is the original depot roof, and the green tiles in the entrance hall came straight out of the old ticket office.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. The practical things. Your membership card is also your locker key — tap it on the locker door to lock, tap it again to open. If you lose it, a replacement is four pounds, so please try not to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You really don't need to bring much with you. Towels are free to borrow: just ask at reception and drop them in the basket by the exit on your way out.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Swimming costumes and goggles you would have to buy, I'm afraid, and the vending machine by the door is honestly a last resort.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Parking is the thing I get asked about most. When we first opened we only had ninety spaces and it was chaos every evening, but the extension last spring took us up to 120, plus twelve accessible bays right beside the door.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The barrier reads your number plate, so there's nothing for you to do. The first three hours are free as long as your card has been scanned inside the building.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the pool timetable is printed on the back of your welcome sheet, but let me flag one thing, because people get this wrong all the time. If you don't like a crowded pool, everybody assumes Saturday morning is the quiet one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It really isn't — Saturday morning is when the swimming club has all six lanes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Our quiet swim sessions are on Sunday mornings, seven until ten. Lane ropes out, no whistles, and the lights are kept low. It's the nicest two hours of the week, in my opinion.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And bookings. Anything with an instructor — classes, the squash courts, the climbing wall — has to be booked through the app. Not the website.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The website is only for memberships, and it will cheerfully tell you a class is available when it's been full since Tuesday. So: the app.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Booking opens a week ahead at seven in the morning, and yes, the popular classes do go in about two minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. The last thing I want to do is point a few of you in the right direction, because Fairhaven is a big building and it's very easy to end up doing exactly the same thing every week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So — if you've never actually learnt to swim, and a lot of adults haven't, there's nothing unusual about it at all, please don't start in the main pool. It's two metres deep at the shallow end and it's full of people doing lengths.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Go to the learner pool instead, round behind the changing rooms. It's warmer, it's chest-deep the whole way along, and there's an instructor in the water every weekday evening.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you're training for something, on the other hand — and we've got a lot of members doing the half marathon in October — the treadmills upstairs will do you no favours whatsoever. Use the outdoor track.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's floodlit until nine, it's properly measured, and on Tuesday evenings there's a group that runs intervals together.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then there are people who simply cannot make themselves exercise alone. I'm one of them, honestly. If that's you, the studio is where you want to be.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There are eighteen classes a week in there, everything from spin to very gentle chair yoga, and you'll be in a room with thirty other people who also didn't want to come.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you're bringing small children in, particularly at lunchtime, then it's the family café on the first floor. There's a play corner, the floor is designed to be dropped on, and nobody minds the noise.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The roof terrace is lovely, but that's the one place we ask people to keep the tables adult-only until two o'clock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if what you actually want is to try something you have genuinely never done before — the climbing wall. You do need a twenty-minute induction first, that's free, and after that you can book it like anything else.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One of our members started at seventy-one, so I don't want to hear about your knees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's me finished. Grab a coffee, have a wander round, and if you get lost — and everyone gets lost near the squash courts — just ask anybody in a red top.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: History, then kit, then parking, then the pool, then bookings. Miss one and the next heading tells you where you are.
teaching.strategy: She is talking to a room, so everything is announced before it is delivered. Five gaps, five short bursts: a building type, a thing you borrow, a count, a day, and one word for how you book.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type the five gaps: two-word place name, plural noun, bare number, day of the week, singular noun. Then check which units are already printed.
teaching.watch_out: Four of these five hand you a wrong value first. The printed frame carries the unit, so repeating it costs the mark.

groups.instruction: Which part of the centre does Marissa recommend for each of these people? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to questions 16-20.

teaching.order_note: She works through the five people in the printed order. If you hear children, the runner has already gone.
teaching.strategy: Eight places, five people, each letter used once. She opens every recommendation with the type of person rather than the place, so listen for the 'if you're' frame first and only then for where she sends them.
teaching.preview_focus: Read all eight options and the five descriptions before she starts. Then cross letters off as you use them: a used letter cannot come back.
teaching.watch_out: One misplaced letter forces a second. Most wrong answers here are places she names in order to warn you away from them.
teaching.bank_note: Three letters are never the answer. The main pool and the roof terrace are each named and then ruled out for the person asking.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
FAIRHAVEN LEISURE CENTRE — NEW MEMBERS
The building was previously the town's ______.
questions.explanation: 'the town's' is printed, so predict a building type and no article of your own. She names the two buildings people guess and cancels both before the answer arrives. 'It wasn't' is the whole cancellation and it is spoken quietly. Two words, no article.

prediction.note: A building type, two words at most. 'The town's' is printed, so no article of your own.

signpost.phrase: And it wasn't the old cinema either

teaching.answer_quote: This was the town's bus depot, right up until 2019.

distraction.signal: Most people guess it was already a swimming pool. It wasn't.
distraction.note: She names two guesses and cancels both before answering. A bare 'It wasn't' is the whole cancellation; do not wait for a louder one.

form.note: Two words: bus depot. 'The town's bus depot' is four and the frame already prints 'the town's'.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Members can borrow ______ free of charge.
questions.explanation: 'borrow' plus 'free of charge' predicts a plural thing you take and give back. 'You really don't need to bring much with you' announces the whole list. Towels are free; costumes and goggles are named a line later as things you must buy. One plural word.

prediction.note: A thing you take and give back, almost certainly plural. 'Free of charge' rules out anything with a price.

signpost.phrase: You really don't need to bring much with you

teaching.answer_quote: Towels are free to borrow: just ask at reception

form.note: She says 'towels'. The singular is also keyed here, but write what you hear and do not write both.

teaching.recovery: If the building's old use went past, forget it. She announces 'The practical things' and the next answer is what you can borrow.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Number of parking spaces since the extension: ______
questions.explanation: 'since the extension' predicts a bare count and tells you a second, earlier figure exists. 'took us up to' is the cue. Three numbers arrive in one sentence: ninety before, 120 after, twelve accessible bays on top. Write the figure that follows 'up to' and nothing else.

prediction.note: A bare count of car spaces. 'Since' guarantees an earlier figure will be given first.

signpost.phrase: the extension last spring took us up to

teaching.answer_quote: the extension last spring took us up to 120, plus twelve accessible bays

paraphrase_link.audio: the extension last spring took us up to

distraction.signal: we only had ninety spaces
distraction.note: Three figures in one sentence. 'Since the extension' is printed, so take the one after 'up to', not before it.

form.note: Write 120 alone. The twelve accessible bays are a separate count and adding them gives a number nobody said.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Quiet swim sessions: ______ mornings, 7-10 a.m.
questions.explanation: 'mornings' plus a printed time predicts a day of the week. 'Our quiet swim sessions are on' is the cue. Saturday is named twice with the word 'quiet' attached to it, then contradicted outright. Write the day that follows 'It really isn't', in the singular.

prediction.note: A day name. The clock time is printed, so the day is the only thing wanted.

signpost.phrase: Our quiet swim sessions are on

teaching.answer_quote: Our quiet swim sessions are on Sunday mornings, seven until ten.

distraction.signal: It really isn't — Saturday morning is when the swimming club has all six lanes
distraction.note: Saturday is spoken twice with 'quiet' attached to it. The answer is the day that follows 'It really isn't'.

form.note: One word: Sunday. The printed 'mornings' already carries the plural, so 'Sundays' is not the keyed form.

teaching.recovery: If the day blurred, stop hunting. She opens the next item with the single word 'bookings'; move your eyes to fifteen and wait.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Classes and courts must be booked using the ______.
questions.explanation: 'using the' predicts a singular thing you book through, with the article already printed. 'has to be booked through' is the cue. Two candidates are named within seconds and the website is cancelled twice, first by 'Not the website' and then by 'only for memberships'.

prediction.note: One thing you book through, singular. 'The' is printed, so do not write it again.

teaching.answer_quote: has to be booked through the app. Not the website.

distraction.signal: The website is only for memberships
distraction.note: Both words are spoken within seconds. 'Not' and 'only' are the two cancellations; write the word she repeats at the end.

form.note: 'App' on its own is enough. Two words is the ceiling, so 'the leisure centre app' is three and scores zero.

teaching.recovery: Nothing more is asked in this half. Use the thirty-second pause to guess anything blank, then read sixteen to twenty.

questions.instruction: Which part of the centre does Marissa recommend for each of these people? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to questions 16-20.
questions.prompt: someone who has never learnt to swim

options.A: the learner pool
options.B: the main pool
options.C: the climbing wall

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and note that she opens every recommendation with the type of person, not the place. 'please don't start in the main pool' is a negation, which tells you the main pool is the wrong letter before the right one arrives. The learner pool follows 'instead'.

prediction.note: Five people, five places, in the printed order. She names the person first and the place second.

signpost.phrase: please don't start in the main pool

teaching.answer_quote: Go to the learner pool instead, round behind the changing rooms
teaching.recovery: If you lost a letter, do not hunt. Every item opens with 'if you're' or 'if that's you', so that phrase is your way back.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The main pool is named first and is the obvious place to swim, so a learner matching on 'swim' takes it before the warning registers.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says outright not to start there: two metres deep and full of people doing lengths.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The studio is described as the place for people who cannot make themselves exercise, and a nervous non-swimmer sounds like exactly that person.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The studio is about company, not about not being able to swim. Nothing there is in the water.

questions.instruction: Which part of the centre does Marissa recommend for each of these people? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to questions 16-20.
questions.prompt: someone training for a race

options.A: the learner pool
options.B: the main pool
options.C: the climbing wall

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the indoor option to be raised first. 'on the other hand' opens the item and the treadmills are dismissed in the same sentence they are named in. The recommendation is the imperative that follows: 'Use the outdoor track.'

prediction.note: The stem says training for a race. Expect an indoor option offered and refused before the real one.

teaching.answer_quote: the treadmills upstairs will do you no favours whatsoever. Use the outdoor track.

distraction.signal: will do you no favours whatsoever
distraction.note: The indoor option is raised and dismissed in one sentence. The recommendation is the imperative that follows it.

teaching.recovery: If this one slipped, listen for 'Then there are people who'. That phrase opens question eighteen and costs you nothing to wait for.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: 'The treadmills upstairs' is the only gym equipment named in the whole talk, and a learner matching training to machines parks the spare letter there.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The treadmills are named only to be rejected, and the weights room is never recommended to anybody.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A Tuesday group running intervals together sounds like an organised class, and organised classes are what the studio is for.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That group runs on the outdoor track. It is a reason for the keyed answer, not a different place.

questions.instruction: Which part of the centre does Marissa recommend for each of these people? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to questions 16-20.
questions.prompt: someone who cannot exercise on their own

options.A: the learner pool
options.B: the main pool
options.C: the climbing wall

questions.explanation: Predict a letter. 'If that's you' is the cue and it comes one clause before the place. She describes the person for two sentences before naming anything, which is the pattern for every item in this group. Nothing is offered and withdrawn here: it is a clean item.

prediction.note: The stem is about needing company. Expect a room with other people in it, named after the description.

teaching.answer_quote: If that's you, the studio is where you want to be.
teaching.recovery: Question nineteen opens with 'If you're bringing small children in'. That phrase is your re-entry point if this one went past.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The interval group on the track is the other place in the talk where people exercise together, and the stem is about not exercising alone.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That group belongs to the runner in seventeen. Each letter is used once, so it is already gone.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The climbing wall comes with an induction and an instructor, which sounds like the supervised option for somebody who needs pushing.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The induction is a safety requirement, not company. She recommends the wall for novelty instead.

questions.instruction: Which part of the centre does Marissa recommend for each of these people? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to questions 16-20.
questions.prompt: someone eating with young children

options.A: the learner pool
options.B: the main pool
options.C: the climbing wall

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect two places that suit children. 'If you're bringing small children in' is the cue. The café is named with its play corner; the roof terrace is named immediately afterwards and fenced off for adults until two. An exclusion spoken quietly still kills the option.

prediction.note: Eating with young children. Expect somewhere with food, and expect a second food option to be ruled out.

signpost.phrase: If you're bringing small children in

teaching.answer_quote: then it's the family café on the first floor

distraction.signal: keep the tables adult-only until two o'clock
distraction.note: The next place named sounds nicer and is fenced off in the same breath. Adult-only cancels it for this stem.

teaching.recovery: The last item opens with 'And if what you actually want is'. Wait for that phrase rather than replaying this one in your head.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The roof terrace is called lovely and is named seconds after the answer, so a learner still writing when it arrives overwrites the café.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The tables there are adult-only until two, which is exactly the lunchtime the stem describes.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The learner pool is warm and chest-deep the whole way along, which sounds like the description of a children's facility.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That is the non-swimmer's answer in sixteen, and the stem here is about eating, not swimming.

questions.instruction: Which part of the centre does Marissa recommend for each of these people? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to questions 16-20.
questions.prompt: someone who wants to try an activity that is new to them

options.A: the learner pool
options.B: the main pool
options.C: the climbing wall

questions.explanation: Predict a letter. The stem's phrase is 'new to them' and she paraphrases it as 'something you have genuinely never done before' before naming anything. The place follows the dash. Clean item, and the last of the five: any letter still blank should be guessed now.

prediction.note: Trying something new. Whichever letters are still unused, one of them is this answer.

signpost.phrase: if what you actually want is to try something you have genuinely never done before

teaching.answer_quote: to try something you have genuinely never done before — the climbing wall
teaching.recovery: This is the last item. Fill every blank letter in the check step; there is no penalty and an empty box is a guaranteed zero.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The weights room is never recommended to anybody, so a learner with a spare letter and no memory of it parks the letter here.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Nothing in the talk attaches the weights room to novelty, or to anything else.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She spends longer on the pools than on anything else, so the main pool stays loudest in memory when the last item arrives.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The main pool is raised once, as the place a beginner should avoid. It is never recommended.

what_makes_this_hard.note: A single voice with nobody to ask for a repeat. She states the popular wrong belief first on four of these ten items, so the first plausible value is usually being cancelled.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: Saturday is spoken twice with the word 'quiet' attached to it before the real day arrives one line later.

pre_teach.gloss: the staff member in charge of the building that shift
the garage where a town's buses are kept
what you use only when nothing else is left
parking spaces kept for disabled drivers
the floating dividers taken out of the pool
will not help you at all
gentle yoga done sitting down
a small area set aside for children to play

signpost_map.phrase: So, a bit of history first
And it wasn't the old cinema either
You really don't need to bring much with you
the extension last spring took us up to
let me flag one thing, because people get this wrong all the time
Our quiet swim sessions are on
The last thing I want to do is point a few of you in the right direction
please don't start in the main pool
If you're bringing small children in
if what you actually want is to try something you have genuinely never done before

teaching.accent_note: American voices, but the money is in pounds and the café is on 'the first floor'. Treat the lexis as mixed: useful ear training, not a clean General American model.

title: Tutorial: an air-quality field-work project

script_json.title: Tutorial: an air-quality field-work project
script_json.scenario: Two geography students discuss their field-work proposal on high-street air quality with their tutor, who criticises their measurement plan and questionnaire before they divide up the remaining tasks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two geography students, Priya and Callum, discussing a field-work project with their tutor, Doctor Hallam. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Come in, both of you. Right — the field-work proposal. I've read it. Before we get into the detail, tell me what happened to the river study, because that's what you pitched to me last month.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Yes, sorry, we did change it. We were going to sample water quality along the Cray, but when we went to book the meters, the second-year group had already taken all four of them for the whole of March.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We did ask whether we could borrow a set from the university across town, but their technician said no. Insurance, apparently.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's a shame. Honestly, though, it's not a disaster — you'd have spent half your word count explaining the chemistry. So now it's air quality on the high street.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's right. Nitrogen dioxide, using diffusion tubes, and then a short questionnaire with pedestrians about whether they actually notice the traffic.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Mm. I like the questionnaire. What worries me is the measurement side. Talk me through where the tubes are going.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Six sites. Three at the pedestrianised end by the market, and three at the junction outside the station.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Six sites is fine. That isn't what I mean. Look at your timings — you've got every tube going up at nine in the morning and coming down at five the same afternoon.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Well, that's a full working day.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It is. But it's one working day. Nitrogen dioxide doesn't sit still — you'll catch a rush-hour spike, a lunchtime dip, and if it happens to rain on your Tuesday you'll have measured the weather, not the traffic.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Diffusion tubes are designed to run for a fortnight.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So we just leave them up for two weeks.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Two weeks minimum, and take them down at the same hour you put them up. That one change will do more for your marks than anything else in this proposal.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine by us — it actually makes life easier. We were dreading a fourteen-hour day in February.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Now. The questionnaire. How long is it at the moment?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Twenty-two questions.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Twenty-two. And how long did it take you to fill in?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: About seven minutes.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And you wrote it. Nobody standing outside a chemist's in February is going to give you seven minutes.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We could always put it online instead — a QR code in the shop windows.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You could, but then you lose the one thing that makes it field work: you, standing there, watching who walks past. No — cut it. Five questions, one side of paper, and you'll get four times the responses.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Five. All right. We'd keep the two about perceived noise, and the one about how they travelled in.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can I raise the other thing that's bothering me? I'm not convinced we'll get a representative sample at all. Half the people on that high street on a weekday are commuters walking from the station car park to the platform.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: They don't live in the borough, they've got no particular view about local air quality, and they're in a hurry.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's a genuinely good observation — and it's a finding, not a problem. Make 'where have you come from today' your first question, and then you can report your results by group.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Residents notice it, commuters don't: that's a far more interesting paragraph than anything you'd get out of twenty-two questions.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Should we be comparing our numbers with anything official?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You should — and that's actually where I'd start, before you order a single tube. The council publishes an annual air-quality report, and there's been a permanent monitoring station on that junction since 2016.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Read the last three years of it, take their baseline, then design your sites so they tell us something the station can't.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The journal literature can wait until you write your discussion, and you've clearly read the department handbook already — your risk assessment was the best I've seen this term.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. Let's divide the work up, because you've got three weeks and a reading week sitting in the middle of them. Who's doing what?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'll take the tubes. I've already emailed the lab and they've got twelve spare, so I'll book those out on Monday and get them labelled.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Good. And the council data?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's me. My cousin works in the planning office — which doesn't help in the slightest, but at least I know who to ask. I'll request the raw monthly figures rather than the summary table.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Ask by email, so you've got a record of what you requested. And the risk assessment will need redoing now the tubes are staying up for a fortnight — different hazards, and you'll be working up a ladder on the lamp posts.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's mine as well, then. I wrote the first one, so I may as well.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Fine. The questionnaire itself?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We thought we'd write that one together, actually. We disagree about half the wording, so it's probably better if we argue it out now rather than in the write-up.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It is. And we'll both pilot it — ten people each, on the Saturday.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's the right instinct. And the mapping? I want to see your sites on a proper base map, not a screenshot of an online one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'll do the maps. I took the mapping module last year, so I can get the traffic-flow layer in underneath as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And I'll draft the method section while she's doing that.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Send me one page a week. Not a polished draft — one page, in whatever state it's in. That's the only thing that keeps a project like this on schedule.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thank you. That's really helpful.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: See you next Tuesday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Five stems, five stages of one conversation. When the tutor changes subject, the previous question is closed.
teaching.strategy: Three voices, and every stem tells you whose view it wants. Track who is speaking as hard as you track what is said: two of these five are lost to attribution rather than to vocabulary, and neither of them is difficult English.
teaching.preview_focus: Underline the name in each stem: Dr Hallam in twenty-two, twenty-three and twenty-five, Callum in twenty-four. Then read the fifteen options once.
teaching.watch_out: Options here are raised by the wrong person or at the wrong moment. A true statement that answers a different question still scores zero.

groups.instruction: Who will be responsible for each task? Write A for Priya, B for Callum, or C for both students, next to questions 26-30.

teaching.order_note: The tasks are handed out in the printed order. If you hear the maps, the questionnaire has already gone.
teaching.strategy: Three letters and five tasks, so letters repeat and none is used up. The tutor names each task as a short question and a student claims it in the next turn: the claim is the answer, never the naming.
teaching.preview_focus: Fix the two voices first, Priya the woman and Callum the man. Then read the five tasks so you recognise each one when the tutor names it.
teaching.watch_out: The speaker who takes a task is often not the one who raised it. 'Both' is a real option here and it is genuinely used.
teaching.bank_note: A, B and C are all used, so no letter is spare. Hearing a name is not the same as hearing somebody accept the job.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: The students abandoned their river study because

options.A: the equipment had already been booked by another group.
options.B: their tutor thought the topic was too broad.
options.C: the sampling sites were too far from the campus.

questions.explanation: The stem asks why they abandoned the study, not what the tutor thought of it. 'tell me what happened to the river study' announces it a turn early. Priya gives the reason at once: the meters were all booked. The tutor's opinion arrives later and answers a different question.

prediction.note: The question word is 'because'. Expect several true statements about the river study and only one causal one.

signpost.phrase: tell me what happened to the river study

teaching.answer_quote: when we went to book the meters, the second-year group had already taken all four of them

paraphrase_link.printed: the equipment had already been booked by another group
paraphrase_link.audio: the second-year group had already taken all four of them

distraction.signal: you'd have spent half your word count explaining the chemistry
distraction.note: The tutor's misgiving is real but it arrives after the decision. Ask yourself whether the statement caused the change or merely followed it.

teaching.recovery: If this one went past, wait for 'What worries me is'. That phrase opens the measurement discussion and question twenty-two with it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The tutor does say the chemistry would have eaten half their word count, so a learner listening for his verdict hears a criticism.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He says it only after they have already changed topic, and calls the change no disaster rather than his idea.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The study was on a river and the tubes are on a high street, so a learner reaching for a difference settles on distance.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Nobody mentions distance from campus at any point. Access to meters is the only obstacle given.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Dr Hallam see as the main weakness of the measurement plan?

options.A: There are too few sampling sites.
options.B: The measurements cover too short a period.
options.C: The two ends of the street are not comparable.

questions.explanation: Expect the tutor to name what is fine before he names what is wrong. 'Diffusion tubes are designed to run for a fortnight' is the verdict. He accepts the six sites explicitly, then says 'That isn't what I mean', which is the moment option A dies. The weakness is the single day.

prediction.note: The stem names Dr Hallam, so track his turns. Expect him to clear one option out of the way first.

signpost.phrase: Diffusion tubes are designed to run for a fortnight

teaching.answer_quote: Diffusion tubes are designed to run for a fortnight.

paraphrase_link.printed: The measurements cover too short a period
paraphrase_link.audio: designed to run for a fortnight

distraction.signal: That isn't what I mean
distraction.note: He raises the number of sites, approves it, then says it is not his point. Approval plus a disclaimer kills an option outright.

teaching.recovery: If you lost the verdict, he opens the next topic with the two words 'The questionnaire'. Move to twenty-three and wait for them.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: 'Six sites' is spoken twice in consecutive turns and a learner who catches only the number assumes the count is the problem under discussion.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He says six sites is fine and immediately adds that it is not what he means.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Callum describes two very different ends of the street, a pedestrianised market and a station junction, which sounds like a comparability problem.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The contrast between the two ends is the design, not a fault. Nobody criticises it.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Dr Hallam advises the students to

options.A: reduce the questionnaire to five questions.
options.B: publish the questionnaire online.
options.C: interview shopkeepers rather than pedestrians.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and watch who proposes what. Callum offers the QR code; the stem asks what Dr Hallam advises. 'No — cut it' is the decision marker and the instruction follows in the same breath. An option raised by the wrong speaker is still the wrong option.

prediction.note: The stem names Dr Hallam. Two of these three will be spoken by somebody else or refused by him.

teaching.answer_quote: No — cut it. Five questions, one side of paper, and you'll get four times the responses.

paraphrase_link.printed: reduce the questionnaire to five questions
paraphrase_link.audio: cut it. Five questions, one side of paper

distraction.signal: We could always put it online instead
distraction.note: Callum proposes it, the tutor refuses it. Before you mark an option, check whose mouth it came out of.

teaching.recovery: If this slipped, Callum opens the next item himself with 'Can I raise the other thing'. That is your cue for twenty-four.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is proposed in the option's own words seconds earlier, and the tutor's reply begins 'You could', which sounds like agreement.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The proposal is Callum's and 'You could, but then you lose' refuses it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A chemist's shop is named in the same breath as the people who will not stop, so shops and pedestrians get paired in one sentence.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The chemist is only where a pedestrian would be standing. Nobody suggests interviewing shopkeepers.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What is Callum worried about?

options.A: The weather will stop people from taking part.
options.B: Many of the people on the street are not local residents.
options.C: Traffic noise will make the interviews hard to record.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and note the stem names Callum, so track the male student's turns. 'Can I raise the other thing that's bothering me' announces his worry explicitly. He then states it in two sentences: the pedestrians are commuters who do not live in the borough. Clean item, no reversal.

prediction.note: The stem names Callum, so the answer is in his turn. He announces the worry before he states it.

signpost.phrase: Can I raise the other thing that's bothering me?

teaching.answer_quote: Half the people on that high street on a weekday are commuters walking from the station car park

paraphrase_link.printed: Many of the people on the street are not local residents
paraphrase_link.audio: Half the people on that high street on a weekday are commuters

teaching.recovery: If you missed his point, Priya asks the next question out loud: 'Should we be comparing our numbers with anything official?'

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Rain and February are raised earlier as risks, so a learner holding a general worry about weather attaches it to the wrong speaker.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The rain point is the tutor's, and it is about the tubes measuring weather, not about people refusing.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Noise is a printed option and the questionnaire contains two questions about perceived noise, so the word appears in exactly the wrong place.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Noise is what they are asking about, not a problem with recording. Nothing is being recorded.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Dr Hallam tells the students to begin by reading

options.A: the council's annual air-quality report.
options.B: journal articles on similar studies.
options.C: the department's field-work handbook.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three readings to be named. 'that's actually where I'd start' is the endorsement and it lands on the council report. The journal literature is deferred to the discussion and the handbook is already read, so both are cancelled in one sentence at the end.

prediction.note: The stem's word is 'begin'. All three readings will be named; only one is given a starting position.

teaching.answer_quote: The council publishes an annual air-quality report, and there's been a permanent monitoring station

paraphrase_link.audio: The council publishes an annual air-quality report

distraction.signal: The journal literature can wait until you write your discussion
distraction.note: Both wrong options are named in the last sentence, after the answer. 'Can wait' and 'already' each cancel one in three words.

teaching.recovery: This closes the first half. Use the thirty-second pause to guess anything blank, then read twenty-six to thirty.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Journal reading is what students expect to be told to do first, and the literature is named in the closing sentence where advice usually sits.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He puts it off until the discussion section, which is the end of the write-up, not the start.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The handbook is praised in the same sentence, and praise sounds like endorsement to an ear listening for approval.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He says they have clearly read it already, so it cannot be where they begin.

questions.instruction: Who will be responsible for each task? Write A for Priya, B for Callum, or C for both students, next to questions 26-30.
questions.prompt: booking the diffusion tubes

options.A: Priya
options.B: Callum
options.C: both students

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, A, B or C, and track the voices rather than the words. 'Who's doing what?' opens the whole set. Priya claims the tubes in her first clause, in the first person, and backs it with what she has already done. A task named by the tutor is not a task claimed.

prediction.note: Only three letters here, so they repeat. Listen for 'I'll' and 'that's me', not for the task word.

teaching.answer_quote: I'll take the tubes. I've already emailed the lab and they've got twelve spare
teaching.recovery: If you lost the voice, the tutor names each task aloud as a short question. 'And the council data?' is the next one.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Callum speaks two turns later, so a learner still writing when his voice arrives attaches it to the task they were writing about.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Callum's claim is the council data. He never mentions the tubes.

title: Lecture: street trees and the modern city

script_json.title: Lecture: street trees and the modern city
script_json.scenario: A university lecture on the history of urban street trees, the species chosen for city streets, what cities now expect trees to do, and why so many street trees die young.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about street trees in cities. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good morning. Last week we looked at parks, which are essentially pieces of countryside that a city has agreed to keep. This week I want to talk about something much stranger: the tree that lives in the pavement. The street tree.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And I want to start with where the idea came from, because it isn't ancient. Medieval cities had orchards inside the walls, and they had a tree on the green, but they did not line their streets with trees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The deliberate planted avenue is a Renaissance invention, and the first city to do it at any scale was Paris, in the sixteen hundreds.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: London followed a century later, and Berlin later still, and in both cases the model was explicitly the Parisian one — a straight road, a double row of limes, and a view at the end of it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, why? If you ask people today why the Victorians planted street trees, they'll usually say for beauty, or for the birds. Neither is right, and the second one would have puzzled them enormously.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The reason given in almost every council minute of the eighteen sixties is shade. Shade for pedestrians, shade for horses, and shade for the shop fronts, because sunlight faded the goods in the window. It's a completely practical argument.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There was a second argument, though, and it's the one I find most interesting, because it was wrong. Before germ theory was accepted, the great fear in cities was bad air — miasma. And trees, it was believed, cleaned that air and therefore prevented disease.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There are pamphlets from the cholera years that recommend planting as a public-health measure, in the same paragraph as widening the sewers.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They were wrong about the mechanism, obviously. But we'll come back to whether they were wrong about the outcome.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — species. If you walk down almost any older street in a British or French city and look up, you're probably looking at one tree: the London plane. And the plane was not chosen because anybody thought it was beautiful. It was chosen because it survives.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It tolerates industrial air, it doesn't mind having its roots in rubble, and it sheds its bark in plates, which takes the soot off with it — a self-cleaning tree, in a city that burned coal.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Where the plane failed, cities moved to limes, and then to a much wider palette after the disease outbreaks of the last thirty years taught us what a monoculture costs.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But survival is exactly where the modern problem lies. The average street tree planted today in a British city has a life expectancy, in some surveys, of under twenty years. A plane in a park will live for three hundred.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So what kills them? Not, usually, pollution, and not vandalism, although both get blamed. The single commonest cause of early death is compaction.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The soil under a pavement is compacted to something close to the density of concrete, deliberately, because that's what stops the paving from moving.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Roots cannot get air or water through it, and a tree that cannot root simply declines for a decade and then dies in a dry summer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings us to what we now ask these trees to do — and we ask a great deal more of them than the Victorians did.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first thing is temperature. A street with a closed canopy can be five degrees cooler at head height, on a summer afternoon, than the identical street next to it without trees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: In a city with an ageing population and no air conditioning, that is not a comfort question, it's a mortality question — which is, I think, the sense in which the miasma pamphlets accidentally got it right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The second is water. A mature canopy intercepts rainfall before it reaches the drains, and the fashionable engineering solution now is to plant trees in structural soil that doubles as a storm-water reservoir. The tree becomes part of the drainage system.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the third is money, which is where management comes in. Once you can put a figure on the cooling and the drainage and the particulates, a tree stops being decoration on the balance sheet and becomes an asset — and assets have to be replaced.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Most local authorities are now required to publish a replanting programme, setting out how many trees they will put back for each one they take down.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The public dimension of this is worth a moment. When Melbourne mapped its urban forest, it gave every single tree an identification number and, as an afterthought, an email address, so that residents could report damage.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What happened instead is that people wrote to the trees. Thousands of letters — some of them, I promise you, love letters. Which tells you something useful about consent: it is much harder to fell a tree that people have written to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, targets, and then I'll stop. The figure you'll see in most strategy documents is a canopy-cover target of thirty per cent — that is, thirty per cent of the city's surface shaded when you look down on it from above. Very few European cities are there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The typical British figure is around sixteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the constraint on getting there is changing. For a century the limiting factor on urban planting was pollution, and we solved a great deal of that. The limiting factor now, on every species list I've read in the last five years, is drought.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The question is no longer what a tree can breathe, it's what it can drink.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Next week we'll look at how you actually value one of these things in cash terms, and I'll ask you to bring the two valuation papers from the reading list.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Booking a holiday cottage

script_json.title: Booking a holiday cottage
script_json.scenario: A man telephones a small letting office to book a self-catering cottage for a week in the spring; the assistant takes his details and then goes through the practical arrangements for the stay.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man booking a holiday cottage and an assistant at a letting office. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good morning, Penvale Cottages, Ruth speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, morning. I'm ringing about the self-catering places you do. We're after a week in the spring, if there's anything left.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, yes, plenty. Spring's a good deal quieter than the summer for us. Let me open a booking form and take a few details off you. Can I start with a surname?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's Whitlow.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sorry, would you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Course. W. H. I. T. E. No, sorry, ignore that, there's no E in it. Let me start again. W. H. I. T. L. O. W. Whitlow.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Whitlow. Right, I've got that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And a number we can get you on in the daytime?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's oh one four seven two, double three oh, nine one five.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh one four seven two, double three oh, nine one five. Lovely, thank you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And how many of you would there be?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Just the two of us this time. We're leaving the children with their grandmother, which is honestly the whole idea of the trip.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two adults, then. And when were you thinking of coming down?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The week beginning the fourteenth of April, if that's still free.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Let me have a look for you. The fourteenth of April. No, I'm afraid that one went on Friday. I could do you the week after, the twenty-first.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The twenty-first is fine. Better for us, if anything, because my brother isn't back from sea until the Wednesday.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The twenty-first it is. Now, I've got two cottages free that week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's Larkspur, which is the one down by the river with the veranda, and there's Bramble, up behind the farmhouse.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Does either of them take a dog?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Bramble does. Larkspur's got the better view, I'll be honest with you, but it's the one with the steps down to it, and we don't allow dogs in that one at all.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then it'll have to be Bramble. The dog is the entire point of the holiday, according to my wife.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Bramble, then. I'll pencil you in. Now, there's a deposit to hold it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: How much are we talking?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's normally a hundred and twenty pounds. But you're booking more than eight weeks ahead, and when people do that it comes down to ninety.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ninety. That's manageable.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And you get it back afterwards, obviously, so long as nothing's broken and the place isn't left in a state.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, a few practical things and then I'll let you get on. Keys.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Do we have to come into the office for those?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can, but it's a twenty-minute drive out of your way. Mrs Ackroyd next door used to keep a spare set for us, only she's moved now. So what everybody does these days is the key safe on the wall by the back door. I'll text you the code the night before.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's easier all round.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Much. Now, parking. There's room for one car right outside Bramble, and for most people that's plenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you bring a second one, though, it goes in the yard by the farmhouse. And I'd ask you not to leave it on the lane, because the milk lorry can't get past.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: One outside, one in the yard if we need it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's it. Then the heating, which does catch people out in April. There's a wood burner in the sitting room and a basket of logs in the porch, and that first basket comes with the cottage. After that there's an honesty box on the shelf.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And if we get through more than that?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Couple of pounds in the box and help yourself. Some people bring their own down in the car, which is fine, though it's a lot to carry for what it costs.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Could we order more through you?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We're not a shop, I'm afraid. The garage out on the main road does bags of kindling, if you're ever desperate.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Last thing, and then I'll let you go. Check-out is ten o'clock on the Saturday, and we ask everyone to strip the beds and leave the linen in the basket on the landing. You don't need to hoover or scrub anything, because there's a cleaner in that morning.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the towels?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: In the same basket, please. Whatever you do, don't put those through the machine yourselves. The last lot came out grey and I had to buy forty new ones.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Message received. That's all very clear, thank you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're very welcome. I'll email the confirmation across within the hour, and there's a little map on the back of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

teaching.recovery: If you are still deciding, let it go. She says Now, parking to open the next question.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The caller asks about the office directly and she answers You can, so a learner listening for a yes hears one.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: You can is permission, not recommendation, and she calls it a detour in the same breath.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A named neighbour holding a spare set is the most concrete thing in the turn, and names stick.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Used to keep, and she has moved away. The arrangement no longer exists.

teaching.recovery: If the two cars blurred together, drop it. That's it, then the heating, opens the next one.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The lane is the last place named, and a learner matching the option's own word hears lane and marks it.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It is the one place she forbids, and she gives the reason: the milk lorry.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She does say there is room outside the cottage, and for one car that is genuinely the arrangement.

options.A: The first basket is included in the price.

option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Some people is not expected, and she adds it is a lot to carry for what it costs.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The caller asks the question in the option's own words, so those words are in the room a second before the answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She refuses: we're not a shop. The garage is a different business, not the office.

questions.prompt: What must guests do before they leave?

options.A: vacuum the cottage
options.B: take the sheets off the beds
options.C: wash the towels

questions.explanation: The stem says must, so predict an obligation and expect optional or forbidden things beside it. Last thing opens it and we ask everyone marks the obligation. Strip the beds is the paraphrase; hoovering is cancelled in the same sentence.

prediction.note: Must means one obligation. Expect an option to be cancelled rather than never mentioned.

signpost.phrase: Last thing, and then I'll let you go

teaching.answer_quote: we ask everyone to strip the beds and leave the linen in the basket
teaching.recovery: Nothing follows this one, so guess it in the check step from the stem's verb. Never leave a box empty.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Hoovering is named in the same sentence as the answer, and cleaning a holiday let before leaving feels obligatory.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: You don't need to hoover, because a cleaner comes in that morning.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The caller raises the towels himself, so the word is spoken twice and feels like a live issue.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Towels go in the same basket. Washing them is the one thing she forbids.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Nothing here is hard to hear. Six of the ten answers are the second value offered for their slot, so the part tests whether you can wait rather than whether you can decode.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: Three quantities in one sentence, and the first is the price a different customer would pay.
