title: Signing up for a first-aid course

script_json.title: Signing up for a first-aid course
script_json.scenario: A man signs up for a certificated first-aid course at the front desk of a community recreation center; the program assistant takes his details and then explains what he has to bring and what he has to pay for.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a man signing up for a course at the front desk of a community recreation center in the United States. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hi there. Are you signing up for a class, or just picking up a schedule?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Signing up, I hope. My employer wants me certified before the fall, and somebody at work said you run the course here. I've left it late, I know, but they only told me on Friday.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We do, twice a year. Let me pull up the sign-up sheet. Can I get a last name?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Vasquez.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How do you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: V. A. S. Q. U. E. Z. Vasquez.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Let me read that back to you. V. A. S. Q. U. E. S.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's a Z on the end, not an S. Everybody does that, don't worry.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Z. Sorry about that, I've fixed it. And a cell number?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sure. Two one four, five five five, oh nine eight three.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two one four, five five five, oh nine eight three. Perfect.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, we run two courses this session, and people mix them up all the time. There's water safety, which is mostly pool work, and there's first aid. Same room, same instructor, completely different certificate at the end.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The water safety one. Um, no, hold on, sorry. It's first aid I need. The certificate my employer asked for is the first aid one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First aid it is. That's the Level 2 certificate, and it's the one most employers around here ask for.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That sounds right. Which night is it?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First aid meets Wednesdays. Six weeks, seven until nine thirty, in the room on the first floor at the end of the hall.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Wednesdays are good for me. And when does the whole thing start?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: September. We were going to open on the ninth, but half the town is away that holiday weekend, so we pushed it back to the sixteenth.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The sixteenth. Okay, I can make that work.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Great. The fee is sixty dollars, and we do take it at sign-up rather than on the first night. That covers all six weeks and the assessment at the end.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can I put it on a card?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You could last month. The card reader has been down since Thursday and nobody can tell me when it's coming back, so today it's cash or a check.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I'll write you a check, then. My checkbook's out in the car, I'll bring it in.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine, I'll hold the spot while you go get it. Nobody else is going to take it in the next four minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Okay. A few things about what to bring, because everybody asks me the same four questions. Two of them are about parking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go ahead. I'd rather know now than turn up wrong.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The workbook first. That one's in the price, and there'll be a copy on your chair the first night. Don't buy one online, people do that every session and then they've paid for the thing twice.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Good to know. I nearly did that already.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The pocket mask is a different story. That one you get from us, twelve dollars, and it's yours to keep afterwards. We handed them out free for years, but they walked off faster than we could order them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the dummies you practice on? Do I need my own?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The manikins are ours. You'll each have one for the whole session, at no charge, and they go back in the crate at the end of every night. Same with the training defibrillators.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. What about parking? I picked up a ticket in that lot last spring.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You'll want a lot pass, and that's not something we hand out with the course. You buy one at the front desk, five dollars.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It sticks inside the windshield and it's good for the whole six weeks, so hang on to it. People bring me the old one back in the spring, which I promise you I do not need.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So the book is free, the mask and the pass I pay for, and the manikin goes back in the crate.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's exactly it. You've got it in one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh, and wear something you can kneel in. Half of this course happens on the floor, and good pants do not survive it. Sneakers, not sandals.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Noted. Thanks for your help.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Any time. Go get that checkbook and I'll print your receipt.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Joining a bushwalking club

script_json.title: Joining a bushwalking club
script_json.scenario: A man telephones the secretary of an Australian bushwalking club to join; she takes his membership details and then explains what walkers must bring and what happens when a walk is called off.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man joining a bushwalking club in Australia and the club's secretary. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Talgarra Bushwalking Club, Bronwyn speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: G'day. I'm after joining, if you're still taking people. A bloke at work reckons your Sunday walks are the best thing going.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We are, yeah, we're always after new walkers. I'll take your details and get you on the list. What's the surname?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Halloran.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How do you spell it?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: H. A. L. O. R. A. N. Ah, no, hang on, there's two L's in it. H. A. double L. O. R. A. N. Halloran.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two L's. Halloran. Got you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the best mobile for you?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh four one two, double six, three nine, four one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh four one two, double six, three nine, four one. Beautiful.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, membership. There's a family one, which is ninety dollars and covers everyone under your roof. There's a single. And if you're a student or you've got a seniors card, there's a concession rate.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's just me, no kids, no partner. And I'm at uni two days a week, if that counts for anything.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It counts, so you'd be on the concession, not the single. Cheaper, and it's exactly the same walks.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, so I'll put you down for the Sunday group?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sunday suits me. When's the next one?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first one you can come on is the eighth of March. No, hang on, sorry, the eighth is the long weekend and we never run on public holidays. Make that the fifteenth.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The fifteenth. I'll put it in the phone while we're talking.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Do that. Now, where we meet. It used to be the pub car park out on the highway, and half the old members still turn up there, poor things. We shifted it two years ago.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We meet at the showground car park now, the gravel one round behind the pavilion. Seven o'clock sharp, and I'll be honest, we do leave without people.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Showground. Righto, I'll be early.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the fee. It's fifty-five dollars for the year on a single. The concession one is forty.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Forty. Can I pay that on the day?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can, or you can do a bank transfer when the newsletter comes out. Either's fine by me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Righto, that's you on the list. I'll flag you as a first-timer so somebody walks with you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, a few things about the walks themselves, because people turn up unprepared and it makes for a long day.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go on, I'd rather hear it now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Water. Two litres minimum, and I don't care how heavy it feels in the car park. There's no tap once you're through the gate. People bring an esky with sandwiches in it and forget the water completely, and then I'm sharing mine.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Two litres. Right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Poles are a personal thing. Half the club swears by them and the other half reckons they're a nuisance on rock. Bring them if you already use them, but don't go buying a pair on our account.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: How do I know whether a walk's too hard for me?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Every walk's got a grade, one to five, and it's in the newsletter that goes out on the Thursday. Don't go off the distance, that's the mistake everyone makes. Six kilometres up a ridge will hurt you far more than fifteen on the flat.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's useful. So grade first, distance second.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if you're still not sure, ring the leader. Her number's on the newsletter as well. Mind you, half of them are out of range by the Saturday arvo, so don't leave it late.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And what happens if the weather turns?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We walk in rain, that's just bushwalking. We don't walk on a total fire ban, and we don't walk if the leader calls it off, which she'll do by text the night before. Don't ring the club on the morning, there's nobody in the office on a Sunday.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Text the night before. Got it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Last thing, and this one actually matters. If you've put your name down and then you can't come, tell the leader. We count heads at the car park and we don't move until the numbers add up. One no-show held twenty of us there for forty minutes in January.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Fair enough. Do I get the money back if I miss one?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No refunds, I'm afraid. It's an annual fee, not a per-walk thing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And no, we don't hand your spot to somebody else either. We're not running a bus service. It's purely the head count at the start.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Understood. I'll text her if anything comes up.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Beauty. See you on the fifteenth, then. Bring the water.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

options.A: an esky of food

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three items to be named. Water is the first word of the turn and minimum is the obligation. The food container is what people bring instead, and the poles are offered as a matter of taste.

prediction.note: Must bring means a requirement, so ignore anything offered as a choice.

teaching.answer_quote: Two litres minimum, and I don't care how heavy it feels
teaching.recovery: If you hesitated, let it go. Her next section opens with Poles, and the grade question follows that.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: An esky of sandwiches is named in the same turn, and food does sound like something a walker must carry.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The esky is what forgetful people bring instead of water. It is the mistake, not the rule.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Poles get a whole turn of their own, which makes them feel important enough to be an answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Bring them if you already use them. She tells him not to buy any.

questions.prompt: How should members judge whether a walk suits them?

options.B: by the distance in kilometres
options.C: by asking the walk leader

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the wrong method to be named loudly. Every walk's got a grade is the answer and it comes first. Distance is then named as the mistake everyone makes, with a worked example to prove it.

prediction.note: A how question. Expect one recommended method and one named as an error.

teaching.answer_quote: Every walk's got a grade, one to five
teaching.recovery: If you missed it, wait for the weather. The cancellation question is next and it is clearly marked.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Two distances are quoted in numbers, and numbers feel like evidence, so the option sounds supported.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Don't go off the distance. The numbers are there to show why distance misleads.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She does tell him to ring the leader, in a full sentence, only two turns later.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That is the fallback if you are still unsure, and she adds that leaders are often unreachable.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: How are members told that a walk is off?

options.A: by a text message from the leader
options.B: by phoning the club on the morning
options.C: through the Thursday newsletter

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and mark the negatives first. Three things are ruled out before the answer lands, and the answer is a relative clause tucked onto the end: she'll do it by text the night before. The newsletter is real, but it carries grades.

prediction.note: Told means a channel. Listen for who contacts whom, and when.

signpost.phrase: we don't walk if the leader calls it off

distraction.note: The newsletter is real and useful, and it answers a different question. Check what the stem asked.

teaching.recovery: If you lost it, her Last thing opens question ten. Nothing before that phrase belongs to it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Ringing the club is the obvious thing to do, and the club and the morning are both named in this turn.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The newsletter is the club's only named publication and it has already been given a job in this talk.

questions.explanation: The stem asks why, so predict a reason and expect true-but-irrelevant facts beside it. We count heads is the reason and we don't move until the numbers add up proves it. The other two are both denied outright in the turns that follow.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Clubs with limited places usually do reallocate them, so the option describes the world the learner expects.

title: Reporting a bag left on a coach

script_json.title: Reporting a bag left on a coach
script_json.scenario: A man telephones the lost property desk of an Australian coach company about a backpack left on a service the day before; the clerk takes the report and explains how and where he can collect it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man who has left a bag on a coach and the lost property clerk at an Australian coach company. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Barrowfield Coaches, lost property. Deb speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hi there. I think I've left a backpack on one of your coaches. Yesterday, on the way home. There's a charger in it that I need for work, so I'm keen to get it back.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, let's see what we can do. I'll take the details and put a report on the system for you. We get a lot of these on the regional runs, so don't panic yet. Surname first?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Doust.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Could you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: D. O. U. S. T. Doust. Like the dust in the air, only with an O in the middle.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: D. O. U. S. T. Lovely. Have you got the ticket in front of you?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I have, yeah, it's in my wallet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There'll be two numbers on it. There's a long one along the top, which is the ticket number, and there's a shorter one underneath the barcode. It's the one under the barcode I want.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Four nine, double two, one six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Four nine, double two, one six. Got it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And you travelled on the Tuesday, you said?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Tuesday the fifth, yeah.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hang on. The fifth was a Monday. If it was definitely the Tuesday, then you're talking about the twelfth.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The twelfth. You're right, I'm hopeless with dates. That's the trouble with travelling for work, every day looks the same.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And which service were you on?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I got on at Coombe Vale and I got off at Marrindale.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, but the service itself doesn't finish at Marrindale. That coach carries on to Danesford, and the driver books anything left on it in at the far end. So on the report this goes down as the Danesford service.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The Danesford one. Fair enough, I'd never have thought of that. I just assumed the service was named after wherever I got off.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Nobody does. And do you remember the seat?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I was in seat fourteen, the aisle one. The bag was in the rack above it, not down by my feet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Seat fourteen. That helps, because the cleaners do the racks last. People leave things up there constantly, since you can't see them when you stand up. And what's in it, apart from the charger you mentioned?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: A jacket. No, sorry, not a jacket, a jumper. A green one, my daughter knitted it, which is why I'm ringing at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A green jumper and a charger. That's plenty to identify it by.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, I've got all of that on the system now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, what happens from here, because everybody asks me the same four things. It saves you ringing me back tomorrow.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go on. I'd rather know than keep ringing you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First, how long we hold things. Anything handed in gets logged and kept for twenty-eight days. After that it goes to the charity shop on the corner, and once it's gone there's nothing I can do about it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Twenty-eight days. That's fair enough. I'll set myself a reminder.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It is, but don't sit on it. Second thing, where you pick it up. It used to be the ticket office at the terminal, which suited everybody. Since March it's been the depot out on Fenwick Road, past the roundabout.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The depot. Is that open on a Saturday?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Saturday mornings only, eight until twelve, and there's one bloke on, so ring the bell and wait. Allow yourself an hour, honestly, because they're digging the road up out there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third thing, and this one catches people out. Bring your licence. Not the ticket. The ticket's no use to me, anybody can print a ticket. I need a photo and a name that matches the report.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Licence, not ticket. I'd have taken the ticket.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They all do. And last, we let you know either way. If the driver's booked it in, you'll get a text tonight. If nothing's come in by Friday, you'll get a text telling you that as well, so please don't ring us every morning.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's good of you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's easier for us, honestly. Right, that's the report lodged. Your reference is the same number off the ticket, so quote that if you do ring, and it saves us both five minutes.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Thanks, Deb. Fingers crossed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No worries at all. Somebody will be in touch tonight either way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

teaching.order_note: She fills the report downwards. Once she asks about the seat, boxes one to four are closed.
teaching.strategy: Every box here is dictated to her by the caller and then repeated by her. Use the repetition as your second pass, but never as your first: two of these six values are wrong the first time they are said.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type the six, and notice that October and green are printed. Box three needs a number only and box six a single noun.
teaching.watch_out: The caller is the one who makes the mistakes here, not the clerk. Two of his answers get overturned within a turn.

groups.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: She numbers them herself: first, second, third and last. Follow her count, not your watch.
teaching.strategy: She announces four things and then delivers them in order, so each stem has a spoken marker in front of it. Write two words at most, and cut the article before you write anything at all.
teaching.preview_focus: Turn each stem into a slot: a length of time, a place, a document, a method of contact. All four are short concrete nouns.
teaching.watch_out: Answers here are one or two words. Copying her whole phrase puts you over the limit and scores zero for content you heard correctly.

questions.prompt: How long is lost property kept before it is given away?
questions.explanation: The stem asks how long, so predict a number and a unit. First is her own numbering and it opens the answer. The period is stated once, in words, and what happens afterwards is the proof you heard the right figure.

title: Hiring a floor sander

script_json.title: Hiring a floor sander
script_json.scenario: A woman telephones a tool hire shop to hire a floor sander; the assistant books the machines and then goes through the charges, the collection point and what the equipment must not be used on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman hiring equipment to sand a floor and an assistant at a tool hire shop. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Kilnmore Tool Hire, Wes speaking.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'm after hiring a floor sander. We've taken the carpet up in the front room and the boards underneath are in a bit of a state. Somebody varnished them in about nineteen seventy and nobody has touched them since.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No worries, we do a lot of those this time of year. I'll start a booking and we'll sort you out. Can I grab a surname?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Quennell.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: How's that spelt?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Q. U. E. double N. E. double L. Quennell. Nobody gets it first time, don't worry.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Q. U. E. double N. E. double L. There you go, first time. And a contact number?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's oh seven, double one, four, three six two, nine oh four.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh seven, double one, four, three six two, nine oh four. Got that.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Right, machines. For a room that size there are two you could take. There's the belt sander, which is the smaller one, and there's the drum sander.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which do people usually go for? I've never done anything like this before, so I'm in your hands.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: For boards that have never been done, the drum, every time. The belt one's fine for touching up a bit of skirting, but honestly you'd be there all weekend with it. I'd put you down for the drum.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The drum one, then. I'll take your word for it, because I certainly don't want to be doing it twice.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And when do you want it? We're open seven till five, and Saturdays till one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Saturday morning, if you've got one free. Actually, no, hang on. My husband's got the car on the Saturday, so that's no good at all. Friday afternoon would be much better.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Friday afternoon it is. That gets you the whole weekend on a two-day rate, which is a bit of luck for you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what do you need off me when I come in?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: There's a deposit. It was eighty pounds right up until the spring, but we've dropped it to sixty now the machines are newer. You get it straight back when the machine comes back in one piece.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sixty. That's fine, I'll bring the card. Do you take it back off the card straight away, or is it held?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And I'd take the edger while you're at it. The drum won't get within four inches of the skirting, so without one you'll have a border of old varnish all the way round the room and you'll be on your knees with a scraper.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then I'd better have an edger as well, hadn't I.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Good decision. So that's the drum, the edger, Friday afternoon, and I'll put the sheets aside for you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Now, the costs, because they're not all charged the same way and people do get caught out.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Go ahead, I'm writing this down.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The drum sander's thirty-five pounds a day. There's a weekend rate of fifty for the two days, which is what you'll actually be on, but the figure that goes on the booking form is thirty-five.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thirty-five on the form. Right.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The edger's eighteen a day, and that one doesn't live in the shop. It's in the yard round the back, so come to the yard gate rather than the counter, or you'll only get sent round anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The yard gate, not the counter. Noted.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sheets are two pounds each. Take a dozen, take twenty, it makes no odds, because you only pay for the ones you use. Bring the rest back unopened and we don't charge you for them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's decent of you. Everywhere else I rang wanted paying for the lot up front.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's not generosity, it's that nobody on earth can guess how many they'll need. Last thing, the extractor. It comes free with the sander and you'd be mad not to take it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's fine on floorboards and old paint. Do not use it on plaster, though. Plaster dust kills the motor stone dead, and that's a two hundred pound repair, and that one does come out of your deposit.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Floorboards yes, plaster no. Understood. I'll keep it well away from the walls.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: You've got it. I'll have the paperwork ready for Friday, so you can be in and out in ten minutes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thanks very much, that's all really clear. I was dreading this phone call, to be honest with you.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No worries at all. See you Friday afternoon.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

teaching.preview_focus: Look at box six: the printed word is an, so the answer begins with a vowel sound. That eliminates half the equipment in the shop before he speaks.

title: Arranging a furniture delivery

script_json.title: Arranging a furniture delivery
script_json.scenario: A man telephones a furniture store to arrange delivery of a couch to his apartment; the scheduling clerk books the date and access and then explains what happens on the day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man arranging a furniture delivery and a scheduling clerk at a store in the United States. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hartsmoor Furniture, delivery scheduling. This is Marisol.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hi. I'm calling to set up delivery on a couch. It came into the warehouse last week, I got the email about it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sure, let's get you on a truck. Can I start with a last name?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Rasmussen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Would you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: R. A. S. M. U. double S. E. N. Rasmussen. Two esses in the middle.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: R. A. S. M. U. double S. E. N. Thank you. And there should be an order number on that email.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Let me pull it up. Okay, here we go. Seven one two, eight four. Hang on, no, that's the quote number from when I came into the store. The order number's the one below it. Double four, one nine, oh three.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Double four, one nine, oh three. That's the one, I've got your couch right here on the screen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, dates. We're only in your neighborhood on Thursdays, so it's a Thursday whatever we do.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Thursday's fine. The sooner the better, honestly, we've been sitting on the floor for a month.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I hear that a lot. The fifteenth is our next run out there, but that truck's already full. The one after is the twenty-second of May, and I can get you on it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The twenty-second it is, then. I'll take it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Great. Now, timing. The crew starts at eight, and I originally had you down for the morning run.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But they're doing a whole building over on Ash Street that morning, so realistically you're looking at from 1.30 onwards. I'd rather tell you now than have you waiting in all day for nothing.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: From one thirty. That's fine, I'll work from home that afternoon.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Perfect. Now, the building itself. Is there an elevator?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: There is, but it's tiny. The couch is going to have to come up the stairs.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's no problem, they do stairs all day. Which entrance do they want?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Not the front one, whatever you do. The front entrance opens straight onto the main street and there's nowhere to stop a truck. They want the rear entrance, off the parking lot.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Rear entrance, off the lot. I'll put that on the ticket in capitals, because otherwise they will try the front.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if nobody's home? Some buildings have a front desk we can use, but yours doesn't, does it?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No desk, no. Leave it with a neighbor if you have to. Apartment 4B, she's retired and she is always, always in.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Apartment 4B. Got it. Okay, you are booked.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, a few things about the day itself, because these are the ones that surprise people.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go ahead, I'm listening.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Packaging. The crew unwraps everything in the room it's going in, and every piece of it goes back out with them. You do not end up with a mountain of cardboard in your apartment.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. The last place we bought from left it all stacked flat in the hallway for a week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We used to do exactly that, years ago, and the building managers hated us for it. Now it all goes back on the truck and gets recycled at our warehouse rather than in your building's bins.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Good. So what do you need from me before they show up?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Clear the hallway between your front door and the room it's going in. Genuinely, that's all. People take their doors off the hinges for us and it has never once been necessary with a two-seater.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And don't move your car for us either. The crew parks on the street and walks it in. You would not believe how many people spend a morning hunting for another space.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Okay. And what about the old couch? Can they take that away?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They can't, I'm afraid, not on a delivery run. What most people do is call the thrift store over on Fenmore. They'll come out for anything that's clean, and they don't charge you for it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's been talk of us starting a removal service of our own, mind you. There's been talk of that for about three years now.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Understood. And the balance on the order?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The balance is due before we load. You'll get a link tonight, you pay it online, and once that clears you're locked in for the twenty-second.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The crew can't take payment, by the way. They don't carry a reader on the truck at all.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Could I just come into the store and pay it at the counter?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You could try, but they'll send you straight back to the link. The counter can't run money against a delivery order, it's a completely different system.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Online it is. Thanks, that was painless.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're very welcome. Thursday the twenty-second, from one thirty, rear entrance.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

teaching.recovery: If you lost it, wait for The balance is due. That opens the last question of the set.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He asks for exactly this in his own words, so the option is spoken aloud a second before the answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: They can't, not on a delivery run. It is refused in the first four words of her reply.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A removal service run by the store would solve his problem neatly, and she gives it a whole turn.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect two refusals. Due before we load fixes the timing and you pay it online fixes the method, both in one sentence. The other two options are then closed off one turn at a time.

title: Enquiring about a physiotherapy service

script_json.title: Enquiring about a physiotherapy service
script_json.scenario: A man telephones a community physiotherapy clinic after a referral from his doctor; the receptionist takes his details, books a first appointment and then explains how the service works.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man arranging treatment for an injured shoulder and a receptionist at a community physiotherapy clinic. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Norland Community Physiotherapy, good morning. Bernadette speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, hello. Um, my doctor's referred me about my shoulder, and she said the referral won't move unless I ring you myself and pick a slot.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: She's quite right, we can't book you without speaking to you. Let me take the details and find you something. Can I start with your surname?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ballantyne.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Could you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Yes, it's B. A. double L. A. N. T. Y. N. E. Ballantyne. It's the Y. N. E. ending, not the I. N. E. one. Everybody gets that wrong.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: B. A. double L. A. N. T. Y. N. E. Lovely, thank you. Now, there'll be a referral number on the letter your doctor gave you, up in the corner.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hang on, I've got it here somewhere. Right. It's P. T., and then four one nine, I think.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: P. T. four one nine? There should be four digits after the letters, not three. Have another look for me.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, so there are. I've missed one out, sorry. It's P. T. double four, one nine.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: P. T. double four, one nine. That's you on the system.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, whereabouts is the trouble? Your doctor's put upper body, which isn't terribly helpful to us.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's the shoulder. The right one. I've had a dodgy left knee for about ten years, but that's not why I'm ringing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right shoulder. And how long's the shoulder been going on?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Two months, give or take. It started the weekend I helped a mate shift a wardrobe up a staircase, and it's got steadily worse since then.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That'll do it. Now, appointments. Mondays are our new-patient day, so whatever we pick, it'll be a Monday.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Monday suits me, I'm on lates that week anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I've got the fifteenth of June free. Shall I put you down for that one?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The fifteenth. Yes, go on then, that works.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Lovely, I'll just... oh, hang on. Sorry, no, I can't do the fifteenth after all. That Monday's the bank holiday and the whole building's shut. Let me move you to the twenty-second.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The twenty-second, then. Crossed out and changed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, time. I could give you eight o'clock, which is the first slot of the day and people always jump at it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Mind you, the eight o'clock is the one that gets moved when the physio's held up at the hospital. The 9.30 is the safer bet, if you can manage it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I'll take the safer one. I'm no use at eight in the morning anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Very sensible. Right, last box on the form, and it's the one everybody ignores. What's going on your feet?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Bring a pair of trainers, because we warm you up on the treadmill before anybody touches the arm. Loose sleeves too, if you've got them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Trainers and loose sleeves. Noted.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's you booked in. Bear with me a moment while this prints.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, while that's chuntering away, there are four things worth knowing about how we run, because they catch people out.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go on. I'm writing this down.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Cancellations first. If you can't make it, ring us. We need a day's notice, and a day's notice means twenty-four hours.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Anything less than that goes down as a missed appointment, and two missed appointments puts you straight back on the waiting list, which nobody wants.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Understood. And roughly how many appointments will I get?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Usually eight. But honestly, don't count them. The thing that actually matters isn't the half hour you spend in here with us.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's the daily routine at home that fixes a shoulder. Ten minutes, twice a day, seven days a week. What we do in the room is check you're doing it properly.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's fair. Will I remember them all, though? I'm hopeless at that sort of thing, I'll be honest with you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You won't have to remember anything. Every exercise comes with a short video, and we text you the link before you've left the building.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, that's clever. My sister's clinic gave her a photocopied sheet and she lost it in a week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We did the sheets for years. Nobody ever found them again either.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And when do you decide whether any of it's working?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We'll have another look at you six weeks in. If the arm's moving further and the pain's dropping off, we hand it back to you and you carry on alone.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And if it isn't shifting by then?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then we talk about a scan. But that's a conversation for week six, not today. The great majority of shoulders like yours settle on their own with the exercises.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Right. Thanks, Bernadette, that's everything I needed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're very welcome. Monday the twenty-second, half nine, and don't forget the trainers.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

teaching.strategy: Every value in this half is either spelled, read back or challenged by the other speaker, so you get two chances at each one. Write lightly the first time and let the confirmation turn decide what stays.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type all six. June and Monday are printed, so box four is a bare number, and the word pair before box six forces a plural.
teaching.watch_out: Two boxes take a value that is corrected after you have already written it. The second value is always the one that counts.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.answer_quote: The 9.30 is the safer bet, if you can manage it

questions.explanation: The frame prints a pair of, so predict a plural noun for something worn in twos. She flags footwear as the thing people ignore, and the instruction arrives two turns later with the reason attached.

questions.explanation: The printed hours fixes this as a number. Cancellations is the section marker. She says a day's notice first and only then converts it into hours, so the figure you need arrives after the idea does.

title: Registering for a charity road race

script_json.title: Registering for a charity road race
script_json.scenario: A woman telephones the registration desk of an American charity road race to enter the five mile event; the registrar takes her details and then briefs her on race-day logistics.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman entering a charity road race in the United States and the man who runs the event's registration desk. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Harbor Mile Road Race, this is Darnell.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, hi. I'm trying to register and the website keeps timing out on me. Can I just do the whole thing over the phone? I've been meaning to sign up since July and I've left it to the last week, obviously.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It does that every year the week entries close. Sure, I can take it here. Let's start with your last name.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Marchetti.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Can you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sure. M. A. R. C. H. E. double T. I. Marchetti. It sounds like a K in the middle, but it's spelled with the C. H.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: M. A. R. C. H. E. double T. I. Perfect. Give me a second and let me pull you a bib number.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're three three oh nine. Hold on, no, scratch that. Three three oh nine just went out to the runner ahead of you. Yours is three three one oh.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Three three one oh. Written down.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Okay. Now, dates. You entered the five mile, right? Not the half marathon?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The five mile. I'm not ready for anything longer this fall, believe me. I did a ten K in the spring and I could barely walk down stairs for three days afterwards.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good, because they're on different weekends. The half's on the fifth of October, but the five mile is the twelfth.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twelfth of October, five mile. Now the fee, and I'm afraid I have bad news on that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Early registration was twenty-eight dollars, but that window closed at the end of August. Anybody signing up now pays thirty-five.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Thirty-five. Well, I'll live, and it's going to the hospital fund anyway. Does that include the shirt, or is that extra on top?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It does, and there's a good one this year. What size do you want? They run small, so most people go up one.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Medium, then. I'll take your word for it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Medium it is. Last thing, packet pickup. That's where you collect your bib and your timing chip.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And where do I go for that?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We used to hand those out from a tent in the parking lot, but the wind took the tent two years running. Now it's all inside the boathouse, down by the water.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The boathouse, right by the water. And is that open on the Saturday, or is it only on the morning of the race?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Saturday noon to eight, and race morning from six. Do not leave it until race morning if you can avoid it. The line is brutal and it moves at about one runner a minute.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Okay. Now there are three or four things about the day itself, and this is where people come unstuck.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go ahead. I'm listening.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Parking. The lot at the boathouse holds maybe eighty cars, and there are two thousand of you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's a free shuttle from the high school every ten minutes, and that's what we want you on. Every year people pay to park downtown and then walk a mile before they've run a step.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Shuttle from the high school. That's easy enough, I drive past it every day on the way to work.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Weather. It's October on the coast, so it could be seventy degrees and it could be absolutely pouring.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We only cancel for lightning, and even then we hold for thirty minutes first and try to start late. Rain, we run. So dress for what's outside, not for what you'd like it to be.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Rain, we run. Understood. I'll dig out the old jacket, then, and stop looking at the forecast every ten minutes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Your timing chip is on the back of the bib this year. Don't fold the bib, don't pin through the chip, and whatever you do, don't put it in your pocket.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Every year somebody runs a great race and never shows up in the results, and it is always the chip. Pin the bib flat on the front of your shirt and forget about it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And you keep the chip afterwards, by the way. They're disposable now. We used to chase people down the finish chute to get them back.

lines.speaker: s2

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The gun's at eight, sharp. We don't hold the start for anybody, not even the mayor.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The last shuttle leaves the high school at seven forty, so if you're on that one you're cutting it fine. Be at the high school by 7.15 and you'll be standing around relaxed instead of running to the start.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Seven fifteen at the high school. Honestly, that was far quicker than the website ever was. Thank you for sitting through all of it with me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It usually is. Marchetti, three three one oh, twelfth of October. You're all set.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is the first place named, it is where the finish is, and parking at the venue is what any runner would try first.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Eighty spaces for two thousand runners. He raises it to rule it out, not to offer it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Paying for parking sounds like the safe, grown-up option, and he describes people doing exactly this.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He offers it as what people get wrong every year, then a mile's walk before the start.

option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Rain, we run. Three words, and they reverse the option completely.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Thirty minutes is stated as a real number, and a stated number feels like an answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The hold applies to lightning, not to any storm. The condition is the whole item.

option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He calls that cutting it fine. It is the time he warns her against, not the time he gives.

title: Opening a savings account

script_json.title: Opening a savings account
script_json.scenario: A woman telephones a building society to finish opening a monthly savings account; the adviser takes her details, books a branch appointment and then compares the society's four savings accounts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman opening a savings account and an adviser at a building society. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Marlow Building Society, savings team. Idris speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hello. I filled in the form on your website for the Regular Saver, and at the very end it told me to ring and finish it off with an actual person.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It does, I'm afraid, and I promise it's the shorter half. Can I have your surname first?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Cowdrey.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And how's that spelled?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: C. O. W. D. R. A. Y. No, hang on, sorry, that's my sister-in-law's. Hers is the A. Y. one. Mine's C. O. W. D. R. E. Y. Cowdrey.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So E. Y. at the end, not A. Y. C. O. W. D. R. E. Y.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's it. It's been going wrong on letters for about fifteen years now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I can imagine. Right, now, the Regular Saver. How much are you thinking of putting in each month?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I honestly don't know. What's the range?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twenty-five is the floor, and you can go as high as you like. There's a bonus rate as well if you add fifty on top of that.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then let's do both. The twenty-five and the fifty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, so I'll put you down for seventy-five pounds a month going in, from the account you gave online.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Seventy-five. That's more than I've ever managed before.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, which day of the month should it come out? Most people pick something just after payday, so it goes before they see it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The fifth, then. That's two days after I'm paid, and I'll never miss it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The fifth. Now, one thing people get caught by on this account, and it's worth me saying it twice. Taking money out.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's no notice at all on the Easy Access account. You ask in the morning, you've got it by the afternoon. But this isn't that account. On the Regular Saver we need thirty days.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Thirty days. That's all right, it's supposed to sit there and be forgotten about.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's exactly the idea. Now, before Friday I need two things from you. Photo identification, and something with your address on it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Would a mobile phone bill do for that?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the one everybody brings, and it's the one we always have to send back, I'm afraid. What you want is a water bill. Nobody has ever queried a water bill.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Water bill and passport. I'll put them by the door tonight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Very wise. Now, the appointment itself. Friday's the only day I've got a free adviser, is that any good to you?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Friday's fine. I'm off that day anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then let's say 2.15. That gives you the whole afternoon and nobody's rushing you out.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Quarter past two on Friday, then. Bring the passport and the water bill and we'll have the account open inside twenty minutes. And if you do need to ring us before Friday, quote four one nine, double two, six. That's you on our system.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: While I've got you, it's worth me running through the other accounts, because people join the wrong one and then find they can't get out of it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go on, I've got a minute.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The Regular Saver you've just opened pays four percent, which is the best we do for anybody starting from nothing. It's really about getting the habit going. At this stage the amount matters far less than the routine does.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a nicer way of putting it than my mother did. And the Easy Access one you mentioned?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two percent, and you can have your money the same day you ask for it. That's your emergency fund, the boiler money. Everybody should have one and hardly anybody does.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Guilty. And there's a bond too, isn't there? My neighbour was going on about it over the fence.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The Two Year Bond, yes, but be careful there, because the rate she'll have heard is out of date. It was six percent until the spring. It's five now, and you can't touch it until it matures, and that's twenty twenty-nine.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Five's still better than anything I've had. I'll think about it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Do. And the last one's the Junior Saver, three percent, opened by a parent or a grandparent for a child and locked until they're eighteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Most people assume it's for university fees. It usually isn't, by the time they get there. The point of it is that the child has a deposit behind them at twenty-two instead of starting from nothing.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's my sister's two sorted, then. Thanks, Idris, you've been very patient.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Not at all. Friday, quarter past two, passport and water bill. See you then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Booking a ferry crossing

script_json.title: Booking a ferry crossing
script_json.scenario: A British visitor telephones an Australian island ferry company to book a return crossing for a family; the booking agent takes the details and then explains where things are on the island.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a British visitor booking a ferry crossing and a booking agent at an Australian island ferry company. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Koolambra Island Ferries, this is Warrick. How're you going?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, hello. Fine, thank you. I'd like to book a return crossing for the September school holidays, if there's anything left at all over the public holiday weekend.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's a bit left, but not a lot. Let's have a look at what I've got. Can I grab a surname?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Frayne.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How do you spell that?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: F. R. A. Y. N. E. Frayne. There's no I in it anywhere, which is what people always put.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: F. R. A. Y. N. E. No worries. Now, what date are you looking at?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Somewhere around the middle of the month, if there's anything going.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's talk of putting an extra sailing on the seventeenth, but nothing's confirmed and I can't sell you a seat on a boat that might not run. What I can do is the eighteenth.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The eighteenth is fine. It's a Friday, isn't it? That gives us the whole weekend on the other side, which is what we wanted.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It is. Now, sailings. There are three of them that day and they're not equal.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The 10.45 is the one everybody wants, and it went a fortnight ago. There's a 7.10 in the morning, which is brutal with kids, and there's the 2.30. I'd put you on the 2.30.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The 2.30, definitely. Nobody in this family is any use at seven in the morning.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fair enough. And how many of you altogether?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Four. Two adults and two children.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Four it is. Now, while I've got the screen up, let me give you the reference.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Actually, hang on, sorry, I said four. It's five. My brother's just decided he's coming, and he'll never let me hear the end of it if I leave him off.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Five. No worries, there's room on the 2.30. Righto, your reference.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's K. B. seven three two.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: K. D. seven three two.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: K. B. B for Bendigo. K. B. seven three two.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: K. B. as in Bendigo. Got it, sorry, that's my handwriting rather than your accent.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: All good. Now, one last thing, and it's the one nobody believes. What to bring.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's cold out on that water, even in September. Don't bother with an umbrella, the wind takes it straight out of your hand. Bring a jumper, a proper one, and pack it at the top of the bag.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: A jumper. In September. Right, I'll take your word for it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Everybody laughs and everybody ends up borrowing one off the crew. Righto, that's you booked. Frayne, five of you, the 2.30 on the eighteenth.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the island itself. Have you been across before?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Never. My sister's been telling me to go for about ten years and I've never got round to it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then let me give you the five names you'll hear over there, because they all sound alike and people end up in completely the wrong one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The ferry docks at Marrawee Point. That's where the island bus is sitting waiting, and it doesn't wait long, so don't stop on the ramp for a photo.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: How long is the bus ride from there? I've got a five year old and she doesn't sit still for anything over half an hour.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twenty minutes, and there isn't another one until the arvo. Oh, and you can't take the car across at all, so leave it at Wallum Flat.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the big gravel yard about a kilometre back from the terminal. It's free if you're on a return ticket, which you are.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. Is there anywhere to buy food, or are we carrying it all?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's exactly one shop on the island, and it's at Cobbers Bay. It shuts at four, so do it on the way out, not on the way back.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: One shop. Right. And my sister swears there are seals somewhere.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Everyone tells you Yarrindi Cove, and everyone's three summers out of date. The colony picked up and moved.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They're on the rocks under Talwyn Head now. It's a forty minute walk from the bay, and you'll smell them a long time before you see them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Forty minutes each way. I'll pack the walking shoes and an esky, then.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Do that. There's a tap at the Point as well, so there's no sense carrying water the whole way round.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: You've saved me a great deal of trouble. Thank you, Warrick.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No worries at all. The 2.30 on the eighteenth. We'll see you at the Point.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

teaching.strategy: Every figure in this half is spoken twice, once as the value that is not available and once as the value that is. Listen for the reason attached to each one, because the reason is what tells you which of the two survives.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type the six. September is printed, so box two is a bare number, and the dates here are given day first as they are in Australia.
teaching.watch_out: A value you have already written and agreed can still be withdrawn a full turn later. Boxes four and five both move.

teaching.strategy: The five place names are spoken exactly as they are printed, so hearing them is easy. What is not printed is why each one matters, so write the purpose beside each letter as he says it and match afterwards.

title: A guided tour of Brackenfield Watermill

script_json.title: A guided tour of Brackenfield Watermill
script_json.scenario: A volunteer guide walks a group of visitors round the outside of a restored watermill using the site plan, then explains how the mill works and what visitors can do there.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a volunteer guide showing a group of visitors round a restored watermill on a Saturday morning. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, morning everybody, and welcome to Brackenfield. I'm Ellen, I've been a volunteer here since the wheel went back in, and I'll be taking you round. Do grab a plan off the pile by the gate, because the site is a great deal more spread out than it looks from the lane.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So. We're all standing just inside the entrance, and the entrance is the thing I want you to hold on to. Turn so the gate's behind you and the mill building is over on your left. Every left and every right I give you from now on is from exactly where you're standing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Straight away on your left, tucked in against the near end of the mill, is the sack store. Little stone shed, tin roof. That's where the grain came in off the carts, and it's where we keep the wheelbarrows now, so it's rather less romantic than it sounds.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, directly opposite that, across the cobbles, you'll see the old hand pump. The pump isn't marked on your plan at all, so please don't go writing anything in for it. What is marked, immediately behind it, is the tea room. Scones, and a queue, from about eleven.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Carry on up the yard with the stream on your right. A few yards short of the footbridge you'll see a set of black timber boards standing in the water. That's the sluice gate. That's what lets water into the wheel, and one of us opens it at ten every morning.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now cross the footbridge. Over on the far bank you've got a long thin strip of reed bed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No, sorry, that's wrong. The reed bed is away downstream by the weir. What's over there, on your right as you come off the bridge, is the willow beds. We cut those every winter and they go off to a basket maker in the village.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then double back over the bridge, and right at the top of the yard, behind the mill, is the orchard. One or two of the older leaflets still call that corner the cider yard, and it was the cider yard, until the restoration. It's the orchard now, and the apples are yours if you can reach them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So that's the ground covered. I'll take questions on any of it at the end. Let's get on, because the wheel starts turning at half past and you'll want to be standing inside the mill when it does.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the tour, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. How the thing actually works, because this is the bit almost everybody gets wrong. The wheel is not sitting in the river. The river is two fields away. The water comes to us along a channel that was dug in the sixteen hundreds, and that channel has a name. It's called the leat. L. E. A. T.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It runs behind the hedge you walked in past, and it drops by about a foot over the length of the site, which doesn't sound like anything at all. But the drop is what does the work. No drop, no flour.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, when can you see it working. Everybody assumes we grind every day of the week. We don't, and we can't, because the stones would be worn down inside a year. The stones turn on Saturday afternoons, from two o'clock, and only then.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then there's the shop, which is inside the tea room, confusingly, and which is staffed entirely by people my age who will talk to you for as long as you let them. We sell what we grind. Wholemeal, and a coarser stoneground that is very good and very slow to cook.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Prices. The small bags, the half-kilo ones, are two pounds. The big bags, and the big bags are the ones you actually want because they freeze beautifully, the big bags are five pounds.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Access now, and I'm sorry about this one. The whole of the ground floor is level, and there's a ramp at the side door, so the wheel and the stones are fine for everybody. Apart from one place. It's the bin floor, right up at the top, that we cannot get anyone to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And while I think of it, the bin floor is called the bin floor because the grain sat in bins up there and came down by gravity. Everything in a mill comes down by gravity. That is the entire idea of the building, and it's why it's tall and thin.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Last thing and then I'll shut up. We are all volunteers here, and we are short of people. If you have ever thought about it, what we ask is two days a month. Not two days a week, which is what people hear, and then they go pale. Two a month. We'll teach you the rest.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. The wheel goes on in about four minutes. If you want to be underneath it when it starts, and you do, follow me round the side. Mind the step there, it's the wettest thing on this site.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
