title: Volunteer briefing at the Northgate Community Kitchen

script_json.title: Volunteer briefing at the Northgate Community Kitchen
script_json.scenario: A volunteer coordinator briefs a group of new volunteers at a community kitchen: the scale of the operation and the housekeeping rules, then the delivery runs and the cold store.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a volunteer coordinator briefing a group of new volunteers on their first evening at a community kitchen. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to sixteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to sixteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hi, everyone. I'm Dana, I run the volunteer side of things here, and this is the twenty minutes where I tell you everything and you remember about a third of it. That's fine. It's all on a sheet by the door as well.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, numbers first, because they surprise people. When I started here we were putting out six hundred meals a week and that felt like a lot. As of this fall we're at nine hundred, out of the same kitchen, with the same four stoves.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You'll report to whoever's on as shift lead. Some evenings that's Priya, tomorrow it's a guy called Halloran, and I'll spell that, because everybody gets it wrong. H. A. L. O. — no, sorry, there are two L's in there. Let me do that again. H. A. double L. O. R. A. N.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Shifts. There are two of them. The morning one is seven till noon and it's mostly baking and prep. The afternoon shift, which is the one most of you signed up for, starts at 3.30 and runs until we're done, which is usually somewhere around eight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What to wear. We used to ask everybody to bring an apron, and you really don't need to any more — there's a whole rack of them by the door. What you do need, and I will send you home over this, is closed-toe shoes. It's a kitchen. There are hot pans in it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Donations. Everybody assumes we're short of food. We're honestly not. This city is extremely generous and there's a truck outside most mornings. What we are permanently short of is freezer space. If you know anybody with a spare chest freezer, I would like their number.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Age. We love having students, we really do, and we ask for one thing: anybody under sixteen has to be signed in by an adult who then stays in the building. Not out in the parking lot. In the building.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the housekeeping done. Anything you forget is on the sheet taped inside the pantry door, and nobody here has ever been in trouble for asking the same question twice.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the briefing, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. Deliveries, because about half of you signed up to drive. We run four routes a week — Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Thursday's been going since the week this kitchen opened, so it is not the new one, whatever the sign-up sheet told you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And everybody assumes Thursday's the long one, because it goes right out to the county line. It isn't. Friday's longer by a good hour. What Thursday is, is the run I'm forever begging people to drive. If you can only do one route a month, make it that one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The walk-in cooler now. There's a parka hanging on the hook beside the door. Wear it, don't wear it, that's entirely up to you. I'd say most people last about four minutes in there without it, and then they come out and put it on.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two things that are not up to you. Do not prop that door open, however much you're carrying, because it wrecks the compressor and it costs us a fortune. And nobody goes into the walk-in on their own. Not ever. If I'm not around, grab whoever is.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Drivers, before you go anywhere, come to the office and pick up your route sheet. One piece of paper, addresses in order, door codes on the back. Please don't work off your cell phone. The addresses change on a Tuesday and your phone doesn't know that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The van, while we're on the subject, is a stick shift, it is older than several of you, and the trick with the back door is that you lift it before you pull it. Everybody in this room will learn that the hard way exactly once.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One last thing, because somebody always asks. We cook lunch and we cook dinner. We have never once done breakfast, and between you and me we never will, because there is nobody on this earth who wants to be dicing onions at five in the morning.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Aprons are on the rack, the tablet by the door is how you clock in and out, and I'll be somewhere near the stoves if it all goes sideways. Thank you for coming. We genuinely cannot do this without you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Six gaps, six headings, top to bottom. If you hear 'Age', the shoes gap has already gone past you.
teaching.strategy: Dana runs a heading and then a gap, six times over. Every heading is a single spoken noun: numbers, shift lead, shifts, what to wear, donations, age. Write the heading words on your page in the pause and use them as a ladder.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type all six before she starts: two figures, one surname, one clock time, two noun phrases. Then mark which gaps already print their unit.
teaching.watch_out: Three of these gaps print their own unit or noun. Repeating it takes a correct answer over the two-word limit and scores nothing.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Question 18's answer comes after 17's. Once she says 'the walk-in cooler', 17 is finished.
teaching.strategy: Both of these are decided by one short clause that follows a much louder wrong one. Dana raises every option out loud, so option-spotting is worthless here. Listen for what she says is not optional, and for what she says people assume.
teaching.preview_focus: Read all six options before the audio restarts, and underline the modal in each stem. You need the options in your head, not under your eyes.
teaching.watch_out: Choosing the option whose words you heard most clearly. Every wrong option here is spoken in almost its printed form.

groups.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Two questions, in speaking order, at the very end of the talk. Neither answer is repeated.
teaching.strategy: These are two-word answers with no printed frame to lean on, so the stem itself has to do the slot-typing. Turn each question into the shape of its answer before the audio restarts: a thing drivers pick up, and a meal.
teaching.preview_focus: Convert each stem into a predicted phrase shape. Note that both answers are things she says once, in a single clause, with no repeat.
teaching.watch_out: Writing a whole spoken phrase. The limit is two words and she speaks in sentences, so you must trim before you write.

NORTHGATE COMMUNITY KITCHEN — VOLUNTEER BRIEFING

- Meals cooked each week at the moment: ______
questions.explanation: 'At the moment' in the frame warns you the figure will be updated, so predict two numbers and expect the second. 'As of this fall' is the switch. She gives the old figure first and marks it as old with 'when I started here'. Write the current one.

prediction.note: A weekly meal count for a community kitchen: hundreds, not thousands, and not a decimal.

teaching.answer_quote: As of this fall we're at nine hundred

distraction.note: The first figure is fenced off by a past-tense frame. Wait for the present tense before you commit a number.

form.note: Write the figure alone. 'Meals' is printed, so '900 meals' goes over the limit and scores zero.

questions.prompt: - Report to the shift lead. Surname: ______
questions.explanation: 'Surname' tells you before the audio that this is transcription, not comprehension. 'I'll spell that' is the cue to put your pen down and take letters. She spells it wrong, says so, and restarts with 'double L'. Take the second run, not a patched first one.

prediction.note: A surname you cannot guess. Stop listening for meaning and start writing single letters.

teaching.answer_quote: tomorrow it's a guy called Halloran, and I'll spell that

distraction.note: Cross the first attempt out completely and write the second one underneath. Patching letters into a half-written name is how this mark goes.

form.note: 'Double L' means two of them. Case is not marked, so a small h costs you nothing.

teaching.recovery: If the meal count slipped past, guess a round hundreds figure and move. This gap needs your pen ready, not your memory.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Shifts
- The afternoon shift starts at ______.
questions.explanation: 'Starts at' plus 'afternoon' predicts an afternoon clock time, which rules out the first time she gives. She describes the morning shift first and labels it as the morning one. The printed word 'afternoon' is doing all the work here.

prediction.note: The frame says afternoon, so any time before noon is a decodable mishearing, not a near miss.

teaching.answer_quote: The afternoon shift, which is the one most of you signed up for, starts at 3.30

form.note: A colon or a point both score. Do not add 'p.m.' — that is a second item in a one-item box.

teaching.recovery: If the surname got away, leave the box and take the second run's letters at the end. The times arrive within seconds.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
What to wear
- Everyone on a shift must wear ______.
questions.explanation: 'Must wear' predicts a piece of clothing, and she offers two. The first is explicitly withdrawn: you don't need to bring one any more. 'What you do need' is the endorsement, and the item after it is the answer. The hyphenated compound counts as one word.

prediction.note: An item of clothing, and an obligation. Expect something optional to be offered first.

teaching.answer_quote: What you do need, and I will send you home over this, is closed-toe shoes

distraction.signal: you really don't need to any more
distraction.note: 'We used to ask' plus 'you don't need to' cancels an item in seven words. Strike it out as you hear it.

form.note: A hyphenated compound is one word, so 'closed-toe shoes' is two and fits. 'A pair of' does not.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Donations
- The kitchen is always short of ______.
questions.explanation: The printed frame's own words, 'short of', are spoken twice and attached to the wrong thing the first time. Predict a noun phrase, and wait: 'What we are permanently short of' is the endorsement. Two words, and neither of them takes an -s.

prediction.note: Two words at most, and something a kitchen runs out of. Do not settle on the first candidate.

signpost.phrase: What we are permanently short of

teaching.answer_quote: What we are permanently short of is freezer space

distraction.signal: Everybody assumes we're short of food
distraction.note: Your own printed words are spoken first, attached to the wrong noun. 'Everybody assumes' is the warning that a reversal is coming.

form.note: 'Space' is uncountable here, so no -s. Two words exactly: no article, no 'more'.

teaching.recovery: Lost the shoes? Let them go. She opens the next item with the single word 'Donations', which is printed on your page.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Age
- Volunteers under ______ must be signed in by an adult.
questions.explanation: 'Under' plus a printed rule predicts an age in the teens, so a figure over about eighteen would be a mishearing you could reject as you wrote it. 'We ask for one thing' announces the rule, and the whole condition arrives in one clause. Write the figure alone.

prediction.note: An age threshold for students. Teens only, so a figure in the twenties is decodably wrong.

teaching.answer_quote: anybody under sixteen has to be signed in by an adult

paraphrase_link.printed: must be signed in by an adult
paraphrase_link.audio: has to be signed in by an adult

form.note: 16 or sixteen, nothing else. Adding 'years' puts a two-item answer in a one-item box.

teaching.recovery: If the freezer gap went past, take it in the check half-minute. Her next word is 'Age', and it is printed on your page.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Dana say about the Thursday delivery run?

options.A: It covers more distance than the other runs.
options.B: It is the run she most needs drivers for.
options.C: It has been added to the schedule recently.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three to be spoken. She kills C before the question even starts and A with a flat 'it isn't'. 'What Thursday is, is' is the endorsement frame, and what follows it is a plea for drivers, not a fact about distance.

prediction.note: All three will be raised out loud. Listen for the one she endorses, not the ones she names.

teaching.answer_quote: the run I'm forever begging people to drive

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The county line is vivid and it is the only distance detail in the talk, so a learner listening for length hears it and stops.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She raises it as what everybody assumes and then flatly denies it: Friday is the longer run, by an hour.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: New volunteers are looking at a sign-up sheet, and Thursday is the run being pushed, which makes it feel like the new one.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says it has been going since the week the kitchen opened, and warns you not to believe the sheet.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Dana tell volunteers about the walk-in cooler?

options.A: Volunteers must never use it by themselves.
options.B: The door should be held open while carrying things.
options.C: The coat by the door has to be worn inside it.

questions.explanation: The stem asks what she tells them, so predict an instruction and expect optional things nearby. 'Two things that are not up to you' is the frame. One instruction is a prohibition on the door; the other is the rule about going in alone, and only one of them is an option here.

prediction.note: Two of these three are things she says are optional or forbidden. Only one is a rule about people.

signpost.phrase: Two things that are not up to you

teaching.answer_quote: And nobody goes into the walk-in on their own. Not ever

distraction.signal: Do not prop that door open
distraction.note: The door instruction comes first, in the option's own words, with 'do not' in front. Hear the polarity before you mark.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Propping a heavy cooler door open while carrying trays is exactly what a new volunteer would do, and the words are spoken.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The instruction is negative: propping it open wrecks the compressor. The option states the opposite of what she says.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The parka is described in detail, and a coat kept by a cold room sounds like protective equipment with a rule attached.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says wearing it is entirely up to you. It is the one thing in that passage she leaves optional.

questions.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: What do drivers collect from the office before every run?
questions.explanation: The stem predicts a thing, small enough to carry, and the limit is two words. 'Before you go anywhere' announces it. She says 'pick up' where your page says 'collect', so the printed verb is never spoken and you must listen for the meaning.

prediction.note: A physical object a driver carries. Two words, so trim any article before you write.

teaching.answer_quote: come to the office and pick up your route sheet

form.note: Two words. 'Your route sheet' and 'a route sheet' are both three and score zero.

teaching.recovery: If the cooler question is still open, guess it now from the stem's modal. This answer arrives inside the next ten seconds.

questions.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: Which meal has the kitchen never provided?
questions.explanation: 'Which meal' fixes the slot to one word from a very small set, so predict the three and wait. 'One last thing' announces the closing item. She names the two they do cook first, then the negative. The answer is the one attached to 'never'.

prediction.note: One word, from a set of three. Write all three in the margin and cross them off.

signpost.phrase: One last thing, because somebody always asks

teaching.answer_quote: We have never once done breakfast

form.note: Breakfast: one word, ea in the first syllable, and no e in the second. 'Breakfeast' scores zero.

teaching.recovery: Last question on the page. If anything above is blank, spend the check half-minute filling it, not rethinking it.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Five of the ten answers are preceded by a plausible wrong value in the same breath, and the North American lexis is a comprehension blocker for learners who have only met British vocabulary.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: The printed words 'short of' are spoken first attached to food, so a keyword-spotting learner writes the decoy with confidence.

title: Opening the Marlow Valley Science Weekend

script_json.title: Opening the Marlow Valley Science Weekend
script_json.scenario: The organiser of a country town's science weekend introduces the event to visitors and volunteers: how it started, what it costs, and which of the town's buildings each activity is running in.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear the organiser of a country science weekend opening the event in front of visitors and volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Morning, everyone, and thanks for turning up this early on a long weekend. I'm Alison, I chair the committee, and I get ten minutes before the first session, so I'll be quick and you can all get a coffee.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A bit of history, because most of you weren't here at the start. This whole thing began as a school project. It was Year eleven — sorry, no, Year 12, I always get that wrong. A group of Year 12 students who wanted to put the telescope somewhere people could actually use it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And it has grown, frankly, beyond what any of us planned. We told the council two thousand people in the grant application, and I remember thinking that was ambitious. Last year we counted just over three thousand through the gates across the two days.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Money. Almost none of it costs you anything. The bus out to the observatory is the one thing you pay for? It's ten dollars a seat, that's the diesel and nothing else, and you book it on the desk at the door, not on your mobile.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Volunteers now. We did hand out those bright orange vests for a couple of years and, look, nobody wore them, so we've stopped. What every volunteer does need is a lanyard from the front desk, because that's what gets you into the back of the pavilion.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. That's the boring half done. The interesting half is where everything actually is, because we have spread ourselves all over this town.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So. Six venues, which for a town this size is showing off a bit. The main exhibition is in the showground pavilion, that has never moved and it never will, and the teachers' session is in there too on the Sunday, same as every year.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The solar car races are down on the tennis courts, both afternoons. Sixteen cars this year, most of them built at the TAFE, and the thing people always say afterwards is that you cannot hear a single one of them coming. Which is very much the point of a solar car.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the primary school is where the under-fives go. There is a colouring-in table in the pavilion as well and every year somebody sits their toddler down at it and waits, but the actual little kids' program, the water tables and the bubbles and the mud kitchen, that's all up at the school.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Astronomy. Obviously that one can't start until it's properly dark, and the only big flat unlit space in this town is the bowls club green. So the telescopes go on the green, from about half past eight, and the bowls club has very kindly agreed not to mind.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The rocket launches used to be behind the school, and we had, let's say, several conversations about that with the neighbours. So this year the launches are at the fire shed, out on the highway, where nobody lives and there is a fire truck sitting right there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the microscope lab is in the old bank. Lovely room, gorgeous ceiling, and it holds twelve people. Twelve. So that is the only session on the whole program where you have to put your name down first, and the list is on the desk by the front door.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Parking. The showground gates will be open, and yes, there is parking in there? But it's about twenty spaces and every one of them is spoken for by an exhibitor's van.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So what we're asking is that everybody leaves the car at the primary school and walks up the footpath. It's four minutes. And no, the main street is not shut all weekend, whatever you may have read. It's closed to cars on the Sunday morning only, for the parade.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what's new. People keep asking whether we're going to three days. There's talk of it, there has been talk of it for years, and it is not happening this year. The genuinely new thing is that the dates have shifted onto the public holiday, which is why the caravan park is already full.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's me done. Program's on the back of your ticket, the uni students in the green shirts know more than I do, and if it rains, everything moves into the pavilion and we all get to know each other rather well.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Four sentences, four answers, in speaking order. Sentence 12's answer cannot arrive before sentence 11's.
teaching.strategy: Each printed sentence is a rewrite of something Alison says, never her own wording. Underline the one word in each sentence that the audio is least likely to repeat, and be ready to hear a different word carrying that meaning.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type the four gaps: a school year, a figure, a thing you pay for, a thing you collect. Two of the four print their own unit.
teaching.watch_out: Two of these four answers are given wrongly first and put right in the same breath. The second value is the one that counts.

groups.instruction:
Where is each of these activities taking place?

Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to questions 15–18.

teaching.order_note: The four venues are named in question order. If you hear the old bank, questions 15 to 17 have already gone.
teaching.strategy: The box holds venue names and she says every one of them out loud, so the letters are easy. The stems are the hard half: each one describes an activity in words she never uses, so match on the reason, not on the noun.
teaching.preview_focus: Read the four stems first and turn each into a property: pre-school, needs darkness, makes noise, limited numbers. Then read the box once and stop looking at it.
teaching.watch_out: One misplaced letter forces a second one wrong, because every venue in this box is used at most once.
teaching.bank_note: The pavilion and the tennis courts are never answers. Each is given a property that fits one of the four stems almost well enough.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Parking comes before the closing announcement, so 19 is settled before 20 begins.
teaching.strategy: Both stems are answered by a clause that corrects something she has just conceded. She says yes and then takes most of it back, twice. The answer is always on the far side of the 'but' or the 'and no'.
teaching.preview_focus: Read all six options. Mark the two that contain an absolute word — no, all, every — because absolutes are what she spends this passage qualifying.
teaching.watch_out: Hearing a thing mentioned and marking it. Every option here is named aloud; only one of them survives the sentence it appears in.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: The event began as a project run by students in ______.
questions.explanation: 'Students in' predicts a school year, so a number was coming. She says the wrong year first and corrects herself inside the same breath, then repeats the right one. The last value stated before she moves on is the answer, and she gives it twice.

prediction.note: An Australian school year. One word plus a number, and the number will be in the teens or below.

teaching.answer_quote: A group of Year 12 students who wanted to put the telescope somewhere

distraction.signal: It was Year eleven — sorry, no
distraction.note: She repairs it in four words and then repeats the right year. Never write on the first number in a sentence like that one.

form.note: 'Year 12' is a word and a number, which fits. 'Year twelve students' is three words and scores zero.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Last year the weekend was attended by about ______ people.
questions.explanation: 'About' plus 'people' predicts a rounded figure, so expect thousands at a town event. She gives the number they promised the council first and frames it as a forecast. 'Last year we counted' is the switch to what actually happened.

prediction.note: A two-day country event: thousands, not hundreds of thousands. A rounded figure, not an exact one.

teaching.answer_quote: Last year we counted just over three thousand through the gates

distraction.signal: We told the council two thousand people in the grant application
distraction.note: A figure inside a past application is a prediction, not a count. Wait for a past-tense verb of measuring.

form.note: Write 3000 or three thousand. 'Just over 3000' is three items and scores zero.

teaching.recovery: If the school year went past, leave it: she says 'Year 12' twice, so guess twelve and put your attention on the figure.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: The only part of the program that visitors pay for is the ______.
questions.explanation: 'Only part' plus 'pay for' predicts a single thing with a price attached, so the price itself is not the answer. 'Almost none of it costs you anything' sets the frame and the exception follows immediately. One word, and the price after it is a decoy for careless pens.

prediction.note: One thing, named once. A price will be spoken next to it, but the frame asks what, not how much.

signpost.phrase: Almost none of it costs you anything

teaching.answer_quote: The bus out to the observatory is the one thing you pay for

paraphrase_link.printed: The only part of the program that visitors pay for
paraphrase_link.audio: the one thing you pay for

form.note: One word: bus. 'Observatory bus' is not what she says, and 'ten dollars' answers a different question.

teaching.recovery: If the visitor figure escaped, write any thousands number and move on. This answer arrives in her very next sentence.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Every volunteer needs to collect a ______ from the front desk.
questions.explanation: 'A' before the gap predicts a singular countable object. She offers the vests first and cancels them with 'nobody wore them, so we've stopped'. 'What every volunteer does need' is the endorsement, and one word follows it.

prediction.note: A singular object a volunteer wears or carries. Expect a withdrawn item to be named first.

teaching.answer_quote: What every volunteer does need is a lanyard from the front desk

distraction.signal: nobody wore them, so we've stopped
distraction.note: 'We did hand out' is a past habit, and 'we've stopped' kills it. Cross the vests out the moment you hear the past tense.

form.note: Lanyard: l-a-n-y-a-r-d. It is one word, and the y in the middle is where it goes wrong.

questions.instruction:
Where is each of these activities taking place?

Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to questions 15–18.
questions.prompt: an activity for children who are not yet at school

options.A: the bowls club
options.B: the fire shed
options.C: the old bank

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the near-miss venue to be named in the same breath. She raises the pavilion's colouring table first and says people mistake it for this. 'The actual little kids' program' is the endorsement, and it is at the school.

prediction.note: Two venues will be linked to small children. Wait for the one she calls the actual program.

teaching.answer_quote: the primary school is where the under-fives go

paraphrase_link.audio: the water tables and the bubbles and the mud kitchen

teaching.recovery: If the lanyard gap is blank, leave it blank for now. The venue letters begin the moment she says 'the primary school'.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She names a colouring-in table in the pavilion in the same sentence, and says every year a parent sits a toddler down at it.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She raises it precisely as the thing people confuse with this, then places the real under-fives program elsewhere.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Solar cars sound like a children's activity, and the races run on both afternoons when families are there.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The cars are built by TAFE students and raced, not handled. Nothing about that venue is aimed at pre-schoolers.

questions.instruction:
Where is each of these activities taking place?

Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to questions 15–18.
questions.prompt: a session that cannot begin until it is dark

options.A: the bowls club
options.B: the fire shed
options.C: the old bank

questions.explanation: The stem never says astronomy and she never says dark-dependent, so match on the reason. 'That one can't start until it's properly dark' is the signpost, and the venue arrives as the only unlit flat space in town. The word telescope is your bridge from the opening.

prediction.note: One venue will be chosen for a physical property, not for what it normally does. Listen for that reason.

signpost.phrase: can't start until it's properly dark

teaching.answer_quote: the only big flat unlit space in this town is the bowls club green

distraction.signal: The solar car races are down on the tennis courts, both afternoons
distraction.note: Floodlit courts feel like the night venue. She never says lights, she says unlit, and that is the property that decides it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The pavilion is the venue she names most often and it is indoors, which a learner reads as controllable darkness.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She only ever puts the exhibition and the teachers' session in the pavilion, and neither depends on the time of day.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Tennis courts are the one outdoor venue most people associate with floodlights, and the races run in the afternoon.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The courts are used for the solar cars, which need sun. She calls the bowls green the only unlit space.

questions.instruction:
Where is each of these activities taking place?

Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to questions 15–18.
questions.prompt: an activity moved because of the noise it makes

options.A: the bowls club
options.B: the fire shed
options.C: the old bank

questions.explanation: The stem predicts a move, so listen for a past location and a present one. 'Used to be behind the school' plus 'several conversations with the neighbours' is the whole story in one line, and 'this year' switches to the current venue.

prediction.note: Two places will be attached to this activity, one of them in the past tense. Take the present one.

signpost.phrase: So this year the launches are at

teaching.answer_quote: So this year the launches are at the fire shed, out on the highway

paraphrase_link.audio: out on the highway, where nobody lives

teaching.recovery: Lost 16? Do not reopen the box. Each venue is named once, in order, so put your finger on the next stem instead.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The pavilion is where everything moves if it rains, so it is already in the learner's head as the fallback venue.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Rockets are not launched indoors, and she attaches the pavilion only to the exhibition and the teachers' session.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The courts are the other outdoor venue, and a learner who has lost track picks the outdoor one for anything loud.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says the exact opposite about the courts: you cannot hear a single solar car coming. That is the quiet venue.

questions.instruction:
Where is each of these activities taking place?

Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to questions 15–18.
questions.prompt: the only session that has to be booked in advance

options.A: the bowls club
options.B: the fire shed
options.C: the old bank

questions.explanation: 'Only' and 'booked' predict a capacity limit somewhere. She gives the room, then the number twice, then the consequence. The booking rule is stated after the venue, so a learner waiting for the word 'book' must hold the venue in mind for a whole clause.

prediction.note: Listen for a small number of places. The limit is what forces the booking, so the figure comes first.

teaching.answer_quote: the only session on the whole program where you have to put your name down first

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The teachers' session sounds like the kind of thing you would register for, and it is in the pavilion.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She never attaches a limit or a list to the pavilion. The booking sentence is about a room that holds twelve.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Sixteen cars implies entries, and entries imply a list, so the courts feel like the venue with paperwork.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The cars are entered by TAFE builders, not by visitors. Nothing in that passage asks a visitor to sign anything.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Alison ask visitors to do about parking?

options.A: leave their cars at the showground
options.B: park at the school and walk in
options.C: keep off the main street for the whole weekend

questions.explanation: The stem asks what she asks, so predict an instruction and expect a concession first. She admits there is parking at the showground and then removes it in the same sentence. 'What we're asking is' is the endorsement, and the closure of the street is limited to one morning.

prediction.note: An instruction, not a fact. Two of these three will be raised and then qualified away.

teaching.answer_quote: everybody leaves the car at the primary school and walks up the footpath

paraphrase_link.printed: park at the school and walk in
paraphrase_link.audio: leaves the car at the primary school and walks up the footpath

distraction.signal: the main street is not shut all weekend
distraction.note: One unstressed 'not' and one 'only' between them decide this option. Mark absolutes in the preview and listen for their limits.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She confirms out loud that the showground gates are open and that there is parking inside, which is the option's own claim.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The twenty spaces are all held for exhibitors' vans, so the concession is withdrawn in the next clause.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A street parade and a closed main street are both mentioned, and closure feels like a weekend-long arrangement.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says it is closed to cars on the Sunday morning only. The option's word 'whole' is what makes it false.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What is new about this year's Science Weekend?

options.A: It has been extended to three days.
options.B: It now includes a session for teachers.
options.C: The dates have shifted to a public holiday weekend.

questions.explanation: 'New' predicts a contrast with previous years, so expect old things to be named as old. She kills the three-day idea as talk and the teachers' session was mentioned earlier as an annual fixture. 'The genuinely new thing is' leaves only one candidate standing.

prediction.note: Two are true of the event but not new. Listen for the word new attached to one.

teaching.answer_quote: the dates have shifted onto the public holiday, which is why the caravan park is already full

paraphrase_link.audio: the dates have shifted onto the public holiday

teaching.recovery: Last question here. If parking is still open, guess it from the stem's verb and spend the check time on the sentences.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She raises the three-day idea herself, in the sentence right before the answer, and says people keep asking about it.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: 'There's talk of it' and 'it is not happening this year' put it in the future, not this year's program.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A teachers' session sounds like an addition, and a learner who missed the earlier mention has no reason to doubt it.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She placed it in the pavilion earlier with the words 'same as every year', which is the opposite of new.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Every matching stem describes an activity in words she never uses, and half the completion answers are given wrongly first. The Australian institutional vocabulary blocks meaning for learners who have never met it.

title: Radio feature: reopening the Norland canal arm

script_json.title: Radio feature: reopening the Norland canal arm
script_json.scenario: A local radio presenter's feature slot on a volunteer trust restoring a disused canal arm: what it was built for, how far the work has got, and what is in the trust's diary.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a local radio presenter introducing a feature about a canal restoration project. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now. If you walk out past the retail park and you take the little gravel track behind the recycling depot, you come to something most people in this town have no idea is there. Half a mile of canal, full of water, and going absolutely nowhere. No boats, no towpath signs, nothing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Everybody assumes a canal means coal. It usually did. Not this one. The Norland arm was cut to bring limestone down off the hills to the kilns at the basin, and coal only ever came back up it, as a return load, on the empty boats.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The plan, when the trust started, was ambitious. Six miles, all the way to the junction, and there's still a drawing on the wall of their hut to prove it. What they have settled on, and what they are actually digging, is three miles.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you want to help, they run work parties. Second Sunday of the month — no, hang on, that's out of date, they shifted it last autumn. It's the first Sunday now. First Sunday, nine till three, and they feed you at one, which I'm told is the real reason people come.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The single biggest obstacle is half a mile up from the basin, where the arm runs under the Ashfield road. There's a culvert there. That's just a pipe carrying the water underneath the road, and it fell in some time in the eighties. Digging that out is a two-year job on its own.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So I asked Sheila Vance, who chairs the trust, what the hold-up really is. I'd assumed money. Everybody assumes money, and the council officer I spoke to talked about funding for a solid twenty minutes. Sheila didn't. She said what they cannot find is bricklayers.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the history and the hole in the ground. What I want to give you now is the practical half, because the trust has three things in the diary and every one of them is open to anybody.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the feature, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things in the diary. And I should say that none of these needs you to know the first thing about canals, which is just as well, because a fortnight ago I could not have told you what a lock was for, and I grew up two streets from this one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The open day. That is in September, and it is the one day in the year they put boats back on the water. Trips run from the wharf all afternoon, there's a brass band that has seen better decades, and there is, inevitably, a cake stall.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Winter talks, Thursday evenings from October. They used to be in the community centre and honestly half the town could never find it. They're in the boathouse now, which is warmer, holds forty, and has a kettle that works.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And membership. It's twelve pounds a year for one person, or twenty for a whole household, and it gets you the newsletter and a vote at the annual meeting, which is a livelier evening than you would ever imagine.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then there's the tunnel. Everybody asks about the tunnel. It was surveyed four years ago, properly, with divers and cameras and a very expensive week, and the brickwork turned out to be sound, which nobody had expected.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So it's not that the tunnel's dangerous. It isn't. It's simply that it sits beyond the second lock, and the second lock is not in this phase of the work at all. The tunnel is not part of what is being restored now, whatever you may have read.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, if this is your sort of thing. You can send them money, and they will take it very gratefully indeed. But when I asked Sheila what she actually wanted, it wasn't cheques. It was people standing in a wet ditch on a Sunday with a spade. Turn up to a work party. That is the answer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The Norland Canal Trust, then. First Sunday of the month, open day in September, and a website address I am not going to attempt to read out on air, because it has a hyphen in it and we would all regret it. It's on our page instead. That's me. Back to the studio.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Announcement: changes to household collections in Sandmouth

script_json.title: Announcement: changes to household collections in Sandmouth
script_json.scenario: A city recycling officer explains changes to household waste collection at a neighborhood meeting: new days, new carts and weights, then what will now happen to each material.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a city recycling officer explaining changes to household collections at a neighborhood meeting. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Evening, folks. Warren, from the city. I know an evening about trash cans is nobody's idea of fun, so I'll be quick, and everything I say tonight is on a card that goes out with next month's water bill anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Days first, because that's the one that catches people. South of the creek, nothing changes, you stay on Tuesdays. But everything north of the creek, which is all of you in this room, moves to Wednesdays from the first of next month.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And carts have to be out at the curb by 6.30 in the morning. Not seven, which is what the old card said, and not when you hear the truck, because by then he's two streets away and he is not coming back for you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Yard waste. That's a seasonal program, and it runs from April right through to the end of November. Outside those months the yard-waste truck simply doesn't come, and every year somebody leaves a pile of leaves out in January and it sits there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, while I'm on carts. The new blue carts are enormous, and people fill them with wet leaves, and then my crew can't lift them. Ninety-six gallons of volume, fifty pounds of weight. Fifty is the limit, and the weight is the one that catches everybody.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh — and I said April for the yard waste. That's wrong, and I would hate you to write it down. It moved this year. Yard waste starts in March now, first full week of March, and it still finishes end of November.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One more thing and then we'll get to the materials. If we miss you, and we do miss people, call it in within 48 hours. Inside 48 hours we come back for free. After that it waits for your next collection day, and there is nothing I can do about that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. That's days, times, weights and misses. The rest of this is the part everybody actually argues about, which is what you can and cannot put in the cart.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the announcement, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So. Under the new system there are three things that can happen to a material. Some of it goes in the blue cart and gets picked up every single week, and that list is longer this year than it has ever been.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Some of it we can't put on a truck at all any more, and that stuff you drive over to the drop-off center on Halstead Road, which is open seven days and takes about four minutes of your life.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And then there's a short list of things we simply cannot take. Not in the cart, not at the drop-off, not from anybody. Those go in the regular trash, or they go back to the store you bought them from.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Cardboard. This is the good news of the evening. Cardboard used to be every other week and everybody hated it, and from next month it's in the weekly cart, flattened, with the tape pulled off. Flattened. I will keep saying flattened.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Glass. And I'm sorry about this one, because it is genuinely a step backwards. The processor we used closed in the spring, so glass is off the trucks. Bottles and jars, you're driving them over to Halstead Road from now on.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Food scraps. Now, the plan on the table in the spring was monthly, and I'll be honest, we very nearly went with monthly, because monthly is cheap. Council said no. So food scraps are in the weekly cart alongside the cardboard, in the green liner bags.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Batteries. Everybody knows batteries shouldn't go in the cart, and everybody puts them in the cart anyway, and twice this year one has caught fire in the back of a truck. Batteries go to Halstead Road. There's a bin for them right by the gate.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And plastic bags. This is the one that upsets people. We took them for years and we cannot take them any more, at the curb or at the drop-off, because they wrap round the sorting machinery and shut the whole line down. Grocery store, out front, every store has a bin.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's it. Wednesdays, 6.30, fifty pounds, and if in doubt, look at the card. And please, please don't put a garden hose in the cart. I don't know why I have to say that every year, but I do.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: A guide's introduction at the Norland Museum of Making

script_json.title: A guide's introduction at the Norland Museum of Making
script_json.scenario: A museum guide takes a group through the ground-floor plan before they set off round the building, then runs through the week's sessions and what each of them costs.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a guide introducing a group of visitors to the ground floor of a small museum. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hello, and welcome to Norland. I'm Priya, I'll be with you for the first half hour or so. There's a floor plan in the middle of your leaflet, and I would get that out now, because this building was three separate workshops before anyone thought of turning it into a museum, and it does not make a great deal of sense from the inside.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. We're all standing in the doorway with the street behind us, and reception is the desk straight in front of you. Keep that desk ahead of you. Every left and right I give in the next few minutes assumes you are facing it from where you are now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first door on your left, just before you draw level with the desk, is the cloakroom. Bags bigger than a shopping bag have to go in there, I'm afraid, and it's free, and there's a code on the back of your ticket.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Directly opposite the cloakroom, so on your right, is the gift shop. It's open the whole time we are, and it is very much smaller than everybody expects, so if there are twelve of you in it, it is full.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now walk past reception and out into the courtyard, which is the open square in the middle of your plan. On the far side of it, straight ahead as you come out, is the print room. That was the boiler house until the refit, and one of the older guidebooks still calls it that, so do ignore your guidebook.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: From the print room, turn right and follow the covered walk. The room in the far corner is the toy gallery. No — sorry, the toy gallery is upstairs, I always do that. The room in that corner is the clock gallery, and it ticks, loudly, and some people find it unbearable.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then keep going down the right-hand side. You'll pass the stairs and then the lift, and neither of those is a question, they're printed on your plan already. Right at the bottom of that side, in the corner nearest the door you came in by, is the lecture theatre.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the ground floor. Upstairs is one long room running the whole length of the building, and you genuinely cannot get lost in it, which is the entire reason I have spent all this time down here with a plan instead of just walking you round it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the introduction, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, what's actually on this week. Four things, and two of them cost money. I'll be honest with you, the two that cost money are the two I would do, and the two that are free are the two everybody turns up for, which is how it always goes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The handling table runs on Saturdays. That's the one where children get to pick things up, and it starts at 10.30 and it runs until we run out of children, usually about one. Five and over, and please stay with them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The print workshop. Now, people expect that to be the Saturday one as well, because everything else on this list is, and it isn't. The print workshop is Sundays, two o'clock, and it takes an hour and a half, and you do come out of it covered in ink.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It was four pounds last year and that barely covered the ink, so from this month it's six pounds, which includes the paper and whatever you print going home with you in a tube.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The building tour is Thursday mornings, eleven o'clock, and that one is completely free. We meet by the sundial in the courtyard, not at reception, because reception is where everybody instinctively waits and then nobody can hear a word I am saying over the till.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And late opening. Now, the poster in the window still says the last Friday of the month, and that poster is wrong and I have told them. It's the last Thursday of the month, until nine, with music in the courtyard.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, that's me. Take a plan on your way through, mind the step going out into the courtyard because everybody catches it, and if a clock stops while you are standing in the corner gallery, I promise you it isn't anything you did.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Arriving at the Kooranda Creek campground

script_json.title: Arriving at the Kooranda Creek campground
script_json.scenario: A campground caretaker walks a group of arriving campers round the site plan, then gives them the site rules and some advice about the creek and their first evening.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear the caretaker of a riverside campground giving an arrival talk to a group of campers. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: G'day, everyone, and welcome to Kooranda Creek. I'm Trev, I look after the place, and I'm going to take five minutes over this plan because the site is longer than it looks and every single year somebody drives up the walking track with a caravan on the back.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So. We're standing just inside the entry gate, and the camp office is that demountable on your right with the flag on it. Keep the gate behind you and the office on your right. Everything I say from here is from where you're standing now, not from wherever you end up.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Straight across the road from the office, so over on your left, is the amenities block. Showers, toilets, and a laundry with two machines that both work, which is not something I could have told you this time last year.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now head up the main road. There's a big galvanised water tank on your right, and that tank is not on your plan at all, so leave it alone. What is on your plan, just past the tank and still on the right, is the camp kitchen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: About halfway up, a track runs off to your right and drops down towards the water. Follow that all the way and you come out at the boat ramp. It's concrete, it's a bit green in the middle, and you can back a trailer down it if you take it slowly.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Back on the main road you'll see the big gum tree, which is the one thing everybody recognises. Opposite the gum, on your left, is the barbecues. No, hang on, that's wrong, the barbies are up by the camp kitchen. Opposite the gum, on your left, is the playground. And the barbies you don't book, by the way. First in, first served.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And then right at the top, where the beach track leaves the site, on your left, is the lookout. Now that used to be the fire tower, and a couple of the older maps still have it marked that way, but there's been no tower up there for twenty years. It's a lookout with a bench, and it's worth the walk.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the lot. Sites are numbered, yours is on the slip I handed you, and if you can't find it, come and find me. I'm usually somewhere between the office and the kitchen with a wheelbarrow.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, the rules, and there are only three of them worth saying out loud. Quiet time. That's nine thirty. Not ten, whatever the old brochure in the office says, because that brochure is older than my ute. 9.30, music off, voices down, and yes, I do walk round.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Supplies. There is no shop on this site, and I know the website used to suggest there was. The nearest shop is at Kooranda township, seven kilometres back down the road you came in on. The servo is another twelve on from that, so if you're low on fuel, deal with it today, not tomorrow.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And generators. Plenty of you will have one and that's completely fine in the daytime. What we ask is that nobody runs generators after dark. They are a great deal louder than the owner thinks they are at two in the morning, and the creek carries sound.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Swimming. People ask me this every day of my life. There's a sign on the gate that says no swimming, and that sign is about ten years out of date, and I have asked three times for someone to come and take it down.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can swim. Above the boat ramp, where it's shallow and sandy, you're fine, and the kids are in there from breakfast till dark. Below the ramp is where the current sits, and that's the stretch that catches people. And no, it's nothing to do with the tide. We're far too far up the creek for tides.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Last thing. If you do one thing this evening, walk up to the lookout before the sun goes. Ten minutes up, and you'll understand why people come back here for thirty years. The fire notices on the office door, read those obviously, but nobody's evening was ever improved by a laminated sign.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: All right. Sites, showers, quiet at nine thirty. Any dramas, the office is open till six and after that I'm in the green van behind it. No worries. Enjoy yourselves.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Service update: the Riverside line closure

script_json.title: Service update: the Riverside line closure
script_json.scenario: A transit information officer briefs regular passengers at a station on a nine-week line closure: the replacement shuttle, journey times, what the buses can carry, and why the work is happening now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a transit information officer briefing regular passengers about the closure of a commuter line. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good evening. My name's Renata, I work in customer information, and I'd rather stand here and take this from you in person than have you find it out on a platform sign at seven in the morning. So. Ask me anything at the end.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The headline. The Riverside line closes on the fourteenth for track work. Now, we announced twelve weeks back in the spring, and I know twelve is the number sitting in your head. That came down. It is nine weeks, and we are held to that publicly.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Where you catch the replacement. The shuttle picks up on Clark Street, outside the hardware store — sorry, no, that's wrong, the hardware store closed in June. Outside the drugstore. Clark Street, outside the drugstore, and there's a temporary sign going up on Thursday.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fares. There was talk in the spring of charging a flat dollar on the shuttle, and I know several of you saw that in the paper. It isn't happening. The shuttle is free for the whole nine weeks. Your monthly passes stay valid on the trains either side, so please don't go buying anything new.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One more before the break. The elevators at Bell Street. They are both out, and they stay out until October, which I know is a serious problem for some of you. There's a staffed ramp at the north entrance from six in the morning until the last train.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. That's the shape of it. The second half is the part that actually affects your morning: how long it is going to take you, what you are allowed to bring with you, and why on earth we are doing any of this now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the briefing, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Journey times, and I'm not going to dress this up. A trip that took you twenty-five minutes on the train is going to take about forty-five on the bus. So allow an extra twenty minutes, and a little more in the rain. And no, before anybody asks, this is not a peak-only service. We looked hard at peak-only and it fails the people who need it most.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Bicycles. And I am sorry about this, because I know how many of you ride to the station. We can take strollers, we can take wheelchairs, every one of these buses is low-floor. We cannot take bicycles. There's no rack on the front and there is genuinely no room in the aisle.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And some good news, finally, because there is some. The new station at Kestrel Park. That was supposed to be two years out, and the closure has actually pulled it forward, because the crews are already down there with the equipment. It opens in the fall.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the schedule, and I want to be straight with you. It is not the train schedule. People keep telling me it's the same timetable and it is not. The trains ran every ten minutes. The shuttle runs every twenty, all day, and that includes the morning peak.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Why now. The signals on that stretch are old. Everybody in this room knows the signals are old, I have had letters about the signals, and yes, they will get replaced while we're in there, because you do not close a line twice.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But the reason for the closure, the whole reason, is the Hollis Street bridge. It is well over a hundred years old, it carries the track across the creek, and it has to come out and go back in. That is what nine weeks buys you. The platform work at Bell Street is a separate project and it's next year.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, what would I tell a regular rider. Don't try to reroute yourself through downtown, because that line is already full at eight in the morning and it will not thank you. Check the app before you leave the house. Every single morning. The shuttle gets held up at the lights and the app knows before I do.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's everything I have. There are printed cards on the table by the gateline, and there is a phone number on them that reaches an actual person rather than a menu, which I fought for. I'll be standing here for another twenty minutes. Thank you all for coming out on a wet evening like this one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Four notes, in the order she gives them. Once she says 'elevators', the first three gaps are behind you.
teaching.strategy: Renata opens every item with a bare noun: headline, fares, elevators. Three of these four answers are the second value in their sentence, because she names what people already believe before she gives what is true.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type the four: a figure, a building, a fare, a month. Then mark the two frames whose unit is already printed for you.
teaching.watch_out: Every wrong value here comes from something people have read: a spring announcement, a newspaper, a closed shop.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Three sentences, three answers, in speaking order. Sentence 17's answer cannot arrive before 16's.
teaching.strategy: Two of these three sentences are rewrites rather than quotations: she says 'we cannot take' where your page says 'unable to carry'. Underline the printed verb in each one and expect a different verb to carry the same meaning.
teaching.preview_focus: Decide what each sentence physically asks for: a number of minutes, a thing a bus holds, a time of year. Two of the three print their own unit.
teaching.watch_out: The minutes sentence sits between two other durations she says out loud, and only the printed word 'extra' separates them.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Schedule, then reason, then advice. Each stem is finished before the next one opens.
teaching.strategy: All three of these are settled by a contrast. She states what people believe, or what is also true, and then marks the real answer with a phrase like 'the whole reason'. Listen for the second half of every sentence.
teaching.preview_focus: Read all nine options in the pause. Then, for each stem, decide whether it wants a fact, a cause or an instruction, because that alone kills some options.
teaching.watch_out: Two of the wrong options here are things she says are true. True is not the test: the stem asks which one answers it.

- The line will be closed for ______ weeks.

teaching.answer_quote: The shuttle is free for the whole nine weeks

distraction.note: 'There was talk of' marks an option that never happened. Strike it out the moment you hear the phrase.

form.note: One word: free. 'Free of charge' is three words and scores zero on a two-word limit.

teaching.recovery: If the shop name got away, put any building and move. She opens this item with the single word 'fares'.

questions.prompt: - Elevators at Bell Street are out of service until ______.
questions.explanation: 'Until' plus 'out of service' predicts a month or a date. 'The elevators at Bell Street' opens the item by name, and the month arrives in the same clause as 'they stay out'. No rival month is offered, so this is a clean transcription item.

teaching.answer_quote: they stay out until October, which I know is a serious problem

teaching.recovery: If the fare gap is empty, write one word and let it go. This item is announced by the word 'elevators', printed above the gap.

questions.explanation: 'Extra' plus a printed unit predicts a bare figure that is a difference, not a total. She gives the old journey time and the new one first, and only the word 'extra' in your sentence tells you that neither of those is the answer.

prediction.note: A difference in minutes, not a journey length. The printed word 'extra' is doing the whole job here.

teaching.answer_quote: So allow an extra twenty minutes, and a little more in the rain

distraction.note: Three durations in one sentence. Keep the printed word 'extra' under your finger and let the two totals go past.

form.note: 20 or twenty. Writing '20 minutes' repeats a printed word and puts you over the limit.

questions.prompt: The shuttle buses are unable to carry ______.
questions.explanation: 'Unable to carry' predicts a plural noun and a list of things that can be carried. She names three that can before the one that cannot. The printed frame is negative, so the answer is the item after 'we cannot', not the ones after 'we can'.

prediction.note: No article before the gap, so plural. Expect a list of things that are allowed first.

teaching.answer_quote: We cannot take bicycles. There's no rack on the front

distraction.signal: We can take strollers, we can take wheelchairs
distraction.note: Two positives arrive before the negative. Your frame says 'unable', so mark that word in the preview and hunt for the exclusion.

form.note: Plural: the frame has no article. 'Bicycle' loses a mark you had already heard correctly.

teaching.recovery: If the minutes figure escaped, write anything plausible. She opens this sentence with the single word 'bicycles'.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: The new station at Kestrel Park will open in the ______.
questions.explanation: 'In the' before the gap predicts a season rather than a month, because a month would not take 'the'. 'And some good news, finally' announces it. She gives the old timescale first and says the closure pulled it forward, then names the season.

prediction.note: 'The' before the gap rules out a month, so expect a season. One word only.

teaching.answer_quote: It opens in the fall

form.note: She says fall, so write fall. 'Autumn' means the same thing and is not the word spoken.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Renata say about the shuttle schedule?

options.A: It runs less frequently than the trains did.
options.B: It keeps to the existing train timetable.
options.C: It operates during peak hours only.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a comparison. She denies the timetable claim twice, then gives both intervals, and the comparison between ten and twenty is what answers the stem. She never uses the word 'frequently', so you have to do the arithmetic yourself.

prediction.note: Two numbers will decide this. Expect an interval for the trains and a different one for the buses.

signpost.phrase: I want to be straight with you

teaching.answer_quote: The trains ran every ten minutes. The shuttle runs every twenty

paraphrase_link.printed: less frequently than the trains did

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She quotes the belief out loud, and a learner who catches 'the same timetable' and not the denial marks it.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says 'it is not the train schedule' and then 'it is not', giving two flat denials before the figures.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Peak-only was genuinely considered, and she discusses it at length in the journey-time passage.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says the shuttle runs every twenty minutes all day, and that peak-only was rejected as unfair.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What is the main reason for closing the line?

options.A: to replace signalling equipment
options.B: to rebuild a bridge over the creek
options.C: to lengthen the platforms at Bell Street

questions.explanation: 'Main reason' predicts several true causes and one ranked above them. The signals are real work and she confirms they will be done, which is exactly why they are the trap. 'The whole reason' is the ranking phrase, and the platform work is placed in another year.

prediction.note: The stem says 'main', so more than one true cause is coming. Listen for a ranking phrase.

teaching.answer_quote: the reason for the closure, the whole reason, is the Hollis Street bridge

paraphrase_link.printed: rebuild a bridge over the creek
paraphrase_link.audio: it carries the track across the creek

distraction.signal: The signals on that stretch are old
distraction.note: The signals are named three times and are genuinely being replaced. 'Main reason' in your stem is what rules them out.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The signals get a whole sentence, they are old, letters have been written, and she confirms they will be replaced during the closure.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She frames them as work done at the same time, not the cause. The stem asks for the main reason.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Bell Street has already appeared twice in the briefing, so the name is familiar and feels connected.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She calls the platform work a separate project and places it next year, outside this closure entirely.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Renata advise regular passengers to do?

options.A: buy a new season ticket
options.B: check the app every morning
options.C: travel on the downtown line instead

questions.explanation: 'Advise' predicts an instruction, and she gives two negative ones before the positive. 'Don't reroute' kills one option and the fares passage killed the other. The instruction that survives is repeated as a two-word sentence, which is her way of underlining it.

prediction.note: An instruction. Two of these three will arrive with 'don't' in front of them.

signpost.phrase: what would I tell a regular rider

teaching.answer_quote: Check the app before you leave the house. Every single morning

paraphrase_link.audio: Check the app before you leave the house

teaching.recovery: Last question. If the reason is still open, settle it in the check half-minute by asking which option she ranked, not which she named.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Tickets and passes are discussed in detail, and a closure feels like a moment to change what you buy.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says existing passes stay valid and asks people not to buy anything new, which is the opposite instruction.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Rerouting through downtown is the obvious workaround and she names it as something people will try.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She names it in order to tell you not to, and gives the reason: that line is already full at eight.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Almost every answer is the second value in its sentence, because she names what passengers already believe before she corrects it. Two questions need a comparison rather than a fact.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: Nothing in the audio says 'less often'. You have to hold ten and twenty in your head and compare them yourself.
