title: Volunteer briefing: the Sandmouth shore survey

script_json.title: Volunteer briefing: the Sandmouth shore survey
script_json.scenario: The organiser of a long-running coastal wildlife survey briefs a room of new volunteers: when and where they walk, what they bring, what the trust supplies, and what happens to the records afterwards.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear the organiser of a coastal wildlife survey briefing a room of new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Evening, all. I'm Marcus, I run the volunteer side of the shore survey, and I want to say at the start that this survey has been going for twenty-two years, which is a lot longer than anybody involved at the beginning expected, and that is entirely because of people who turned up on cold mornings.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First thing, and it governs everything else: we survey at low tide. Not whenever suits, but an hour either side of low water, which is why the dates on your sheet look so random. Some of you will be standing on a beach at half past six in the morning. New people walk it far too fast, incidentally, but that sorts itself out by the second time.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Each team takes one stretch of shore. Now, when we set this up the stretches were a kilometre long and it very nearly finished everybody off, so they came down. They're five hundred metres now. Five hundred, marked at each end with a post, and you walk it twice, once out and once back.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Teams of three. One person on the water's edge, one on the strandline, one writing everything down, and you swap over halfway because the writing is the cold job. Three is the number that works. If you arrive as a pair we'll put you with somebody, so don't lose sleep over it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Kit. We used to keep a box of spare binoculars in the hut and, predictably, there are two left and one of those has no lens cap. So you bring your own binoculars. Boots you will want, a board to lean on is a good idea, and a pencil rather than a pen, because a pen freezes and a pencil doesn't.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if something goes wrong on the day, you don't ring me, you ring the survey coordinator. Her surname is Gilroy. I'll spell it. G. I. L. E. R. — no, sorry, ignore that, there is no E in it. G. I. L. R. O. Y. Gilroy. Her number is on the bottom of every sheet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. That's who, where and when. The second half is what you actually do once you're standing on a beach in the dark wondering why you volunteered.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the briefing, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Equipment. Almost all of it you bring yourself, as I've said. The only thing we hand out is a quadrat, which is a square metre frame you put down on the sand and count inside. One per team, they live in the box by the hut door, and they do genuinely have to come back.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Weather. We go out in rain. We go out in wind. We went out in snow two winters ago and it was the best count this survey has ever recorded. The one thing that stops us is fog. If you can't see the far post from where you're standing, don't start. Ring the coordinator and go home.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, what happens to your sheets. The council does get a copy, and a lot of people assume that is the point of the whole thing, and it isn't. Everything goes to the national recording scheme, where a county recorder verifies it before it counts as a record. That is why the dates matter so much.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The one thing new people get wrong, every single time, is this. Lateness I can forgive, the tide can't but I can. What I cannot undo is an empty sheet. You walk a stretch with nothing much on it and you write nothing down. An empty square is data, and it is the most useful data we have. Record the common things.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Training. There's a morning at the field centre in April, and I know several of you have already put your name down for it, and I'm about to save you a Saturday. You don't all need it. If you're leading a team you do, because you're the one signing the sheet off. If you're walking in a team, you don't.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Boots, board, binoculars and low tide. Sheets are in the box by the door, take three. And before anybody asks me again, no, there is no online version of the training, whatever the newsletter told you. Go and get a cup of tea.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Five notes in speaking order. When he says 'that's who, where and when', this whole set has closed.
teaching.strategy: Marcus opens each item with one bare word: tide, stretch, teams, kit, coordinator. Two of the five answers replace a value he has already given, and both replacements are marked with a plain past tense before them.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type all five: an adjective, a distance, a small number, a plural object, a surname. Mark the surname gap now, because that one needs your pen ready.
teaching.watch_out: The kit item names four things and only one of them fills the printed frame. The frame's words 'their own' decide it.

groups.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Equipment before weather, in that order. Neither answer is repeated later in the talk.
teaching.strategy: No printed frame to lean on here, so the stem has to do the slot-typing for you. One asks for a physical object and one for a weather word, and each arrives after Marcus has listed several things that do not qualify.
teaching.preview_focus: Turn both stems into a shape before he restarts: a thing you are handed, and a single weather word. Both answers are one word.
teaching.watch_out: Writing the whole spoken phrase. He defines the equipment in a full clause, and only the noun before that clause is the answer.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Records, then the common mistake, then training. Each stem closes before the next one opens.
teaching.strategy: Each of these three is decided by something Marcus contradicts: an assumption about the council, an instinct about what is worth recording, and a booking several of them have already made. Listen for the sentence that begins with a denial.
teaching.preview_focus: Read all nine options in the pause and decide which stem wants a fact, which wants an error and which wants a rule. Mark every absolute word you see.
teaching.watch_out: Two wrong options here are things he states as true. True is not enough: the stem decides which truth answers it.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
SANDMOUTH SHORE SURVEY — VOLUNTEER NOTES
When and where
- Surveys are always carried out at ______ tide.
questions.explanation: 'Tide' is printed, so the gap can only be one of two words and you can write both in the margin before he starts. 'It governs everything else' announces it, and he repeats the idea as 'low water' in the next clause, which is your confirmation.

prediction.note: One word, and only two words in English can fill it. Decide both in the pause and cross one off.

teaching.answer_quote: we survey at low tide. Not whenever suits

form.note: One word: low. 'Low tide' repeats a printed word and takes the answer over the limit.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: - Each team walks a stretch of shore ______ metres long.
questions.explanation: 'Metres' is printed, so predict a bare figure and expect a change of unit nearby. The original length is given in kilometres and fenced off with 'when we set this up'. 'They came down' is the switch, and he repeats the new figure straight after it.

prediction.note: A distance in metres, so the figure will be in hundreds. The unit is printed: write the number only.

teaching.answer_quote: They're five hundred metres now. Five hundred, marked at each end with a post

distraction.signal: the stretches were a kilometre long
distraction.note: The first length is in a different unit and a past tense. Two warnings in one clause, so keep your pen still.

form.note: 500 or five hundred. Adding 'metres' repeats a printed word and scores zero for going over.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: - Each team should have ______ people in it.
questions.explanation: 'People in it' predicts a very small figure, so anything above about six would be a mishearing you could reject as you wrote it. He opens the item with the number itself, lists the three jobs, and then repeats the figure. A clean item with two chances at it.

prediction.note: A team size for walking a beach. Single figures only, and he lists the jobs to confirm it.

teaching.answer_quote: Three is the number that works

form.note: 3 or three. 'Three people' repeats a printed word and takes you over the limit.

teaching.recovery: If the distance escaped, write a hundreds figure and move. He opens this item with the number itself, in the first two words.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Kit
- Volunteers must bring their own ______.
questions.explanation: 'Their own' plus no article predicts a plural object, and four objects are named in this passage. Only one of them is attached to the phrase 'you bring your own'; the rest are advice. The trust's spares are mentioned only to explain why they are gone.

prediction.note: No article before the gap, so plural. Four objects are named and only one carries an obligation.

teaching.answer_quote: So you bring your own binoculars

distraction.signal: Boots you will want, a board to lean on is a good idea
distraction.note: Three more objects follow the answer, all recommended and none required. 'You will want' is advice, not an instruction.

form.note: Binoculars is always plural and always has one n and two c-free syllables: b-i-n-o-c.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: - Queries on the day: ring the coordinator, surname ______.
questions.explanation: 'Surname' warns you before the audio that this is pure transcription. 'I'll spell it' is the cue to stop listening for meaning. He puts a letter in that does not belong, says so, and starts the spelling again. Take the second run, not a patched first.

prediction.note: A name you cannot guess. Put the pen on the paper and take single letters, not meaning.

teaching.answer_quote: Her surname is Gilroy. I'll spell it

distraction.signal: no, sorry, ignore that, there is no E in it
distraction.note: Cross the first attempt right out and take the second from the start. Patching a letter out of a half-written name loses the mark.

form.note: Six letters, no E. He says the whole name after spelling it, so use that as your check.

teaching.recovery: If the kit gap is blank, put a plural object and move. This one needs your pen down and your ear on single letters.

questions.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: What is the only piece of equipment the survey provides?
questions.explanation: 'Only piece of equipment' predicts one object, and he has already said volunteers bring everything else. 'The only thing we hand out' is the cue. He names the object and then defines it, so the answer is the noun before the definition, not the definition.

prediction.note: One object, probably a term you have never met, and it will be defined immediately afterwards.

signpost.phrase: The only thing we hand out

teaching.answer_quote: The only thing we hand out is a quadrat, which is a square metre frame

form.note: Quadrat, not quadrant. It ends -rat, and the definition he gives is what lets you hear that.

teaching.recovery: If the surname is unfinished, leave the box and come back in the check time. This half opens with the single word 'equipment'.

questions.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: Which weather condition stops a survey going ahead?
questions.explanation: 'Which weather condition' predicts one short word, and he lists three that do not stop it before the one that does. 'The one thing that stops us' is the endorsement. The reason he gives afterwards, about seeing the far post, confirms it.

prediction.note: One weather word, uncountable, so never an -s. Several harmless ones will be named first.

signpost.phrase: The one thing that stops us

teaching.answer_quote: The one thing that stops us is fog

form.note: One word, three letters, no -s. 'Foggy' is an adjective and does not fit the stem.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Marcus say happens to the completed survey sheets?

options.A: They are verified by a national scheme.
options.B: They have been collected for ten years.
options.C: They are used mainly by the local council.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect an assumption to be raised first. He confirms the council gets a copy and then says outright that this is not the point. What follows is where the data actually goes and who signs it off, which is the stem's answer.

prediction.note: One option will be true but not the point. Listen for the phrase 'and it isn't'.

signpost.phrase: and a lot of people assume that is the point

teaching.answer_quote: Everything goes to the national recording scheme, where a county recorder verifies it

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A figure for the survey's age is given at the very start, and any number in a talk this dense feels like an answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He says twenty-two years, not ten, and he says it in the opening sentence, nowhere near this question.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The council genuinely does receive a copy, and he says so in the sentence that opens the topic.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He raises the council only to deny it is the purpose: people assume that is the point, and it isn't.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Marcus say new volunteers most often do wrong?

options.A: They turn up after the survey has started.
options.B: They record nothing when they find nothing.
options.C: They cover the ground too quickly.

questions.explanation: 'Most often' predicts a ranking, so expect other real errors to be named. He forgives lateness in the same breath, and walking too fast was mentioned early and dismissed as self-correcting. The error he cannot undo is the empty sheet.

prediction.note: A ranking question. Two of these are real mistakes he mentions but does not rank first.

signpost.phrase: The one thing new people get wrong

teaching.answer_quote: You walk a stretch with nothing much on it and you write nothing down

paraphrase_link.printed: record nothing when they find nothing

distraction.signal: Lateness I can forgive
distraction.note: Lateness appears inside the answer sentence itself, which is exactly why it catches people. 'I can forgive' demotes it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Lateness is named in the same sentence as the answer, and a tide-dependent survey makes arriving late sound serious.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He forgives it explicitly in four words and then contrasts it with what he cannot undo.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He does say new people walk far too fast, and it is the only mistake described as typical of beginners.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He adds that it sorts itself out by the second survey, which rules it out of 'most often gets wrong'.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Marcus say about the training morning?

options.A: Everyone taking part has to attend it.
options.B: Only volunteers leading a team need it.
options.C: It can be completed online instead.

questions.explanation: 'About the training' is open, so predict a rule with an exception. He notes that several people have already booked and then says plainly that not everyone needs it. The split follows immediately: leaders yes, team members no. The online option is denied at the very end.

prediction.note: Expect a rule that applies to some people and not others. Listen for who signs something off.

teaching.answer_quote: If you're leading a team you do, because you're the one signing the sheet off

distraction.signal: there is no online version of the training
distraction.note: The online option appears only inside its own denial, and it appears after the answer. Do not revisit a settled item.

teaching.recovery: Last question. If the common-mistake item is still open, settle it on the ranking word 'most', not on what he named loudest.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He says several volunteers have already put their names down, which makes attendance sound like the default expectation.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The next sentence is 'You don't all need it', which cancels the option in four unstressed words.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A newsletter apparently said so, and learners hearing 'online version' in the final line assume it confirms the option.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He raises it only to deny it: there is no online version, whatever the newsletter said.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Marcus concedes a true thing before every answer he actually wants you to write, so five of these ten items reward waiting one clause longer than feels comfortable.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: The wrong option is named inside the answer sentence itself, four words before the thing that is actually being ranked first.

title: The Yarralea harvest festival programme

script_json.title: The Yarralea harvest festival programme
script_json.scenario: A festival committee member walks arriving visitors round the showground plan and then takes them through the weekend programme, the costs and the rules about dogs.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a member of a festival committee welcoming visitors to a country harvest festival. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Righto, welcome to Yarralea, and thanks for coming out. I'm Bec, I'm on the committee, which mostly means I carry things. There's a plan of the ground printed on the back of your ticket, and I'd get that out now, because this place is a good deal wider than it appears from the highway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So. We're standing just inside the main gate, and the information tent is the white one straight in front of you. Keep the gate behind you, the oval in the middle, and the river away over on your right. Every left and right I give you is from where you're standing this minute.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First thing on your left, before you even get to the information tent, is the produce tent. Jams, pumpkins, the biggest zucchini you will see in your life, and the judging's at ten on the Saturday morning if you want to watch grown adults argue about scones.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Directly opposite that, on your right, you'll see the ticket caravan, and the caravan isn't on your plan and never has been. What is on your plan, immediately behind the caravan, is the craft shed. Woodwork, quilts, and the bloke who plaits whips.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now walk up the left-hand side of the oval, past the grandstand. Right in the top corner on that side is the wood chop. No, hang on, that's not right, the wood chop is out on the oval itself. The thing in that top corner is the cooking stage.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Straight across the top of the ground, over on the other side, are the sheep yards. You'll smell those before you see them, and that is where the dog trial runs on the Sunday morning, so it's worth knowing where they are.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And then coming back down the river side, between the sheep yards and the gate, is the medical tent. That corner used to be the fire brigade display and it was for years, so if somebody tells you the truck's in there, it isn't, it's parked out on the road now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the ground. It looks enormous on paper and it takes about eight minutes to walk the whole way round, so nobody needs to panic about missing anything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, what's on and when. It's all in the program, which is two dollars from the information tent and worth it for the map alone. Sunday is much the quieter of the two days, and yes, you can bring the dog on either day, before anybody asks me that again.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The cooking stage. The demonstration is on the Friday, two o'clock, which surprises people because everything else is on the weekend, but the chef flies out on the Saturday morning and there's nothing anybody can do about that. It's free and there's seating for about eighty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sheepdog trial, Sunday morning, and that one you do pay for. It's five dollars a head, kids under twelve are free, and every cent of it goes to the flying doctor. Not fifteen, by the way. I've heard people saying fifteen and I have no idea where that started.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the night markets, both evenings, down along the river path with the lights in the trees. They run till late, but last entry is 9.30, because the gates are locked at ten and we have had people wander up at five to ten and be genuinely heartbroken.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Dogs. Look, half this town brings a dog. There's a sign at the gate that says no dogs, and that sign belongs to the sportsground, not to us, and I have asked for it to come down. Dogs are fine here. What we do ask is that anywhere near the sheep yards they're on a lead, and a short one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if you want one piece of advice off me. Get here at nine and walk the whole ground before anybody else is awake, because at eleven you will not be able to move. And no, you can't book a seat at the sheepdog trial. It doesn't work like that. You turn up and you stand where you can see.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's me. Bins are by the grandstand, there's water at the information tent, and if you lose a child, bring them to us and we'll keep them until somebody claims them. Have a lovely weekend.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Label the plan of the showground below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Bec walks one loop round the oval and never doubles back. Each answer puts you next to the following one.
teaching.strategy: The oval is the fixed point on this plan and every position sits round the edge of it. Fix the gate behind you and the river on your right before the audio starts, and the walk becomes a circle you can follow with a finger.
teaching.preview_focus: Find the gate, the oval, the grandstand, the information tent and the river. Then decide which numbers are near the gate and which are up at the top.
teaching.watch_out: Two things she names sit in the middle of the ground or off it entirely. Neither belongs in a numbered box round the edge.
spatial_cues: walk up the left-hand side of the oval
Straight across the top of the ground
coming back down the river side
between the sheep yards and the gate

groups.instruction: Complete the table below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Read across each row, then down. Reading down the When column mixes three different kinds of answer.
teaching.strategy: Four rows, three gaps, and every row is opened by its own name. The filled cells fix the shape of each gap before she speaks: a day, a figure in dollars, a clock time. Nothing in this table should surprise you.
teaching.preview_focus: Read the filled cells first. Two rows already print their day, so those rows cannot want one, and only the last row can want a time.
teaching.watch_out: The cost row carries three numbers in one breath, and only the printed word 'dollars' picks out the one that belongs in your box.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Dogs come before the closing advice, so 19 is finished the moment she says 'one piece of advice'.
teaching.strategy: Both of these are settled by Bec contradicting something: a sign at the gate, and an assumption that you can reserve a place. Listen for what she says belongs to somebody else, and for what she says does not work like that.
teaching.preview_focus: Read all six options and underline the absolutes: no, only, whole. Then decide whether each stem wants a rule or a recommendation.
teaching.watch_out: Marking an option because you heard its words. Both wrong options in this pair are spoken and then contradicted in the same sentence.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Bec say about bringing dogs to the festival?

options.A: Dogs are not permitted anywhere on the ground.
options.B: Dogs must be kept on a lead near the sheep yards.
options.C: Dogs are only allowed on the Sunday.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a sign to be quoted and dismissed. She explains that the no-dogs sign belongs to the sportsground and says dogs are fine here. 'What we do ask' is the endorsement frame, and one place gets a condition attached to it.

prediction.note: Expect a condition rather than a ban. A written sign will be quoted before the real rule.

teaching.answer_quote: anywhere near the sheep yards they're on a lead, and a short one

paraphrase_link.printed: kept on a lead near the sheep yards
paraphrase_link.audio: near the sheep yards they're on a lead

distraction.signal: There's a sign at the gate that says no dogs
distraction.note: A sign quoted inside the audio is a decoy, not a rule. Wait for the speaker's own present-tense sentence.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The words 'no dogs' are spoken aloud, and a sign at the gate is exactly the sort of thing a candidate treats as the answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says the sign belongs to the sportsground and she has asked for it to come down, then says dogs are fine.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Sunday is singled out twice, as the quieter day and as the day of the dog trial, so it feels attached to dogs.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says outright that you can bring the dog on either day, before anyone even asks the question.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Bec advise visitors to do?

options.A: arrive early and walk round the whole ground
options.B: buy a programme at the information tent
options.C: reserve a place at the sheepdog trial

questions.explanation: 'Advise' predicts a recommendation, and she marks it with 'one piece of advice off me'. The reason follows: by eleven you cannot move. The booking option is denied in the same line, and the programme was mentioned earlier as a purchase, not a recommendation.

prediction.note: A recommendation, not a rule. One of the three will be flatly denied in the same passage.

signpost.phrase: if you want one piece of advice off me

teaching.answer_quote: Get here at nine and walk the whole ground before anybody else is awake

paraphrase_link.printed: arrive early and walk round the whole ground
paraphrase_link.audio: Get here at nine and walk the whole ground

teaching.recovery: Last question on the page. If the dogs item is open, decide it now on the phrase 'what we do ask', not on the sign.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She recommends the programme warmly, calls it worth the money for the map alone, and gives its price.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That is information about what is on sale, given long before the advice frame arrives.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The sheepdog trial is the one ticketed event, and paid events are usually the ones you book.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says you cannot book a seat at all. You turn up and stand where you can see.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Five answers arrive only after a wrong value has been raised, and three of those wrong values come from something written down: a caravan, a sign, and a rumour about a price.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: The wrong name is placed in a corner and then moved to the middle of the oval, so both names share one direction.

title: Tutorial: planning a canteen food-waste project

script_json.title: Tutorial: planning a canteen food-waste project
script_json.scenario: Two students take the first draft of a food-waste project to their tutor, who dismantles their assumptions about access, measurement and the questionnaire, then rules on the extras they want to add.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Robyn and Dev, discussing a food waste project with their tutor, Doctor Ashfield. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Come in, both of you. Right, the food waste proposal. I've read it twice, and I want to start with something you've tucked away at the bottom of page two.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The bit about the kitchen.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The bit about the kitchen. You've written, and I'm quoting you here, we hope to have access to the kitchen. Hope isn't a research design. Has anybody actually said yes?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Um, sort of. I emailed the catering office. Well, the general address. Which I'm now realising is probably not the same thing at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It isn't. Her name's Ferris, she runs the canteen, and she answers her own email within a day. I've put us in for Thursday morning.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Good. Then that's the first thing that happens, before you buy a single set of scales. Everything else in this proposal is guesswork until she's said yes in writing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fine. So the plan is, we weigh what comes back on the plates. Every lunchtime, for a fortnight.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And the kitchen?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The kitchen's the same thing, though, isn't it? Food that nobody ate.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It really isn't. What comes back off a plate is a portioning problem. What gets cut off a carrot before service is a purchasing problem. Different causes, different fixes, and if you tip them into one bin you can't tell us anything about either.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we weigh them separately.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's two sets of scales, though. And I'd rather we did the plates properly than did both of them badly.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Mm. That's a fair worry, and I did wonder about telling you to drop the kitchen side altogether. But you've got four weeks, and Ferris will lend you her own scales. So, no.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Both, then.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Both, weighed separately, and that's the version I want to see on Monday.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Now. You originally pitched me a supermarket study. What happened to that?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: They said no. Well, not exactly no. The manager was quite keen, actually, but then head office wanted a form signed by somebody who doesn't even work in the building.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And it would have been six weeks of waiting for that signature. We've got four weeks in total.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Which is the right call, and I want it in your write-up. A project that dies on paperwork is a finding about the sector, not a failure on your part.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Can I ask about the questionnaire?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Go on.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's twelve questions at the moment. We wanted to ask people what they think about food waste generally.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And they'll all tell you it's terrible, and then scrape half a plate into the bin. Everybody's opinion on waste is excellent. Their behaviour isn't. Ask them what they had, how hungry they were when they queued, and whether they finished it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: When do we hand it out? While they're queuing?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Catch them on the way to the bins, when they can see what they've left. In the queue they're guessing.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So less attitude, more what actually happened.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: More what actually happened, and four questions maximum. That's the questionnaire I'll sign off.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One more thing. Dev wants photographs of the trays coming back.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: For the poster, mainly. I'm not counting anything off them.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then take them. But you don't need ethics approval to weigh a bin, and you do need it the moment a photograph could identify somebody. A tray with a phone sitting on it identifies somebody. Get the form in this week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: This week. Understood.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. You've got a list at the back of things you'd like to add if there's time. Let's go through them, because some of them are free and some of them are a whole term's work.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First one's the delivery records. What the kitchen orders in, week by week.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Ferris keeps those on a spreadsheet and she'll email them to you on Thursday. Take them. That's one afternoon of your life and it doubles the size of your data set.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then interviews with the serving staff. They watch what comes back all day, every day.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: They do, and it's the most interesting thing on your list. It's also four consent forms, a transcription, and a coding scheme you haven't been taught yet. Not in four weeks.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Not this time, then.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Third. A pilot day.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Just to check the scales work and the tray trolley doesn't get emptied before we reach it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Do it. But not the way you've described it, because you've written pilot day as though it's a rehearsal. It isn't. Decide beforehand what would make you change the method, and write that down, or you'll pilot it, find something awkward, and carry on regardless.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fourth. We wondered about running the same fortnight in the halls kitchen, so we'd have a comparison.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Mm. Two sites, half the depth. And the halls kitchen is self-catering, so you'd be setting a canteen against three hundred people cooking for themselves. That isn't a comparison, it's a second project.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Fair enough.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And the last thing on the list, the online survey of the whole department.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That was mine. Two hundred responses instead of forty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It would be two hundred responses about how people feel, and we've just spent twenty minutes agreeing that feelings aren't your data. Although. If you asked one thing, one, how many days a week do you eat here, you'd have a denominator. Do that, and only that, and think hard about the wording.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One question. How many days a week.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Exactly that. Right. Monday, the revised proposal, and Ferris's yes in writing. Off you go.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: The five answers arrive in the order they are printed. Once she reaches the questionnaire, twenty-one has gone.
teaching.strategy: All three options in each of these is said out loud by somebody in the room. Do not listen for the option's words; listen for which one the tutor stands behind, and for the four-word clauses that quietly cancel the other two.
teaching.preview_focus: Underline the question word in each stem: must do first, finally decide, why, focus on, say about. Read all fifteen options before the audio starts, not while it runs.
teaching.watch_out: Every wrong option here is spoken by a student. The tutor is the only voice whose verdict counts.

groups.instruction: What does Doctor Ashfield decide about each of the following additions? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.

teaching.order_note: She takes the list in the order it is printed. If you hear the online survey, the pilot day has gone.
teaching.strategy: Three verdicts, five items, and she never uses any of the three printed words. What she gives you instead is a shape: praise, then a cost, then either go ahead, plan it again, or leave it out entirely.
teaching.preview_focus: Letters can repeat, so do not cross any off. Decide what more planning would sound like: a condition, a but, an instruction about how rather than whether.
teaching.watch_out: Two items get warm praise before the verdict lands. Take the verdict from the tutor, never the enthusiasm from a student.
teaching.bank_note: Every letter is used at least once and two of them twice. A letter you have not used yet is a hint, not a rule.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Ashfield say the students must do first?

options.A: buy the equipment they need
options.B: obtain written permission from the canteen manager
options.C: contact the catering office

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three actions to be named aloud. The tutor's phrase that's the first thing that happens marks the instruction, and she defines it as a yes in writing. The email has already been sent, so it cannot be a next step. Take the endorsed action, not the mentioned one.

prediction.note: The stem says first, so listen for an ordering word, not for the most important-sounding task.

signpost.phrase: that's the first thing that happens

teaching.answer_quote: Everything else in this proposal is guesswork until she's said yes in writing

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Scales are the only concrete equipment in the discussion, and buying them sounds like the obvious opening move in a weighing study.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She names the scales only to say what must happen before you buy them.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Dev describes emailing the catering office in his own words, so a learner matching on catering hears an action attached to the right topic.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That email has already been sent, and both other speakers say it went to the wrong place.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What do they finally decide about the two kinds of waste?

options.A: to collect them in a single container
options.B: to record them as two separate measurements
options.C: to leave the kitchen waste out

questions.explanation: Predict a settled outcome, because the stem says finally. The tutor floats dropping the kitchen side, then refuses her own suggestion, and the agreed version is stated last and shortest. Single-bin collection is only ever described as the thing that would destroy the data. Take the quiet closing line.

prediction.note: Finally means the last position stated, and in a tutorial the settled one is usually the shortest.

signpost.phrase: that's the version I want to see

teaching.answer_quote: Both, weighed separately, and that's the version I want to see on Monday

distraction.signal: I did wonder about telling you to drop the kitchen side
distraction.note: She voices the option she is about to refuse. Hold your pen until somebody says what they will actually do.

teaching.recovery: If twenty-one went past, restart here: she asks And the kitchen out loud, and that question opens this one.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Dev argues that plate waste and kitchen waste are the same thing, and one bin is the simplest reading of that claim.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The tutor uses one bin as her example of what would make the data useless.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The tutor herself says she considered telling them to drop the kitchen side, and it is the loudest sentence in the exchange.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She reports considering it and then rejects it in two words: So, no.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Why did the students abandon their supermarket study?

options.A: The store manager was unwilling.
options.B: The approval would have taken too long.
options.C: Their tutor had advised against it.

questions.explanation: The stem asks why, so predict a reason and expect more than one to be offered. Dev opens with They said no and takes it back in the same breath. The reason that survives is arithmetic: six weeks of waiting against four weeks of project. Take the reason nobody withdraws.

prediction.note: A why stem in Part three nearly always gets two reasons, one of which is withdrawn.

signpost.phrase: but then head office wanted a form signed

teaching.answer_quote: it would have been six weeks of waiting for that signature

distraction.signal: Well, not exactly no
distraction.note: Three words undo the first sentence. When a speaker restates, stop writing and wait for the version that survives.

teaching.recovery: Lost this one? Move your eyes to twenty-four now: Robyn asks about the questionnaire and that question opens the next item.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Dev's first two words are They said no, and a refusal is exactly what the stem invites you to listen for.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He corrects himself immediately and says the manager was keen.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The tutor says Which is the right call, so a learner hears her approving and back-dates the advice to before the decision.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She is endorsing a decision she is hearing about for the first time in this tutorial.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Ashfield want the questionnaire to focus on?

options.A: opinions about food waste in general
options.B: what people did with their own meal
options.C: the time people spend queuing

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the printed words to be planted in a wrong option. Dev says the exact phrase in option A one turn early. The tutor's contrast, opinion excellent, behaviour not, announces her preference, and she then lists three questions that are all about the meal in front of you.

prediction.note: Focus on means a preference, so wait for a contrast pair: not this, but that.

signpost.phrase: Everybody's opinion on waste is excellent. Their behaviour isn't.

teaching.answer_quote: Ask them what they had, how hungry they were when they queued, and whether they finished it

paraphrase_link.printed: what people did with their own meal

distraction.signal: what they think about food waste generally
distraction.note: The option's own words are spoken, by the wrong speaker, as the thing about to be rejected. Check who said it.

teaching.recovery: If you were still weighing this, jump on the word photographs. That single noun opens the last question of the set.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Dev speaks the option almost word for word, and a learner matching printed words to spoken words gets a perfect hit.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It is the students' current draft, and the tutor's whole answer is an argument against it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Queuing is mentioned twice in thirty seconds, once inside the tutor's own list of good questions.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She talks about when to hand the form out, not about measuring how long anyone queued.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Ashfield say about the photographs?

options.A: They will need ethics approval.
options.B: They will not be used in the analysis.
options.C: They can be taken without extra paperwork.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and predict a negative, because permission questions are usually answered with a not first. She says no approval is needed to weigh a bin, then flips: you do need it the moment a photograph could identify somebody. The mark sits in the second half of one sentence.

prediction.note: Say about is a wide stem, so the deciding word will be a small one: do, don't, only, unless.

signpost.phrase: you don't need ethics approval to weigh a bin

teaching.answer_quote: you do need it the moment a photograph could identify somebody

paraphrase_link.audio: you do need it the moment a photograph

distraction.signal: Then take them
distraction.note: Two clauses, opposite polarity, one breath. Wait for the full stop before you commit to a permission answer.

teaching.recovery: Nothing else is asked in this half, so guess from the slot in the check minute and leave no box empty.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Dev says outright that the photographs are for the poster and that he is not counting anything off them, which answers a question nobody asked.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It is true, and it is Dev's statement, not the tutor's, and the stem asks what she says.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Her reply opens with Then take them, and the next clause opens with a denial about approval, so the ear stops on permission granted.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That clause is about weighing the bins. Photographs are the exception she names in the same sentence.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Ashfield decide about each of the following additions? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: The kitchen's delivery records

options.A: Go ahead with it as planned.
options.B: Plan it in more detail first.
options.C: Leave it out of this project.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a cost to be named for every item. Here she names none. Take them is an instruction with no condition attached, and the two reasons that follow are both in favour. This is the calibration item: it tells you what an unqualified yes sounds like in her mouth.

prediction.note: Listen for a condition. No condition and no but means the plain go-ahead letter.

teaching.answer_quote: she'll email them to you on Thursday. Take them

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She opens the section by warning that some items are a whole term's work, which primes the ear for a refusal.

options.A: Go ahead with it as planned.

She calls this the most interesting item on the list, which is the warmest thing she says all tutorial, then prices it in consent forms and training they have not had. Not in four weeks is the verdict, and it is four words long.

prediction.note: Praise is not a verdict. Wait for the word that turns the sentence: also, but, however.

teaching.answer_quote: a coding scheme you haven't been taught yet. Not in four weeks

distraction.signal: it's the most interesting thing on your list
distraction.note: The praise and the refusal share one turn. Score the last clause, never the warmest one.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: They do, and it's the most interesting thing on your list is an eight-word endorsement, and it arrives first.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The very next word is also, and everything after it is a cost she says they cannot meet.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Consent forms, transcription and coding all sound like planning tasks, so the item reads as merely underprepared.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She does not ask for a better plan. She rules it out for this project in four words.

option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The next word is But, and she then rewrites what a pilot day has to contain.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The tray trolley problem sounds fatal, so a learner who catches only the difficulty hears an item being written off.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Robyn describes the plan fluently and nobody interrupts her, so the proposal sounds accepted by default.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Silence during a proposal is not agreement. The tutor's verdict arrives in the following turn.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The self-catering objection sounds like a design flaw that better matching of the two sites could repair.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She calls it a second project, which removes it from this one rather than rescheduling it.

option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Two conditions ride on it: one question only, and the wording has to be reworked.

title: Tutorial feedback: a report on remote call-centre work

script_json.title: Tutorial feedback: a report on remote call-centre work
script_json.scenario: A professor gives two students feedback on a draft report about a call center's move to remote working, then rules on which of their six data sources can be used and where each one belongs.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Jodie and Trent, discussing a draft report with their professor, Professor Linden. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: OK, come on in. So, this is the draft on remote work at the call center, and I'd rather be useful than polite, so I'll start with the thing that costs you the most points.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The conclusion.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: No, actually, the conclusion is the best page in here. It's the research question. You've asked whether remote work improved performance, and then you've measured four different things and called all of them performance.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Handle time and resolution rate, yeah.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Plus absence. And turnover.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Two of those are performance. Two of them are retention. They can move in opposite directions, and in your own data they do. So the question has to name which one you're testing, or the report spends nine pages arguing with itself.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we pick one.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You pick one, and you say why. Let's be specific. Which one does the company actually care about?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Turnover. They said so in the first meeting. They lose about a third of the floor every year, and it costs a fortune to train replacements.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then that's your question, and everything else in here becomes context. Three sentences of rewriting, and this is a much better report.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Can I ask about the literature section? I put in eleven sources and it still felt thin.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It is thin, but not because eleven isn't enough. It's thin because nine of them agree with you.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Isn't that good?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It's comfortable. There's a whole literature saying remote work makes call centers worse, and you've cited one paper from it, in a footnote, and moved on. Half of what you do cite is about office teams anyway. Bring that argument into the body and answer it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hold on. If we bring in the counter-argument, doesn't that weaken our own conclusion?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The opposite. An argument that has never met an objection isn't an argument, it's a preference. And your grader has read that literature.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. And the referencing? I think I mixed two versions of the department style.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You did, and it's the one thing in here the rubric marks mechanically. Pick the version on the syllabus and be boring about it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Could we ask for an extension?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You could, and I'd probably give you one, but then you'd be revising in the middle of your other finals.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The department deadline is the twenty-eighth. Don't aim for that. Aim for the Friday before, because the writing center is booked solid for the last three days of every semester.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The raw material. You've listed six things at the back of the draft. Let's take them in the order you've got them, because two of them have a problem.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The turnover file first. Human resources sent it over as a spreadsheet.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one's your spine. It goes back five years, it's already anonymized, and I'd build the whole results section around it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then the exit interviews. Those are pretty personal.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Those are fine, actually. Human resources ran them, everybody signed a consent form at the time, and the names came off before you ever saw them. Use them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And Marcus's notes? He's the team leader on nights, and he wrote down what people told him about working from home.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And did any of those people know they were being written down? No. So the team leader's notes stay in your drawer until Marcus goes back and asks them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then the shift logs. About four hundred rows of clock-in times.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Four hundred rows isn't a finding, it's an exhibit. One summary table in the body, and the rows themselves go at the back where nobody has to read them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The customer survey's ours. We ran it in March.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You did, and it's the freshest thing in the pile. Two pages of it in the body, please, not eleven.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the benchmark report? The industry one, with the sector averages.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Which edition?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The one on the association's website.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That edition is six years old, and the whole sector changed after it came out. Cite it if you want a before picture, but you can't use it as your comparison, because it describes a world that stopped existing.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Two more things. Trent, in your email you said you'd redo the graphs.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I said tables. The graphs are Jodie's.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The graphs are mine, and honestly they're the bit I'm least sure about.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then start with them. Every graph in here needs a caption that says what the reader is supposed to notice, not just what the axes are.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And when do we see you again?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Come to office hours on Tuesday, both of you, and bring the rewritten question on one sheet of paper. Not the whole draft. One sheet.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: One sheet. Got it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Good. And Trent, the tables. Tuesday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Five answers, one section of feedback each, in the printed order. When she reaches referencing, twenty-three has gone.
teaching.strategy: Feedback tutorials run on a fixed rhythm: a student names a worry, the professor accepts a fragment of it and replaces the rest. The keyed answer is always her replacement, never the student's version of the problem.
teaching.preview_focus: Mark who each stem asks about. Four of these five ask what the professor says, so a student's sentence can never be the answer however well it fits.
teaching.watch_out: Both students diagnose their own draft out loud, and both diagnoses are wrong in a way that sounds modest.

groups.instruction: Which source does Professor Linden describe in each of the following ways? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A to F, next to questions 26 to 28. You may not need to use all the letters.

teaching.order_note: The six sources are taken in the order the students listed them, so each letter is decided and then gone.
teaching.strategy: Here the printed stems are the paraphrases and the box is the plain speech: she names each source out loud. Listen for her verdict, then find the letter, and never try to hold all six verdicts in your head at once.
teaching.preview_focus: Read the three stems and turn each into one word: permission, appendix, out of date. Three words is what you can actually hold for two minutes of audio.
teaching.watch_out: Three letters are never used, and each of the three is built to look right for exactly one stem.
teaching.bank_note: Three of the six are never keyed. Each of those three is set up to look like the answer to exactly one of the stems.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

teaching.order_note: These two close the tutorial, so they arrive in the last forty seconds, one after the other.
teaching.strategy: Two gaps, and the grammar around each one has already told you what shape the word is. After ten minutes of letters your hand will want to write a letter here, so re-read the instruction line before the audio restarts.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type both gaps in the pause: a is a singular noun, a possessive before the gap is a thing belonging to the professor.
teaching.watch_out: A plural on the first gap and a three-word phrase on the second are the two cheap ways to lose these.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Professor Linden say is the main weakness of the draft?

options.A: The conclusion is not supported by the evidence.
options.B: The research question is too broad.
options.C: Two of the measures point in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the students to guess first. Jodie offers the conclusion; the professor says no and names the research question instead. Four things measured and all four called performance is what too broad means here. The opposite-directions point is the symptom she then describes, not the weakness she names.

prediction.note: Main weakness means one thing, so expect the other two options to be true but smaller.

teaching.answer_quote: You've asked whether remote work improved performance, and then you've measured four different things

paraphrase_link.audio: measured four different things and called all of them performance

distraction.signal: The conclusion.
distraction.note: A student answers the question before the tutor does. Treat a student's guess as a decoy until the tutor confirms it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Jodie says the word conclusion in the silence where the answer should be, and a learner keys the first noun that fills the slot.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The professor calls the conclusion the best page in the draft.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She does say the measures move in opposite directions, and it is the most technical-sounding sentence in the exchange.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That is the consequence of the loose question, and she uses it as evidence for the answer.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What do they agree the report should measure?

options.A: how quickly calls are handled
options.B: how many staff leave
options.C: how often staff are absent

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and note that all four candidate measures are read out early, so option spotting is worthless. Her question, which one does the company care about, is the signpost. Trent answers with the company's own reason: a third of the floor gone every year. Clean item, and it rewards waiting for the reason.

prediction.note: Agree means look for the second speaker to confirm, not for the loudest single claim.

signpost.phrase: Which one does the company actually care about?

teaching.answer_quote: They lose about a third of the floor every year, and it costs a fortune to train replacements

paraphrase_link.audio: They lose about a third of the floor every year

teaching.recovery: If twenty-one is still nagging, drop it. Jodie says So we pick one, and the answer to twenty-two lands in the next turn.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Handle time is the first measure named in the whole discussion, and first-mentioned is the commonest wrong reflex in this paper.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It is one of four measures listed, and nobody attaches the company's interest to it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Absence is the measure that sounds most like a people problem, which is what a company worried about staff would obviously track.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Jodie lists it and drops it. Nobody attaches a cost or a company view to it.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What is Professor Linden's criticism of the literature section?

options.A: It contains too few sources.
options.B: Most of the sources take the same position.
options.C: Too many sources are about office-based teams.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and watch the ownership of the complaint. Jodie says the section felt thin, which is her diagnosis, not the professor's. The professor keeps the word thin and changes the cause: nine of eleven agree with you. The office-teams point is a second remark, made in passing.

prediction.note: The stem names the professor, so a student's self-criticism cannot be the key however true it sounds.

signpost.phrase: but not because eleven isn't enough

teaching.answer_quote: It's thin because nine of them agree with you

paraphrase_link.audio: nine of them agree with you

distraction.signal: I put in eleven sources and it still felt thin
distraction.note: The student supplies a diagnosis one turn early. Park it, and wait for the tutor to keep or replace the cause.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Jodie says thin, gives a number, and the professor's first two words are It is thin, which sounds like agreement.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Her next clause denies the count is the problem: not because eleven isn't enough.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She really does say half the citations are about office teams, and it is the last criticism in the turn, so it is freshest.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It arrives after the word anyway, which marks an aside rather than the criticism she is making.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Why does Professor Linden want the counter-argument in the report?

options.A: It will make the conclusion stronger.
options.B: The assignment brief requires it.
options.C: It will show that they have read widely.

questions.explanation: The stem asks why, so predict a reason, and Trent has just supplied the wrong one by asking whether it weakens the conclusion. Her single word Opposite is the whole answer, and the sentence after it explains the mechanism. Reading widely is a side benefit she mentions last, about the grader, not about the argument.

prediction.note: A why stem after a student's worry is nearly always answered by reversing the worry.

teaching.answer_quote: An argument that has never met an objection isn't an argument, it's a preference

paraphrase_link.audio: An argument that has never met an objection isn't an argument

distraction.signal: And your grader has read that literature
distraction.note: True, and about a different person. Check the stem's question word before you take the last thing said.

teaching.recovery: If this one went, the next stem is about submitting. Jodie's word extension is your cue that twenty-five has started.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She invokes the rubric out loud half a minute later, and a learner ties the nearest requirement to the nearest question.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The rubric sentence is about referencing style, and nobody says the brief demands a counter-argument.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Her final clause names the grader and the literature together, which is exactly what showing wide reading sounds like.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That clause tells them who will notice. The reason she gives is what an objection does to an argument.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Professor Linden advise about handing the report in?

options.A: to submit it before the official deadline
options.B: to apply for an extension
options.C: to use the writing center in the final week

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect two dates, because deadline advice always names the official one first. She gives the twenty-eighth, cancels it in three words, and names the Friday before. The extension she offers and then talks them out of, and the writing center is her reason, not her advice.

prediction.note: Advice stems reward the imperative. Listen for aim, don't, come, and ignore everything descriptive.

teaching.answer_quote: Aim for the Friday before, because the writing center is booked solid

distraction.signal: Don't aim for that
distraction.note: The official date is spoken so it can be cancelled. The date that survives is the one with an imperative in front of it.

teaching.recovery: This closes the first half. Use the pause to guess anything blank, then read the six sources in the box before she starts.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She says outright that she would probably grant one, which is as close to an offer as a tutor ever gets.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The word but follows immediately, and she describes revising during finals as the cost of taking it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The writing center is named in the same sentence as the answer, and using it sounds like sensible advice.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says it is fully booked in the final days, which is the reason for finishing early, not a recommendation.

questions.instruction: Which source does Professor Linden describe in each of the following ways? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A to F, next to questions 26 to 28. You may not need to use all the letters.
questions.prompt: It cannot be used until the people in it have been asked.

options.A: the customer survey
options.B: the exit interviews
options.C: the HR turnover file

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect consent to be raised about the wrong source first. Trent flags the exit interviews as personal and the professor clears them. The notes fail on one test only: nobody in them knew they were being recorded. Her rhetorical question is the signal, and the verdict follows it in one clause.

prediction.note: Permission questions turn on whether people knew, not on how private the material sounds.

signpost.phrase: And did any of those people know they were being written down?

teaching.answer_quote: the team leader's notes stay in your drawer until Marcus goes back and asks them

paraphrase_link.audio: the team leader's notes stay in your drawer

teaching.recovery: If twenty-five is still open, leave it. Each source is announced by name by a student, so the next letter always has a spoken label.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is the only source the students collected from members of the public themselves, which sounds like the consent-heavy one.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She calls it the freshest thing in the pile and asks for two pages of it in the body.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Trent says they are pretty personal, which is the exact worry this stem describes, and he says it first.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The professor clears them: consent forms were signed and the names were removed before the students saw them.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Staff records sound like the most confidential item on any list of six.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says it is already anonymized and makes it the spine of the results section.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Published material feels like the kind of thing you need permission to reproduce.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Her objection to it is age, and she explicitly allows them to cite it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Clock-in times are about identifiable individuals, so a learner reasoning from privacy alone lands here.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She never raises consent about them. Her whole objection is that four hundred rows belong at the back.

questions.instruction: Which source does Professor Linden describe in each of the following ways? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A to F, next to questions 26 to 28. You may not need to use all the letters.
questions.prompt: It belongs in an appendix rather than in the body of the report.

options.A: the customer survey
options.B: the exit interviews
options.C: the HR turnover file

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and listen for the word back, which is her shorthand for an appendix. Four hundred rows is an exhibit is the judgement, and the instruction splits the source in two: a summary table in the body, the rows at the back. Only one source gets that treatment.

prediction.note: The word appendix is never spoken. She says at the back, which is the same instruction in plainer words.

signpost.phrase: Four hundred rows isn't a finding, it's an exhibit

teaching.answer_quote: the rows themselves go at the back where nobody has to read them
teaching.recovery: Lost this one? The next stem is about age, and the word edition is spoken twice before that answer arrives.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She tells them to cut it down, and cutting a source down sounds like moving most of it out of the body.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She asks for two pages of it in the body, which is the opposite instruction.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Interview transcripts are long, and long things feel like appendix material by default.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She says only Use them, with no instruction about where they go.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is a spreadsheet, and raw spreadsheets are the classic appendix item.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She calls it the spine and builds the whole results section on it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She restricts it to a before picture, which sounds like relegating it to the back.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: A restriction on what it can prove is not an instruction about where it sits.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Material she refuses to let them quote sounds like something to file at the back out of the way.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She keeps it out of the report entirely, drawer included, not merely out of the body.

questions.instruction: Which source does Professor Linden describe in each of the following ways? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A to F, next to questions 26 to 28. You may not need to use all the letters.
questions.prompt: It no longer describes the industry accurately.

options.A: the customer survey
options.B: the exit interviews
options.C: the HR turnover file

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect an age word. Her question, which edition, is the signpost, and six years old is the finding. Then she half-licenses it: cite it as a before picture. That permission is the trap, because it is permission to do something the stem is not asking about.

prediction.note: Two sources have dates attached. Only one has a date she treats as a problem.

signpost.phrase: but you can't use it as your comparison

teaching.answer_quote: you can't use it as your comparison, because it describes a world that stopped existing

distraction.decoy: using the benchmark as the comparison
distraction.signal: Cite it if you want a before picture
distraction.note: She grants one use and bans another in one sentence. Hold the letter until you hear which use she is banning.

teaching.recovery: The letters are finished after this. Move your eyes to the two sentence gaps now, because their answers arrive quickly.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is the only source with a month attached to it, and dates on the page invite the age question.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: March is this year, and she calls it the freshest thing in the pile.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Exit interviews are historical by definition, since everyone in them has already left.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Nobody raises their age. The only question about them is consent, and it is answered.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: She says it goes back five years, which is the only other number of years in the whole discussion.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: A five-year run is the point of a turnover file, and she builds the results on it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Four hundred rows of old clock-in times sound like the most dated material on the list.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Nothing is said about when they were collected. Her objection is length.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Notes from the night shift feel like a snapshot of a moment that has passed.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: They are ruled out on consent, and she offers a route to using them later.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: Every graph in the report needs a ______ explaining what the reader should notice.
questions.explanation: Predict a singular noun, because the printed a fixes it. Then start with them announces the instruction, and the word arrives three words later. She defines it in the same breath, which is how you spell it: a line under a graph telling the reader what to see. One word, no plural.

prediction.note: One thing per graph, and the printed a rules out a plural however many graphs there are.

teaching.answer_quote: Every graph in here needs a caption that says what the reader is supposed to notice

paraphrase_link.printed: explaining what the reader should notice
paraphrase_link.audio: says what the reader is supposed to notice

form.note: Captions is wrong even though there are several graphs. The printed a decides the number, not the audio.

teaching.recovery: If the letters overran into this gap, listen for Jodie asking when they meet again. Thirty is answered in the reply.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: On Tuesday the students will bring one sheet of paper to Professor Linden's ______.
questions.explanation: Predict a place or a time slot, because a possessive stands in front of the gap. Jodie's question is the cue, and the answer is the first thing in the reply. Tuesday and one sheet are both printed already, so anything you write beyond the two words is over the limit.

prediction.note: A possessive before the gap means a thing belonging to her, so two words at most.

signpost.phrase: And when do we see you again?

teaching.answer_quote: Come to office hours on Tuesday, both of you

form.note: Two words. Adding on Tuesday takes you to four and scores zero, and Tuesday is already printed.

teaching.recovery: Last gap on the paper. In the check half-minute, fill anything blank from its slot type rather than leaving a zero.

what_makes_this_hard.note: The students diagnose their own draft out loud and both diagnoses are wrong. Six named sources then arrive in ninety seconds, and only three of them are keyed anywhere.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: She permits one use of the report and forbids another inside a single sentence, and the permission comes first.

a signed agreement to have your words used
evidence shown at the back, not discussed
typical figures across a whole industry
the marking scheme the grader works from
completely full, with no slots left
set times when a tutor sees students without an appointment

Which one does the company actually care about?
but not because eleven isn't enough
Let's take them in the order you've got them
And did any of those people know they were being written down?
