title: Choosing a method for a campus cycling study

script_json.title: Choosing a method for a campus cycling study
script_json.scenario: Two students bring five possible research methods for a study of why people stop cycling to university, and their supervisor cuts the list down before turning to the design of the survey itself.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Tegan and Hamish, discussing research methods for a cycling study with their supervisor, Doctor Brennan. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Righto, come in, both of you. So, the cycling project. You've got four possible methods on this sheet and about seven weeks, so we're going to lose some of them this morning.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Five, actually. I added the app one on the tram this morning?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Five. Even better. Start me off with the survey, because that's the one you've already drafted.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Online. We'd push it out through the faculty mailing lists, and put a poster up in the bike cage.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And how many responses would you need before it told you anything at all?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Two hundred. We'd probably get four hundred, because everyone on this campus has an opinion about the bike cage.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then that's your backbone. Everything else you do this semester hangs off it, and it's the only one of the five that gets you numbers you can put in a table.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the interviews? I wanted to sit down with people who've stopped riding.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: So did I, at your age. How long is each one?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Forty minutes? Maybe an hour once you've transcribed it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: An hour each, twenty people, and there goes your whole mid-semester break. Do six.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Six isn't a sample.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Six isn't a sample, no. Six is where your quotes come from, and your quotes are what make the survey numbers mean something to a reader. Different job entirely.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fair.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then the gate counts. There's a sensor on the footpath by the sports centre, and I reckon we could sit there with a clicker on a couple of mornings as well.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Hang on. If there's already a sensor, then somebody already has that number. Ring facilities, ask for last year's, and don't spend a single morning of your life counting bikes by hand.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we drop the counting.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You drop the counting and you keep the number. Those are two different sentences.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Trip diaries next. A fortnight, and everyone writes down every trip they make.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Everyone won't. Ten people will, if you buy them coffee, and ten good fortnights of diaries would be the most interesting thing in your write-up. Ten. Not everyone.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the app? It'd track the routes automatically.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It would, and it'd also track them to their GP, their house and their Friday night. You'd need a separate ethics application for that, and the committee doesn't sit again until week nine.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Week nine's too late.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Week nine is after your data collection finishes. So that one's gone, and I'd say so in your methods chapter. Explaining what you couldn't do is worth marks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The survey itself. You've got twenty-six questions in this draft, which is about twenty too many, but I want to talk about the first one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Do you ride to uni. Yes or no.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And what do you do with everybody who says no?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Nothing. They're not our population.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: They're exactly your population. Your question is why people stop, so the interesting person is the one who used to ride and doesn't. If your first question sends them to the end of the form, you've thrown the study away.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we make it a frequency? Never, sometimes, used to, still do?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's better, and it's one question doing the work of two.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The sample, though. We're pushing it through the faculty lists, so that's engineering and science mostly.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Which is where most of the bikes are, so I can see why. But your finding will be about engineering students, not about the campus.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We could hand out cards at the tram stop. The Parkes Road one. Sorry, no, not Parkes Road, the other one, by the sports centre. That's where the riders actually come past.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Do that. And print them properly, don't rely on a code they have to scan, because half of them won't stop long enough.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: When should we open it?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Not in week one. Everybody's timetable is still moving in week one and half of them haven't found the bike cage yet.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And not the week before the mid-semester break, because nobody rides in the week before a break. Week four. Two weeks open, then close it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Do we have to tell people we're recording the interviews?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Someone in our tutorial said you have to write your own consent form for every project.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Someone in your tutorial is wrong. Hamish, you did Doctor Mowbray's methods unit last year. She'll have a template, and hers has already been approved. Use that one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what's the one thing you'd tell us not to do?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Don't start writing your methods chapter at the end. Write it as you go, this week, while you can still remember why you dropped the app. In six weeks you won't, and the examiner marks the reasoning, not the data.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: This week.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: This week. Off you go. And no worries about the app, it was a good idea, it's just the wrong term for it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: What does Doctor Brennan decide about each of the following methods? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.

teaching.order_note: The five methods are taken in the order they are printed, one verdict each, and none of them is revisited.
teaching.strategy: He asks the same two questions of every method: what would it get you, and what would it cost you in weeks. The verdict is always the second answer, and it is usually one short imperative.
teaching.preview_focus: Letters repeat here, so cross nothing off. Decide in advance what a small number sounds like: a figure under twenty, or a word like a handful.
teaching.watch_out: Two methods survive in a smaller form than the students proposed. Shrinking a method is not the same as dropping it.
teaching.bank_note: One letter is used once and the other two are used twice. Nobody says main, small or ruled out aloud.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Five answers across the second half, in the order he raises them: wording, sample, timing, consent, next step.
teaching.strategy: In this half he is repairing the survey, so every stem has a design decision behind it. Two of the five are proposed by a student and only confirmed by him, so keep tracking who is speaking even after the letters start.
teaching.preview_focus: Read the five stems and notice three of them ask what he advises. Underline advises, decide and should, then read all fifteen options once.
teaching.watch_out: Two options quote instructions he really gave, but gave about a different part of the project and at a different time.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Brennan decide about each of the following methods? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: an online survey

options.A: It will be the project's main method.
options.B: It will be used with a small number of people only.
options.C: It has been ruled out.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and expect the first item to be the one that sets your calibration. He asks what the survey would get them, hears a number, and calls it the backbone that everything else hangs off. No cost is named and no condition is attached, so this is what an unqualified yes sounds like.

prediction.note: The method the others depend on is the main one, whatever order it is discussed in.

teaching.answer_quote: Then that's your backbone. Everything else you do this semester hangs off it

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Two hundred and four hundred are both said aloud, and a learner listening only for numbers hears a sample size being negotiated.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Those figures are what makes it the big method, not a restriction on it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He opens by warning that some methods are going to be lost this morning, which primes a refusal for whatever comes first.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The warning is about the list. This is the item he builds everything else on.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Brennan decide about each of the following methods? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: face-to-face interviews

options.A: It will be the project's main method.
options.B: It will be used with a small number of people only.
options.C: It has been ruled out.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a number. He does the arithmetic out loud, an hour times twenty, and the figure that survives is the second one. Do six is two words and it is the whole verdict. Hamish then argues it is not a sample, which is true and is not a refusal.

prediction.note: When two numbers are spoken for one method, the smaller and later one is nearly always the decision.

teaching.answer_quote: An hour each, twenty people, and there goes your whole mid-semester break. Do six

distraction.signal: twenty people
distraction.note: He says twenty to price it, not to plan it. The number attached to an imperative is the one that counts.

teaching.recovery: If twenty-one is still open, let it go. Tegan names each method aloud before he answers, so the next one has a spoken label.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He says the quotes are what make the survey numbers mean something, which sounds like promoting the interviews above them.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He calls it a different job, and the survey is the thing the quotes are attached to.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Six isn't a sample is spoken flatly by Hamish and repeated by the supervisor, which sounds like the method collapsing.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He repeats it in order to agree with the words and reject the conclusion. The six stay.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Brennan decide about each of the following methods? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: counting riders by hand at the gates

options.A: It will be the project's main method.
options.B: It will be used with a small number of people only.
options.C: It has been ruled out.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and read the stem carefully: it says by hand. Hang on marks the objection, and the reason is that a sensor already produces the number. He then splits the two things apart in the next turn, keeping the data and dropping the morning of clicking.

prediction.note: The stem names the activity, not the data. A number can survive while the way of getting it does not.

teaching.answer_quote: don't spend a single morning of your life counting bikes by hand

paraphrase_link.audio: don't spend a single morning of your life counting bikes

distraction.decoy: sitting at the sensor with a clicker
distraction.signal: sit there with a clicker on a couple of mornings
distraction.note: Hamish proposes it in detail and nobody objects for a full turn. Silence during a proposal is not agreement.

teaching.recovery: Missed it? He immediately restates the split: you drop the counting and you keep the number. That sentence gives you the verdict again.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Gate counts would give the biggest numbers in the whole project, and he does tell them to obtain last year's figures.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Asking facilities for an existing file is not a method they are carrying out.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A couple of mornings sounds exactly like the reduced version he applied to the interviews a minute earlier.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He does not shrink this one. He removes the hand counting entirely.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Brennan decide about each of the following methods? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: trip diaries

options.A: It will be the project's main method.
options.B: It will be used with a small number of people only.
options.C: It has been ruled out.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and listen to the first two words. Everyone won't cancels the student's version of the method without touching the method itself. Ten people will is the replacement, and he says ten twice and not everyone once, which is as clear as this script gets.

prediction.note: A verdict that begins by contradicting a quantity is shrinking the method, not deleting it.

teaching.answer_quote: Ten people will, if you buy them coffee

distraction.signal: A fortnight, and everyone writes down every trip
distraction.note: The student's word everyone is the thing being denied. One contracted won't decides this item, so listen through it.

teaching.recovery: If this one went, Tegan says And the app, which is the last method on the list and opens the final item of the set.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He calls ten good fortnights the most interesting thing in the write-up, which is the strongest praise in the first half.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Interesting is not central. The backbone was decided several minutes earlier and never changes.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The previous method was dropped one turn earlier, and refusals in this tutorial have been arriving in pairs.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The next clause gives a number and a condition, which is a plan rather than a refusal.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Brennan decide about each of the following methods? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: tracking journeys with a phone app

options.A: It will be the project's main method.
options.B: It will be used with a small number of people only.
options.C: It has been ruled out.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a timetable to decide it. The privacy point is the reason and the committee date is the mechanism: week nine falls after the data collection ends. So that one's gone is the verdict, and he even tells them to write the refusal up.

prediction.note: A date can rule a method out on its own. Compare the date given with the time the project has.

teaching.answer_quote: So that one's gone, and I'd say so in your methods chapter
teaching.recovery: This closes the set. Use the pause to fill any blank letter from the two you have used least, then read the five new stems.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Automatic route tracking would produce more data than anything else on the list, and he begins by agreeing it would work.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It would is agreement about capability, and the next clause turns it into a privacy problem.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He has already rescued two methods by shrinking them, so a small pilot group is the fix the learner is now expecting.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He offers no reduced version here. The committee date removes the option for this project entirely.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What is Doctor Brennan's objection to the survey's first question?

options.A: It excludes the people the study is about.
options.B: It should ask how often somebody rides.
options.C: It makes the form too long.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and note that he asks a question before he objects: what do you do with everybody who says no. Hamish answers wrongly and the correction is the answer. A frequency scale is the repair Tegan proposes afterwards, so it is a solution, not the objection.

prediction.note: An objection stem wants the fault, not the fix. The fix usually arrives one turn later and sounds better.

teaching.answer_quote: the interesting person is the one who used to ride and doesn't

paraphrase_link.printed: excludes the people the study is about
paraphrase_link.audio: sends them to the end of the form

teaching.recovery: If you missed it, wait for the word sample. Hamish says it aloud and it opens the next item cleanly.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Tegan proposes the frequency scale in the very next turn and he approves it, so the words sit right beside the answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It is the repair for the fault, and the stem asks what the fault is.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He says outright that twenty-six questions is about twenty too many, and length is a real criticism he makes.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He makes it as an aside about the whole draft, then says he wants to talk about the first question instead.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Where do they decide to hand out survey cards?

options.A: outside the engineering faculty
options.B: at the tram stop by the sports centre
options.C: in the bike cage

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a place name to be given and taken back, because that is what people do with directions. Tegan names Parkes Road, corrects herself in the same turn, and lands on the stop by the sports centre. The supervisor's Do that confirms it two seconds later.

prediction.note: Two of the three places have already been mentioned in the first half, so recognition alone will not decide this.

teaching.answer_quote: not Parkes Road, the other one, by the sports centre

distraction.signal: Sorry, no, not Parkes Road
distraction.note: The wrong stop and the right stop are four words apart. Never write a place name until the speaker has finished the sentence.

teaching.recovery: If the correction lost you, the next stem is about timing, and Tegan asks when should we open it out loud.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The faculty lists are the current plan and engineering is named twice in the exchange immediately before the answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The faculty lists are the problem being solved, not the place they choose for the cards.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The bike cage was the poster location in their original plan and it is where the cyclists actually are.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It belongs to the online survey plan from the first half and nobody revisits it here.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: When does Doctor Brennan say the survey should open?

options.A: in the first week of semester
options.B: in week four
options.C: in the week before the mid-semester break

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the wrong weeks to be named first, each with a reason. He rejects week one because timetables are still moving, then the week before the break because nobody rides then. What is left arrives as two words with no reason attached, which is how settled decisions sound.

prediction.note: Three time phrases, two of them behind a not. The one without a negative is the answer.

signpost.phrase: And not the week before the mid-semester break

teaching.answer_quote: Week four. Two weeks open, then close it
teaching.recovery: If you lost the week, wait for Hamish. His question about recording the interviews opens the next item.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Week one is the first week named and it comes with a full sentence of explanation, which sounds like justification rather than rejection.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The sentence begins with Not, and the explanation is a reason to avoid it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The break is mentioned twice in this script and the second mention is in the same breath as the answer.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He rules that week out because nobody rides then, which would destroy the response rate.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Brennan advise about the consent form?

options.A: to write one specifically for this project
options.B: to use one that already exists
options.C: to ask the ethics committee to supply one

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and watch who is being quoted. Tegan reports what someone in her tutorial said, and reported advice is never the answer to a stem naming the supervisor. He contradicts it in five words and sends them to a colleague's approved template instead.

prediction.note: The stem names Doctor Brennan, so any advice attributed to somebody else is a decoy by construction.

signpost.phrase: Someone in your tutorial is wrong

teaching.answer_quote: She'll have a template, and hers has already been approved

distraction.signal: Someone in our tutorial said you have to write your own
distraction.note: Reported speech is quarantined speech. When you hear said, hold the fact loosely until the person in the stem responds.

teaching.recovery: If this one slipped, Tegan asks him for the one thing not to do. That question opens the last item of the paper.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is stated plainly, as a rule, by a student, and rules stated as rules are the easiest thing in the paper to write down.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The supervisor's next sentence calls it wrong, which is as direct a contradiction as this genre offers.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The ethics committee was discussed at length in the first half, so it is the institution already in the learner's head.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The committee was raised about the app and its next sitting is too late for anything.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Brennan tell the students to do this week?

options.A: get the gate-count figures from facilities
options.B: start writing the methods chapter
options.C: submit an ethics application

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and pin the stem's time phrase. Three instructions have been given in this tutorial and only one of them carries this week. He gives it twice, once as a negative about leaving it to the end and once as the positive, with a reason about forgetting.

prediction.note: This week is the whole stem. Three instructions are live; only one has a time attached.

signpost.phrase: Don't start writing your methods chapter at the end

teaching.answer_quote: Write it as you go, this week, while you can still remember why you dropped the app

paraphrase_link.audio: Write it as you go, this week

distraction.signal: Ring facilities, ask for last year's
distraction.note: The other imperative in this tutorial is Ring facilities, and it was given ten minutes before the stem's this week.

teaching.recovery: Nothing follows this. In the check half-minute, sweep for empty boxes first and fill each from its slot type.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Ring facilities is a clear imperative he really gave, and it is the only task in the tutorial with an outside body attached.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It was given in the first half about a method they dropped, and no time is attached to it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Consent and ethics are both discussed a minute earlier, so the paperwork is fresh in the ear when the stem arrives.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He rules the extra application out because the committee sits too late, so nothing is being submitted.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Five methods are decided in ninety seconds and two of them survive in shrunken form, which is neither a yes nor a no. The verdicts are short and the reasons are long.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: He drops the activity and keeps the data in the same breath, so half the item survives and half of it does not.

pre_teach.gloss: Australian short form of university
a street railway; the stop is a meeting point
the week off in the middle of a teaching term
a locked enclosure for parking bicycles
records people keep of every journey they make
the panel does not meet to make decisions
the part of a report explaining how it was done

signpost_map.phrase: And not the week before the mid-semester break
Someone in your tutorial is wrong
And what's the one thing you'd tell us not to do?
Don't start writing your methods chapter at the end

teaching.accent_note: Australian lexis and conventions are authentic here; the voices are British approximations. Note the rising tone on Tegan's statements: in Australian English a rise can mean checking in, not asking.

title: Reviewing field work: a sand-dune vegetation survey

script_json.title: Reviewing field work: a sand-dune vegetation survey
script_json.scenario: Two students go through a weekend of dune field work that partly failed, and their tutor separates what is recoverable from what is not before planning the resurvey with them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Nell and Bethan, going over a weekend of dune field work with their tutor, Doctor Kessel. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right, sit down, both of you. So the dune survey. I've been through the sheets you handed in, and I want to start with something that isn't your fault. There's a lot in here that works, and two things that really don't.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The tide.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The tide. You laid your first transect out at low water on the Saturday, and by the time you'd finished quadrat six the sea was over your first three.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We did get the readings, though. All six of them, before the water came up.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Six is short for a transect anyway. The handbook says ten.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Six would have been survivable. The problem is different. A dune transect is meant to be a gradient from wet to dry, and yours goes wet to dry and then back to wet. It doesn't describe anything.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we redo it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You redo it, and this time you start at the top of the dune and walk down, so the sea can't catch you. And take the tape out before you take the quadrat frame out, not after.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can I ask about the grid references? We lost the ones for transect two.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You didn't lose them. You never took them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We took them on my phone. I had signal in the car park, and then nothing at all on the beach.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: On a phone with no signal, on a beach. Look, it doesn't matter how now. What matters is that transect two has no location, so it isn't a transect, it's a list of plants.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the counts? Bethan and I got different numbers in the same quadrat.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Twice. Marram grass, quadrat four. I had thirty and Nell had eleven.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Were you counting shoots, or were you counting plants? Because those are two completely different numbers, and they both went in the same column.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Shoots.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Plants. Or clumps, I suppose.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: There it is. Marram spreads underground, so one plant can put up forty shoots. Neither of you is wrong. You just never wrote down which of the two you were counting, and that goes in your method before you go back.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What about transect three? We never got to it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Leave it. Three transects was ambitious for a weekend, and two good ones beat three rushed ones. Write in your limitations that you planned three and ran two, and say why.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ross's group did three. We could borrow theirs.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You could, and then it'd be Ross's field work with your name on the front of it. No. Two is honest. An examiner can spot a borrowed transect from the handwriting on the sheet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And is any of it any good?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Your species identification is the best I've had from a second year. Bethan, you keyed out two sedges that I'd have had to look up. That's the part I'd build the write-up around, not the transects.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The resurvey. Let's get the practical side fixed now, so that you don't repeat any of this in a fortnight. I've got twenty minutes, so I'll ask and you answer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We're free the weekend after next.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You're not going at a weekend. The wardens only open the gate to vehicles on a Wednesday, and you're carrying quadrats and a tape.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Wednesday it is, then.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Wednesday. And be on site by nine, because the light goes early in November and half your photographs from last time are unusable.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The photographs. What do you actually want in them?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Every quadrat, from directly above, with a scale bar lying along the edge of the frame. Without a scale bar the photograph is a nice picture of some grass.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Scale bar. We've got one.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Do we record everything to species? The handbook says species.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The handbook is written for a whole-summer project. For yours, genus is fine for the grasses, and it'll save you an hour a transect. Species only for the sedges, because that's where your marks are.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How many of us do we need?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Four. Two on the tape and two recording.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Three would do it if you're organised, but four is safer with the tide. Take four.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I'll type the data up when we get home.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Don't. Type it into the shared sheet in the car park before you leave the site, while you can still read your own handwriting and remember what your abbreviations meant.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Car park. Fine.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And send me the two transects by the Friday. Not the write-up. Just the numbers. I'd rather see two honest transects on the Friday than a polished excuse on the Monday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: One answer per fault, in the order he works down the sheets. Nothing here is revisited later.
teaching.strategy: This is a post-mortem, so every stem is about a fault and the students name a plausible fault first every time. Wait for the tutor to accept, replace or split it, because he does one of those three in every exchange.
teaching.preview_focus: Underline the noun in each stem: data, transect, counts, transect three, strongest part. Those five nouns are your only map through six minutes of talk.
teaching.watch_out: The students diagnose themselves out loud and are wrong four times out of five. Score the tutor only.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Five practical decisions in five short exchanges, in the printed order. Nothing here is returned to later.
teaching.strategy: After twenty minutes of choosing letters your hand wants to write a letter. These are words. Slot-type all five gaps in the pause: a day, a piece of equipment, a level, a number, a place.
teaching.preview_focus: Read what is printed either side of each gap. Two gaps have the in front of them, which means a specific named thing, not a description.
teaching.watch_out: Every one of these five is proposed wrongly by a student first, so the first word you hear in each slot is the wrong one.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Why does Doctor Kessel say the first transect cannot be used?

options.A: The sea covered some of the quadrats before they were read.
options.B: The readings were taken at different states of the tide.
options.C: The transect was too short.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the flooding to be described before the fault is named. He says outright that six quadrats would have been survivable, then gives the real problem: a gradient that runs wet, dry and wet again. That shape is what different states of the tide produces.

prediction.note: The vivid detail comes first in a post-mortem. The fault that is keyed arrives after a but or a however.

teaching.answer_quote: yours goes wet to dry and then back to wet. It doesn't describe anything

paraphrase_link.audio: goes wet to dry and then back to wet

distraction.signal: the sea was over your first three
distraction.note: The picture arrives before the diagnosis. Hold the letter until somebody says what the picture means.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The sea genuinely covered three quadrats, it is the most memorable image in the exchange, and it comes first.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Bethan says the readings were taken before the water came up, and he does not dispute it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Nell says six is short and quotes ten from the handbook, which is a number-backed criticism in a discussion about faults.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: His first three words reject it: six would have been survivable.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What is the problem with the second transect?

options.A: Its position cannot be established.
options.B: The list of species is incomplete.
options.C: It has to be repeated on the same day as the first.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and notice the correction two turns earlier: they did not lose the references, they never took them. He then refuses to discuss how and says what matters, which is the signpost. No location means no transect, and the species list is exactly what survives.

prediction.note: Problem stems reward the sentence beginning what matters, because that is where a tutor puts the mark.

teaching.answer_quote: transect two has no location, so it isn't a transect, it's a list of plants

distraction.signal: We lost the ones for transect two
distraction.note: Lost and never taken sound alike and mean opposite things. Let the tutor's version overwrite the student's.

teaching.recovery: If twenty-one is still open, abandon it. Nell says And the counts, which opens the next item in four words.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: His last four words are a list of plants, and a learner catching only the end hears something wrong with the species list.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The list is the thing that is intact. It is the location attached to it that does not exist.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Repeating work is the topic of the previous turn, and start at the top and walk down is a real instruction about redoing a transect.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That instruction belongs to the first transect, and nothing is said about doing two on one day.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: Why did the two students record different numbers?

options.A: One of them counted carelessly.
options.B: They were counting different things.
options.C: One of them was unsure what she was looking at.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and treat the tutor's question as the item. He asks shoots or plants, gets two different answers, and says there it is. Neither of you is wrong rules out any careless-counting option in four words, and the fix he gives is a recording instruction, not a counting one.

prediction.note: When a tutor asks a question instead of answering one, the answer is in the two replies he gets.

teaching.answer_quote: Neither of you is wrong. You just never wrote down which of the two you were counting

paraphrase_link.audio: never wrote down which of the two you were counting

teaching.recovery: Missed it? Nell asks about transect three next, and the number three is your cue that a new item has started.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Thirty against eleven is a gap so wide that carelessness is the natural explanation, and both figures are spoken clearly.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He says explicitly that neither of them is wrong, which cancels every error-based option.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Bethan hedges twice in three words, plants, or clumps, I suppose, and hedging sounds like uncertainty about the plant.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Her hesitation is about the unit she counted, not about the species. He confirms both counts are valid.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Kessel advise about the third transect?

options.A: to run it during the resurvey
options.B: to leave it out and explain the decision
options.C: to use another group's readings for it

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect an offer to be made and refused, because that is the rhythm of the whole tutorial. Leave it is the verdict, and the instruction that follows tells them to write the gap up as a limitation. Borrowing from Ross is proposed afterwards and killed in one turn.

prediction.note: Advise stems want an imperative. Two of these three are described, and only one is ordered.

teaching.answer_quote: Write in your limitations that you planned three and ran two, and say why

paraphrase_link.audio: Write in your limitations that you planned three and ran two

distraction.signal: We could borrow theirs
distraction.note: The decoy arrives after the answer here. A later proposal cannot overwrite a verdict already given.

teaching.recovery: If you lost this one, Nell asks whether any of it is any good. That question opens the last item of the set.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The resurvey is already agreed for the first transect, so extending it to the third feels like the obvious tidy solution.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Nothing is said about running three on the return visit, and he calls three ambitious for the time they have.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Bethan makes the suggestion in plain words, and he answers You could, which is two syllables of apparent agreement.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The rest of his sentence names it as Ross's work with their name on it, then says No.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Kessel say was the strongest part of their work?

options.A: identifying the plants
options.B: setting out the transects
options.C: keeping to the timetable

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect one thing to be praised and one to be excluded in the same sentence. Best I've had from a second year is the endorsement, the two sedges are the evidence, and not the transects at the end removes the option a learner is most likely to still be holding.

prediction.note: After five minutes of faults, the praise arrives once and briefly. Listen for a superlative.

signpost.phrase: That's the part I'd build the write-up around

teaching.answer_quote: Your species identification is the best I've had from a second year

paraphrase_link.audio: Your species identification is the best I've had

distraction.signal: not the transects
distraction.note: The last two words of the turn cancel an option. Stay on the sentence until the full stop.

teaching.recovery: This closes the first half. Use the pause to guess any blank letter, then slot-type all five gaps below.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Transects are what the whole discussion has been about, and the word appears in his praising sentence itself.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It appears there behind the word not, which is exactly how an option is cancelled in this paper.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: They finished six quadrats before the tide reached them, which sounds like working to a schedule under pressure.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: They failed to reach the third transect at all, and he calls the plan ambitious for the time available.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: The resurvey must take place on a ______ because of the vehicle gate.
questions.explanation: Predict a day, because a is printed and the printed reason is a gate. Nell offers a weekend and he refuses it in five words. Bethan's confirmation is your last warning that the answer is arriving, and he repeats the day on its own to open the next turn.

prediction.note: The printed reason is the vehicle gate, so expect the day the gate opens, not the day they are free.

teaching.answer_quote: Wednesday. And be on site by nine, because the light goes early in November

paraphrase_link.audio: the light goes early in November

form.note: Wednesday has a d after the Wed that nobody pronounces. Write the d or the mark goes.

teaching.recovery: If twenty-five is still bothering you, drop it now. Nell says The photographs, which announces the next gap by name.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Photograph every quadrat from above with a ______ in the frame.
questions.explanation: Predict a piece of equipment, because a is printed and the sentence is an instruction. Nell's question is the cue, and the answer is the third thing in his reply. He then says the word again in the following clause, which is your free second chance at the spelling.

prediction.note: A thing you put in a photograph, and a is printed, so singular and at most two words.

signpost.phrase: What do you actually want in them?

teaching.answer_quote: with a scale bar lying along the edge of the frame

paraphrase_link.audio: along the edge of the frame

form.note: Two words exactly. Adding lying or a scale bar for size takes you over and scores zero.

teaching.recovery: Lost it? He repeats the same two words in the next clause of the same turn, so wait rather than panic.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: The grasses only need to be recorded to ______ level.
questions.explanation: Predict a single technical noun, because level is printed after the gap. Bethan quotes the handbook, which is not the person the notes are recording. He overrules it for this project, gives the answer, and then names the exception, which is the sedges.

prediction.note: A printed noun after the gap fixes it as one classifying word, not a description.

signpost.phrase: Do we record everything to species?

teaching.answer_quote: genus is fine for the grasses, and it'll save you an hour a transect

distraction.signal: The handbook says species
distraction.note: A rule quoted from a document is not the tutor's instruction. Wait for the person to answer for himself.

form.note: Genus, not genius. One letter apart in writing and nowhere near each other in meaning.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: There should be ______ people in the resurvey team.
questions.explanation: Predict a small figure, because people is printed after the gap and a field team is single digits. Two numbers are offered in one sentence and the conjunction decides it: three would do it, but four is safer. Then he says the answer again on its own as an imperative.

prediction.note: A team on a beach, so a single digit. Anything above eight is a decoding error, not a near miss.

signpost.phrase: but four is safer with the tide

teaching.answer_quote: Three would do it if you're organised, but four is safer with the tide. Take four

distraction.signal: Three would do it if you're organised
distraction.note: Two figures, one sentence, one but between them. The figure after the but is the instruction.

form.note: Four or the digit both score. Writing four people repeats the printed word and scores zero.

teaching.recovery: Missed the number? Bethan says she will type the data up, and his one-word reply opens the final gap.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: Enter the data in the shared sheet in the ______ before leaving.
questions.explanation: Predict a place, because in the is printed and the sentence already names the file. Bethan proposes doing it at home and his first word cancels that. The place he names is the last one anybody would choose, which is why it is the answer and not a guess.

prediction.note: The is printed, so a specific place on or beside the site, in one or two words.

teaching.answer_quote: Type it into the shared sheet in the car park before you leave the site

form.note: Two words. The car park is three, because the article counts and the frame already prints it.

teaching.recovery: Last gap. In the check half-minute, re-read every frame and cut anything that repeats a printed word.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Every item begins with a student's wrong diagnosis, so the first plausible answer in each exchange is a decoy by design. Two of the five faults are split in half rather than accepted or refused.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: The correction lands two turns before the answer, and the words lost and never taken sound almost identical at speed.

title: Preparing a symposium talk on sleep and study

script_json.title: Preparing a symposium talk on sleep and study
script_json.scenario: Two students take a twenty-two slide draft of a conference talk on student sleep to their supervisor, who cuts it back, fixes the opening and the graph, and then decides where each remaining item belongs.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Marisa and Frankie, preparing a symposium talk with their supervisor, Doctor Vance. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: OK. The symposium is in nine days, so let's make this useful rather than encouraging. Talk me through what you've actually got.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twenty-two slides. Literature first, then the method, then our results, and then a section on what it means for the university.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Twenty-two slides. Right. And which of those four sections does your audience already know?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The literature. They're all sleep people. Half of them wrote it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We were told to review the literature, though. It's in the assignment description.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You were told to review it in the paper. In the talk, everybody in that room can recite it, and you'll spend six of your minutes telling forty specialists what they published themselves. One slide, then get to your own data.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the method? That's four slides at the moment.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The method's fine. Long, but fine, and nobody in that room will question it. Leave it alone for now and come back to it if you run short.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So how do we open? I had a question, like, how many of you got seven hours last night?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Open with the finding. Just say it. The students who moved their alarm an hour later gained forty minutes of sleep and lost nothing on the tests.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Ooh, or we open with the video of the sleep lab. Everybody loves the sleep lab.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Everybody does love the sleep lab, and it will eat ninety seconds and tell them nothing a still picture couldn't. Open with the number. Frankie's sentence, exactly the way she just said it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the graph? The one with the two lines on it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The two lines is the right graph and the wrong version of it. You've got a legend, gridlines, a title, axis labels in eight point, and somewhere underneath all that, two lines. Delete everything except the two lines and make them thick enough to read from the back of the room.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. And timing?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We've got twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fifteen. It's fifteen this year, they cut it when they added the poster session.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It's fifteen on the program, and fifteen means twelve, because the chair takes three for questions and she will not let you run over. Build a twelve-minute talk and rehearse it with a clock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twelve. Right.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And send me the slides by Monday night. Not Tuesday. The technician loads everything on Tuesday morning, and if yours isn't in the folder you're presenting off your own laptop, which never works in that room.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. You've got five things left that you want in there and about four minutes of room. Let's put each one somewhere, and then you can stop arguing about it on the bus.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The method diagram. The flow one, with the four weeks across the top.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one goes up. It's the only thing in your whole talk that can't be said in a sentence, and that is exactly what a screen is for.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sample sizes next. We've got a table with the numbers for each of the three groups.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Doctor Vance said last week that every talk needs its numbers on screen.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: I said every paper needs its numbers. Nobody has ever read a table of three columns from twenty feet away, so put that one in the handout and leave the screen alone.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The quotes. We've got two really good ones from the diary entries.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Read them. Don't show them. If a quotation is up there the room reads it faster than you can say it and then stops listening to you. Two quotations, read aloud, are thirty of the best seconds in your talk.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Limitations. We've got a whole slide on them.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You've got a whole slide apologizing. Take it down, and put the two real ones into a sentence when you get to the findings. On a slide a limitation looks like a confession. In a sentence it looks like judgment.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the references?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Nobody wants a wall of references at the end of a twelve-minute talk. Put them on the handout in six point, and if somebody wants one they will ask you afterwards, which is a much better conversation anyway.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So that's one slide gone, one added, and the graph rebuilt from scratch.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And nine days. Send them Monday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Three answers in the first three minutes: the fault, the opening, the graph. None of them is revisited.
teaching.strategy: Doctor Vance decides everything in this half, and he always agrees with a fragment of what a student said before replacing the rest. Listen for the second half of his sentences, because the first half is usually the concession.
teaching.preview_focus: Underline criticism, begin and graph in the three stems. Then read the nine options once, so you are recognising rather than reading when he starts.
teaching.watch_out: Both students propose openings and one of them is charming and wrong. Enthusiasm is not endorsement.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: These two close the first half, one after the other, and both are settled in a single turn each.
teaching.strategy: Two gaps and four candidate values will be spoken, because both of these items are negotiated in numbers and days. Write nothing until the supervisor speaks, since the students are guessing out loud on both.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type both gaps now: one wants a figure and one wants a day. Note that minutes and night are already printed, so neither goes in your box.
teaching.watch_out: Repeating the printed unit after the figure is the cheapest zero available on this page.

groups.instruction: Where does Doctor Vance say each of the following should go? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.

teaching.order_note: Five items, five verdicts, taken in the printed order. When you hear references, everything above it is decided.
teaching.strategy: He never uses the words slide, handout or aloud as a set. He says goes up, put that in the handout, read them, take it down. Convert each of those phrases into a letter the moment you hear it.
teaching.preview_focus: Letters repeat, so cross nothing off. Decide what each letter would sound like as an instruction, not as a description of a place.
teaching.watch_out: Two items are refused the screen for opposite reasons, and both refusals begin with a sentence that sounds like agreement.
teaching.bank_note: One letter is used once and the other two are used twice. Nobody ever says the word handout except him.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What is Doctor Vance's main criticism of the draft talk?

options.A: It spends too long on material the audience knows.
options.B: It contains too many slides.
options.C: The method section is too detailed.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the slide count to be echoed back flatly, which sounds like the criticism but is only a set-up. His actual question is which section the audience already knows, and the answer is the literature. Six minutes telling specialists what they published is the fault he names.

prediction.note: Main criticism means one thing. Expect at least one other fault to be raised and cleared.

signpost.phrase: In the talk, everybody in that room can recite it

teaching.answer_quote: you'll spend six of your minutes telling forty specialists what they published themselves

paraphrase_link.audio: everybody in that room can recite it

distraction.signal: Twenty-two slides. Right.
distraction.note: A flat repetition is not yet a verdict. Wait for the sentence that says why the number matters.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He repeats twenty-two slides back at them in a tone that clearly means too many, and it is the first number in the discussion.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He never returns to the count. He goes straight to which section is worth the audience's time.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Frankie raises the four method slides herself and he does call the section long, which is a criticism in almost any other tutorial.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The word after long is fine, and he tells them to leave the method alone.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: How do they decide to begin the talk?

options.A: with a video of the laboratory
options.B: with their main finding
options.C: with a question to the audience

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect three openings on the table, one from each speaker. His reply agrees with the video for a whole clause before killing it on time. Open with the number is the instruction, and he then points back to Frankie's sentence rather than repeating it.

prediction.note: Three people propose three openings. Only the supervisor's verdict counts, and it comes last.

teaching.answer_quote: Open with the number. Frankie's sentence, exactly the way she just said it

distraction.signal: Everybody does love the sleep lab
distraction.note: He repeats the enthusiasm word for word before cancelling it. Agreement repeated back is usually about to be withdrawn.

teaching.recovery: If twenty-one is unresolved, guess it and move. Frankie says And the graph, which opens the next item by name.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: It is proposed with real warmth and he opens his reply by agreeing with it in the proposer's own words.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He prices it at ninety seconds out of twelve minutes and says a still picture would do the same job.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Marisa's show-of-hands question is the first opening offered, and audience questions are a standard way to start a talk.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Nobody responds to it at all, and silence in a tutorial is not agreement.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
questions.prompt: What does Doctor Vance say about the graph?

options.A: It should be replaced by the figures.
options.B: Almost everything on it should be removed.
options.C: Its axis labels should be made larger.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and hear the shape of his sentence: right graph, wrong version. He then lists five things that are on it and tells them to delete everything except the two lines. The eight-point labels are inside that list of deletions, not an exception to it.

prediction.note: When a list is read out fast, ask whether it is a list of keeps or a list of deletions.

signpost.phrase: the right graph and the wrong version of it

teaching.answer_quote: Delete everything except the two lines and make them thick enough to read from the back of the room

paraphrase_link.printed: everything on it should be removed
paraphrase_link.audio: Delete everything except the two lines

teaching.recovery: If you lost it, Marisa says And timing, which is two words and opens the first written gap of the paper.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He has just told them to open with a number, so a learner carrying that verdict forward hears numbers beating pictures again.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That instruction was about the opening sentence. Here he keeps the graph and strips it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Axis labels in eight point is the most specific complaint in the turn, and enlarging text is the obvious repair for a small font.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The labels are inside the list of things to delete, so there is nothing left to enlarge.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: The talk itself should be planned to last ______ minutes.
questions.explanation: Predict a figure, because minutes is printed after the gap. Three numbers are spoken in four turns and two of them are students guessing. His reformulation, fifteen means twelve, is the moment the value is fixed, and he repeats it in the instruction that follows.

prediction.note: A conference slot, so two digits at most. Anything over thirty is a decoding error, not a near miss.

teaching.answer_quote: fifteen means twelve, because the chair takes three for questions

distraction.signal: We've got twenty minutes
distraction.note: One student corrects the other, then the supervisor corrects them both. Write only after the third number.

form.note: Twelve or the digit both score. Writing twelve minutes repeats a printed word and scores zero.

teaching.recovery: If the numbers ran away from you, the next gap is a day, and he opens that turn with the words send me the slides.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: The slides must reach Doctor Vance by ______ night.
questions.explanation: Predict a day, because night is printed after the gap. He gives the day, then names a different day twice in the reason that follows. Only the first one has a deadline attached to it; the other two describe what the technician does.

prediction.note: Night is printed, so your box holds the day only, and a second day will follow it.

signpost.phrase: And send me the slides by

teaching.answer_quote: send me the slides by Monday night. Not Tuesday

distraction.signal: Not Tuesday
distraction.note: The second day is spoken twice and the first only once. Count the negatives, not the repetitions.

form.note: Monday only. Night is printed, so adding it takes you to two words for no marks.

teaching.recovery: This ends the first half. In the pause, read the five items in the box below before he starts working down them.

questions.instruction: Where does Doctor Vance say each of the following should go? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the method diagram

options.A: Show it on a slide.
options.B: Put it in the handout.
options.C: Say it aloud only.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and use this first item to calibrate his vocabulary. Goes up means on the screen, and the reason he gives is the test he applies to everything after it: a slide is for the thing that cannot be said in a sentence. Nothing is qualified here.

prediction.note: The first item of a set is usually the clean one. Use it to learn what each letter sounds like.

teaching.answer_quote: It's the only thing in your whole talk that can't be said in a sentence
teaching.recovery: If twenty-five is still open, leave it. Each item is announced by name by a student, so the next letter has a spoken label.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A four-week flow diagram is detailed, and detail is what handouts are for in most people's experience of talks.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He gives the opposite reason: it cannot be said, so it has to be seen.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He has just spent the first half cutting slides, so a learner primed for deletion hears another one going.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: This is the one item he adds to the screen rather than removing from it.

questions.instruction: Where does Doctor Vance say each of the following should go? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the table of sample sizes

options.A: Show it on a slide.
options.B: Put it in the handout.
options.C: Say it aloud only.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and listen for who is being quoted. Marisa reports something he said last week and reports it wrongly. He corrects the quotation in seven words, gives the reason nobody reads a table from a distance, and sends the table off the screen.

prediction.note: Reported advice is quarantined advice. Wait for the person quoted to confirm or repair it.

signpost.phrase: I said every paper needs its numbers

teaching.answer_quote: put that one in the handout and leave the screen alone

paraphrase_link.audio: put that one in the handout

distraction.signal: Doctor Vance said last week that every talk needs its numbers on screen
distraction.note: A rule quoted back at its author is a decoy until he confirms it. Here he changes one word and the letter changes.

teaching.recovery: Missed it? He repeats the same instruction as leave the screen alone at the end of the turn, so the verdict comes twice.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Marisa states it as a rule he himself gave, and rules attributed to the person in the stem are the easiest thing to write down.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He replaces talk with paper, and that single change moves the table off the screen.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The next item is settled by reading it out, and a learner running one item behind carries that verdict backwards onto this one.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Nothing is said about reading the sample sizes out. The instruction is about where the table sits.

questions.instruction: Where does Doctor Vance say each of the following should go? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the two participant quotations

options.A: Show it on a slide.
options.B: Put it in the handout.
options.C: Say it aloud only.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and take the two imperatives as a pair. Read them, don't show them is the whole verdict in five words, and the reason is that a room reads faster than a speaker talks. Thirty of the best seconds in your talk tells you these are spoken, not printed.

prediction.note: Two short imperatives back to back, one positive and one negative, are a complete verdict.

teaching.answer_quote: Two quotations, read aloud, are thirty of the best seconds in your talk
teaching.recovery: If twenty-seven cost you time, jump on the word Limitations, which Frankie says on its own to open the next item.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Marisa calls them two really good ones, and a strong quotation on a slide is a standard move in student presentations.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: His second imperative forbids it directly, and the reason he gives is about the screen.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The handout has just been used for the item before this one, and quotations are the kind of thing readers like to keep.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The handout is not mentioned in this turn at all. He wants them heard in the room.

questions.instruction: Where does Doctor Vance say each of the following should go? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the study's limitations

options.A: Show it on a slide.
options.B: Put it in the handout.
options.C: Say it aloud only.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and notice that he renames the slide before he judges it: a whole slide apologizing. Take it down removes the screen, and put the two real ones into a sentence puts them in his mouth. The confession and judgment contrast is the reason, not the verdict.

prediction.note: Into a sentence is his phrase for spoken. It has already meant that twice in this discussion.

signpost.phrase: You've got a whole slide apologizing

teaching.answer_quote: Take it down, and put the two real ones into a sentence when you get to the findings

paraphrase_link.audio: put the two real ones into a sentence

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Frankie says they already have a whole slide on them, and the students' own version of an item has been right once already.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Take it down is the second thing he says, and it is an instruction about that exact slide.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Limitations are the kind of small print that belongs on paper, and the handout is already in play for two other items.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: He puts them into the spoken findings section instead, where he says they read as judgment.

questions.instruction: Where does Doctor Vance say each of the following should go? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 26 to 30. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the list of references

options.A: Show it on a slide.
options.B: Put it in the handout.
options.C: Say it aloud only.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the last item to be the quickest. Nobody wants a wall of references kills the screen, and six point is a size that only makes sense on paper. The offer to answer questions afterwards is a courtesy, not a third destination.

prediction.note: A font size is a strong hint on its own. Six point means paper, because nobody projects six point.

signpost.phrase: Nobody wants a wall of references

teaching.answer_quote: Put them on the handout in six point

paraphrase_link.audio: on the handout in six point

teaching.recovery: Last letter on the paper. In the check half-minute, fill any blank with the letter you have used least in this set.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A reference slide at the end is what almost every student talk actually does, so world knowledge answers this before he does.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: His first five words rule the screen out, and the diagram is the only thing he puts up.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: He does talk about somebody asking afterwards, and an answer given afterwards sounds like something said rather than printed.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That is a conversation after the talk. The references themselves have already been placed on paper.

what_makes_this_hard.note: He agrees with a clause and cancels the sentence four separate times, and one student quotes his own advice back at him incorrectly. The verdicts are all two or three words long.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: The correction turns on one substituted word, paper for talk, and the wrong version is stated first and confidently.

pre_teach.gloss: a room where sleep is recorded and measured
the faint background lines behind a graph
a very small size of printed lettering
speak for longer than the time allowed
printed pages given to an audience to keep
the weaknesses a study admits to
a slide crowded with sources nobody can read

signpost_map.phrase: In the talk, everybody in that room can recite it
the right graph and the wrong version of it
And send me the slides by
I said every paper needs its numbers
You've got a whole slide apologizing
