title: Working out what a reading list is for

script_json.title: Working out what a reading list is for
script_json.scenario: A lecturer takes two students through a reading list for a unit on small-town coastal tourism, explaining what each source is actually for, then settles the essay question, the workload and the deadline.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Owen and Jarrah, discussing a reading list with their lecturer, Doctor Weir. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right, come in, both of you. So, the reading list for the coastal tourism unit. Nine items on it, and you have both told me separately that it's too long, which it is.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Heaps too long. I read four of them before uni started and I still couldn't tell you what the argument of the unit actually is.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's because four of those nine don't contain an argument. They're on the list for something else entirely. Let's go through the five that matter, because knowing what a source is for is most of the skill in a reading list.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Start with Halloran? That's the one everybody in the seminar keeps quoting.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Halloran is the argument. The whole unit is a response to that chapter, and if you only read one thing properly this semester, make it that one. Twice, with a pen in your hand.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the tourism board figures? The annual ones, with all the tables at the back.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: There's no argument in there at all. It's a spreadsheet with a foreword. But it's the only place you'll find bed nights by month for the last ten years, and every essay in this unit needs at least one number out of it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we don't read that one, we mine it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Exactly. Now, the harbour article. Or, sorry, articles, because there are two of them with almost the same title. The one you want is Sandmouth harbour and the winter economy, not Sandmouth harbour since the ferry. The ferry one describes what happened. The winter one asks why.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The winter one.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The winter one, and it's the second argument of the unit. It disagrees with Halloran about who actually benefits from a summer season, and your essay lives in the gap between those two readings.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the old planning report? The green one in the library, the one with no cover.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one used to be the core reading, back when the council was still working from it. It's been superseded twice since then. Read the summary if you like the history, but nothing in it is current, and nobody will give you marks for citing it as evidence.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Last one on my list. The podcast series.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Doctor Weir put it at the top of the list, so I assumed it was the important one.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: I put it first because it's twenty minutes and it's free, not because it's the best thing on there. It's an interview, it's charming, and it's one person's memory of a town. Listen to it on the bus. Don't cite it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The essay. You've got a choice of two questions this semester, and I want to talk you out of one of them before either of you gets attached to it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The one about seasonality?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one's fine. It's the second question, the one about resident attitudes, that I'd steer you away from, because you'd need survey data nobody has collected and the pair of you would end up quoting the podcast at me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So both of us do seasonality?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Both of you do seasonality, and you'll write completely different essays anyway, because Jarrah will argue from the figures and Owen will argue from Halloran. That's fine. That is precisely what a seminar is for.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can we use the same figures, though? The same table out of the annual report?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You can use the same table. You can't use the same sentence about it. I've had that go wrong twice this year and it is a very boring conversation to have in my office in November.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And how much of the list do we actually have to read?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: For the essay, three of the nine, properly. For the exam in November, all nine, but skimmed. Those are two completely different jobs, and every year somebody does them the wrong way round and runs out of time.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: When do you actually want the essay?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The unit outline says week six. Ignore the outline. It was written before the public holiday moved. It's week seven now, and I've put that on the noticeboard outside my office as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Week seven. No worries.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And bring one page of notes on Halloran to the seminar on Thursday. One page, handwritten, and not a summary you've had generated for you overnight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Handwritten. Understood.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Handwritten. See you Thursday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: What does Doctor Weir say each of the following sources is for? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.

teaching.order_note: Five sources in the order the students raise them. Once she reaches the podcast, everything above it is settled.
teaching.strategy: She tells you the job of each source before she tells you her opinion of it, so the keyed information is usually the first clause of her turn. The warmth or coldness that follows is decoration you can ignore.
teaching.preview_focus: Turn the three options into three listening targets: an argument word, a numbers word, and a past-tense or history word. Those are what you are hunting.
teaching.watch_out: Two sources are described warmly and are still only background. Enthusiasm and usefulness are different things here.
teaching.bank_note: One letter is used once and the other two are used twice. The words argument and background are hers, not the box's.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

teaching.order_note: Three answers across the second half, on the essay question, on shared sources, and on how much to read.
teaching.strategy: Every one of these three is answered with a contrast: this one is fine but that one is not, you can do this but not that, three properly but nine quickly. Catch the second half of the contrast and you have the letter.
teaching.preview_focus: Underline advises against, the same source and for the essay. Two of the three stems are about limits, so listen for can't, don't and not.
teaching.watch_out: Each stem has a true statement attached to the wrong half of her contrast sitting in the option list.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: The two written answers close the tutorial and arrive in the last forty seconds, one turn apart.
teaching.strategy: After ten minutes of letters, these two gaps want words. Both are instructions rather than opinions, so they arrive as imperatives and they arrive quickly, with no discussion around them at all.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type both gaps: one wants a figure after the printed word week, the other wants a plural noun after one page of.
teaching.watch_out: Repeating week or page after your answer takes you over the limit and turns a correct answer into a zero.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Weir say each of the following sources is for? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the Halloran chapter

options.A: It sets out an argument the unit responds to.
options.B: It supplies figures you will need.
options.C: It is only background.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and use the first source to learn her vocabulary. She names the job in four words before saying anything else, and the sentence that follows makes the whole unit a reply to it. Read it twice with a pen is advice about how, not a different verdict.

prediction.note: The first item of a set is nearly always clean. Use it to fix what each letter sounds like.

teaching.answer_quote: Halloran is the argument. The whole unit is a response to that chapter

paraphrase_link.printed: an argument the unit responds to
paraphrase_link.audio: The whole unit is a response to that chapter

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Owen says everybody keeps quoting it, and a source everybody quotes sounds like the one people take their evidence from.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: Quoting an argument is not taking figures from it, and she names no data in this source.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A chapter that a whole unit was built on can sound historical, as though the field has moved past it.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She calls the unit a response to it, which makes it live rather than superseded.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Weir say each of the following sources is for? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the tourism board's annual figures

options.A: It sets out an argument the unit responds to.
options.B: It supplies figures you will need.
options.C: It is only background.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and take the opening negative as information, not as a verdict. No argument rules out one letter immediately. Then but turns the sentence, and she says every essay in the unit needs a number from it, which is as strong a statement of usefulness as she makes anywhere.

prediction.note: A source with no argument is not automatically background. Wait for what it does have.

signpost.phrase: There's no argument in there at all

teaching.answer_quote: it's the only place you'll find bed nights by month for the last ten years

paraphrase_link.audio: every essay in this unit needs at least one number out of it

teaching.recovery: If twenty-one is unresolved, guess it now. Each source is named aloud by a student, so the next letter always has a label.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The word argument is the first thing said about it, and a learner catching the noun rather than the negative hears the wrong letter.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The sentence is There's no argument in there at all, which removes that letter rather than choosing it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Four of the nine were dismissed at the start as being on the list for something else, and this one has no argument in it.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: The next clause makes it compulsory for every essay in the unit.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Weir say each of the following sources is for? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the article on the harbour and the winter economy

options.A: It sets out an argument the unit responds to.
options.B: It supplies figures you will need.
options.C: It is only background.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and read the printed stem carefully, because two articles share almost the same title and she corrects herself mid-sentence to separate them. The one that asks why is the second argument of the unit, and your essay is placed in the gap between it and Halloran.

prediction.note: The printed stem names one of two near-identical titles. Match on the words after the word and.

signpost.phrase: it's the second argument of the unit

teaching.answer_quote: it's the second argument of the unit. It disagrees with Halloran about who actually benefits

paraphrase_link.printed: an argument the unit responds to
paraphrase_link.audio: the second argument of the unit

distraction.decoy: the article on the harbour since the ferry
distraction.signal: Or, sorry, articles, because there are two of them
distraction.note: She corrects a singular into a plural, which is your warning that two titles are about to be separated. Read the stem again.

teaching.recovery: Lost among the titles? Jarrah says The winter one on its own, which tells you which article the verdict belongs to.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: An article about a winter economy sounds like the kind of thing that would carry seasonal figures, which is the essay topic.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She describes it as disagreeing with Halloran, which is an argument rather than a data source.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: The other article with nearly the same title is called a description of what happened, and descriptions are background.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: That verdict belongs to the ferry article, which is not the one printed in this stem.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Weir say each of the following sources is for? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the old council planning report

options.A: It sets out an argument the unit responds to.
options.B: It supplies figures you will need.
options.C: It is only background.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and let the tense decide it. Used to be the core reading is past, and superseded twice is the confirmation. She then licenses the summary for the history and forbids it as evidence, which is exactly the difference between background and a source you can use.

prediction.note: Used to be is never a current verdict. It tells you what the source has stopped being.

signpost.phrase: It's been superseded twice since then

teaching.answer_quote: Read the summary if you like the history, but nothing in it is current

distraction.signal: used to be the core reading
distraction.note: The strongest description of this source is in the past tense. Check the verb before you take the noun.

teaching.recovery: If you slipped, Jarrah says Last one on my list, which is a four-word warning that the final item has begun.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Core reading is the most important-sounding phrase in the whole discussion, and it is attached directly to this source.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: It is attached in the past tense, and she says twice that nothing in it is current.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: A council planning report is the sort of document that contains tables, and one data source has already been keyed in this set.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She mentions no figures in it at all and forbids citing it as evidence of anything.

questions.instruction: What does Doctor Weir say each of the following sources is for? Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to questions 21 to 25. You may use any letter more than once.
questions.prompt: the podcast series

options.A: It sets out an argument the unit responds to.
options.B: It supplies figures you will need.
options.C: It is only background.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and notice that Owen reasons from the order of the list rather than from anything she has said. She explains the ordering as length and cost, describes the source as one person's memory, and closes with two imperatives: listen to it, do not cite it.

prediction.note: Position on a list is not a verdict. Wait for her to say why the order is what it is.

signpost.phrase: I put it first because it's twenty minutes and it's free

teaching.answer_quote: It's an interview, it's charming, and it's one person's memory of a town

paraphrase_link.audio: one person's memory of a town

distraction.signal: Doctor Weir put it at the top of the list, so I assumed it was the important one
distraction.note: A student explains the lecturer's thinking for her. Wait for the person named to say what she meant.

teaching.recovery: This ends the set. In the pause, fill any blank with a letter and then read the three new stems before she starts.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: Owen states, confidently and in full, that it is the important one, and confident sentences are the easiest to write down.
option_diagnosis.why_wrong: She corrects the reason for its position in the next turn and then forbids citing it.

option_diagnosis.why_tempting: An interview about a town's history sounds like a source of detail, and it is the only source she tells them to consume in full.

title: Lecture: peat bogs and the carbon they hold

script_json.title: Lecture: peat bogs and the carbon they hold
script_json.scenario: A university lecturer explains how peat forms, what drainage does to it, what a four-year monitoring study found, and why the cheapest repair is so hard to organise.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about peat bogs and the carbon they hold. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Morning, everyone. Last week we finished with woodland soils, and today I want to go to the other end of the scale — to ground that looks like nothing at all and holds an extraordinary amount of carbon. Peat. I'll take the formation first, then what's gone wrong, and then the repair work.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, formation. Peat is just plant material that has died and then failed to rot. And the reason it fails to rot is water. Where the rain coming in is greater than what the ground can drain away, the soil stays waterlogged, and waterlogged ground has almost no oxygen in it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And once the oxygen's gone, the bacteria that would normally break everything down simply can't work. So the material piles up instead. Very slowly, mind you — a healthy bog puts on well under a millimetre a year.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, one plant does most of this work, and it's worth having the name because everything else follows from it. The moss is sphagnum. I'll spell that: S. P. H. A. G. N. U. M. It holds many times its own weight in water, and it turns the ground around it acid.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Keep that going for a few thousand years and the peat builds into a dome that sits above the surrounding water table. When it does that, we call it a raised bog, and a raised bog is fed by nothing but rainfall. No groundwater at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Before I leave the formation, a quick aside, because somebody always asks. Peat preserves things. Leather, wooden trackways, the occasional unfortunate traveller. There's a bronze-age walkway on the Norland moors that came out of the ground in one piece. It's the reason bog archaeology exists as a field.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Anyway. Back to the carbon, because that's the reason any of this is on your reading list.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — the damage. And almost all of it starts the same way. Somebody cuts ditches across the moor to drain it, so that the ground will carry sheep, or trees, or both. And the ditches work. That's the trouble. They work beautifully.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Once the water table drops, peat meets air for the first time in millennia and it starts to oxidise. The surface sinks. Across the Norland survey the average was around two centimetres a year. Sorry, no — two is the gentle end. On the worst of the drained sites, make that five.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And there's a second loss that people underestimate, and it is fire. Dried peat will burn underground, sometimes for months on end. And no, it isn't the grazing that finishes a drained site off, whatever you read in the papers. It's the fire.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So that's the mechanism. Now the findings, and this is the part that changed the policy.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The Norland team measured gas exchange on twelve moors for four years, drained and undrained side by side. And the headline is simple enough. A healthy bog takes in a little more carbon than it gives off. A drained one gives off far more than it takes in. It has flipped from being a store to being a source.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The other number worth writing down is what happens when the water goes back. Rewetting doesn't restore the bog — that takes centuries — but on those sites it cut the annual carbon loss by around seventy per cent within three years.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Repair. And the good news is that the cheapest technique is also the best one, which almost never happens in this subject.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You block the ditches. Somebody walks the line with a digger and puts a dam in every few metres, and the dams are made of peat — cut from beside the ditch, dropped in, trodden down. No concrete, no plastic, nothing imported at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the thing that stops it isn't the digger and it isn't the money. A scheme on this scale costs less than resurfacing a mile of road. What stops it, every time, is ownership. One moor can have eleven or twelve owners with different ideas, and you need every one of them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things to take away. Water is what makes the store, the ditch is what breaks it, and the obstacle at the end is a legal one and not a technical one. Next week, saltmarsh, which does the same job faster and is even less popular.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

- A drained bog gives out more carbon than it takes in, so it has become a net ______.

teaching.answer_quote: It has flipped from being a store to being a source

distraction.note: The first noun in a 'from X to Y' sentence is never the answer. Wait for the word after 'to' before you write.

form.note: Singular: the frame prints 'a net'. 'Sources' scores zero even though the study covered twelve moors.

teaching.recovery: If you lost this, do not reread it. She flags the next one herself with 'The other number worth writing down'.

questions.explanation: 'Per cent' is printed, so predict a bare figure that could be a percentage. She announces it as a number worth writing down. Two figures land in one clause, seventy and three, and only the one attached to 'per cent' answers the printed frame.

title: Lecture: putting nutrients into everyday food

script_json.title: Lecture: putting nutrients into everyday food
script_json.scenario: A public-health lecturer defines food fortification, compares the salt and flour programs, and argues that the difficult part of the work is measurement rather than chemistry.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about adding nutrients to everyday food. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. Good morning. Today we're on fortification, which is the practice of putting a nutrient into a food that people are already eating anyway. I want to do three things: define it properly, walk you through the two big programs, and then explain why the hard part of this work has almost nothing to do with chemistry.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, definition first. Fortification is not supplementation. A supplement is a pill, and a pill needs somebody to remember it every single day, forever. Fortification puts the nutrient into something that's already in the kitchen. And the food you pick to carry it — we call that food the vehicle.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Choosing the vehicle is most of the job, and it's harder than it sounds. It has to be something nearly everybody buys, in roughly the same amount, whether they're wealthy or poor, in the city or way out in the country. That rules out an enormous amount of the grocery store straight away.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The working rule is that a vehicle has to reach at least sixty per cent of households before the program is worth running. Sorry — sixty was the old figure, from the early days. The threshold most agencies use now is ninety.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings me to the one food that clears that bar everywhere. The first vehicle anybody used, and still the most successful one, was salt. Everybody buys salt. A wealthy household and a poor household buy almost exactly the same quantity of it, and that is very nearly unique.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what iodized salt prevents is a swelling at the base of the neck. The gland is the thyroid — I'll spell it, because it's all over the reading: T. H. Y. R. O. I. D. Starve it of iodine and it grows, sometimes enormously.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, one aside, and then I'll get back to the programs. The salt producers fought this for years, and not on health grounds. On taste. There were blind tastings, there were letters to the newspapers, and it turned out nobody could tell the difference. A nice little story about how a technical fix becomes a political fight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Anyway. The second program, and the more recent one, is folic acid. And here the vehicle is not salt, it's flour, because the mills add it before the grain ever leaves the site.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The timing is the whole point of that one. Folic acid protects the neural tube, and the neural tube closes inside the first month — often before anybody knows there's a pregnancy at all. Which is exactly why a pill can't do this job and a loaf of bread can. You don't have to know, and you don't have to comply.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the hard part. It isn't the chemistry. The chemistry was settled decades ago and it hasn't moved since. What's hard is the monitoring. You have to know how much is actually in the sack at the far end of a supply chain, and in most places nobody measures it twice.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — the table on your handout. Three nutrients, and one characteristic problem each.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Iodine first. Salt is cheap and it's everywhere, but iodine is volatile. Leave a sack out on a loading dock and you lose a good part of it. So the problem in the iodine row is sunlight, and the fix is nothing cleverer than opaque packaging.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Folic acid next. Students often write birth weight in that box, and birth weight is a genuine finding, but it belongs to a completely different program. The aim in the flour row is early pregnancy, and it's early pregnancy that goes in that cell.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Vitamin D. Different vehicle again. This one goes into milk, and in some countries into breakfast cereal as well, but milk is the standard and milk is what your table wants. It works because the fat carries it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the problem in that row is dose. It's set by law in most places, yes, but the enforcement is loose, and if you test cartons off the shelf the amount varies by brand — sometimes by a factor of three.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, to close. The nutrient is the easy part of a fortification program. The vehicle decides whether it reaches anybody at all, and the measuring decides whether it stays honest once the news coverage has moved on. Next week we'll look at what happens when a government quietly stops funding the testing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Definition, then salt, then flour, then the difficulty. Hearing the word flour means 31 to 34 have already gone.

title: Lecture: the cost of the things people send back

script_json.title: Lecture: the cost of the things people send back
script_json.scenario: A business-school lecturer explains what happens to returned online purchases, why processing them costs more than the goods are worth, and what one retailer's fee trial actually did.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about returned goods and what they cost retailers. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Morning, all. Right. Today's topic is the least glamorous thing in retail, and I'd argue the most interesting: what happens to the parcel after somebody decides they don't want it. I'll do the definitions, then the scale of it, then a trial that one of the big groups ran and what it actually showed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Definitions. Everything you've studied so far moves goods outwards, from the factory to the customer. When a parcel travels the other way, that whole system has its own name, and the term you want is reverse logistics. Reverse, because the goods are going backwards up a chain built to push them forwards.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the scale. If you ask people at a barbecue how many online orders come back, they'll guess one in twenty. In clothing the real figure is about a quarter? Sorry — a quarter was two seasons ago. On last year's numbers it's closer to thirty per cent.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the reason that number matters so much is that a return is not simply a sale that didn't happen. It's a sale that didn't happen plus a whole second set of labour costs. Somebody has to receive it, open it, inspect it, decide on it, repack it and relist it, and all of that is done by a human being.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's also a customer behaviour driving it that we didn't have ten years ago. Shoppers order the same shirt in three sizes, intending from the outset to keep one. That practice has a name in the trade. It's called bracketing, and on some product lines it's now the majority of orders.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So why do people send things back? The survey answer everybody quotes is quality. And quality does appear, and it's a real category. But it's a distant second. The reason given on about two-thirds of clothing returns is fit. Just fit — it didn't fit.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick digression, because it's a good story. There's a warehouse out past Halstow that exists purely to open parcels. Forty people, one job, no shop attached, and it runs on a public holiday roster because the peak is the first week of January. Anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Back to the money. Here's the thing that decides everything downstream. Processing one returned garment costs somewhere between eight and fourteen dollars, and on a lot of fast fashion that is more than the margin on the item was in the first place.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which is why so much of it never goes back on a shelf. And no, it isn't the freight that decides that — freight is cheap and it's getting cheaper. It's the inspection labour. If checking the garment costs more than the garment earns, the rational move for the firm is landfill.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, the trial. The Kellwood group, who specialise in mid-price clothing, spent eighteen months testing what happens if you charge for returns. Flat fee, small, on the app and on the mobile site. Here are four findings, and they're on your sheet as sentences.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first one is the one everybody expects and nobody thinks through. Yes, the return rate dropped, by about a fifth. But total customer spending fell as well, and it fell by enough to wipe out the saving. People didn't return less. They ordered less.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second finding. Of the garments that do come back, roughly half can't be sold as new, and those don't get destroyed any more — they go to clearance outlets, which are a genuinely profitable business now rather than a dumping ground.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, and this is the one I'd put in an exam answer. The single biggest reduction in returns came from something almost free. They published accurate measurements on every product page. Not size labels, which are meaningless across brands. Actual centimetres, garment by garment.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the structural one. Returns are still buried inside general operating costs at most firms, so nobody owns the number. Kellwood's finance team realised that nothing changed until returns appeared as a separate line in the accounts. Once it had a line, it had an owner.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things to take away from all that. The customer behaviour is rational, the firm's response is rational, and the outcome is a warehouse full of shirts that nobody will ever wear. Next week, packaging, which is the same problem with better public relations.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

teaching.order_note: Definitions, scale, behaviour, then money. Once she says 'Right, the trial', every gap in this set has gone.
teaching.strategy: Her first sentence lists three moves and your notes follow them. Four of these six gaps are single technical terms she defines out loud, so listen for the framing verbs: called, the term you want, has a name in the trade.
teaching.preview_focus: Slot-type all six. Two are terms she will define, one is a percentage, and 35 sits after a possessive, so it needs a singular noun.
teaching.watch_out: Three answers here are named only after a wrong candidate has been offered and dropped. Never write on the first plausible noun.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

teaching.order_note: She numbers the four findings aloud. Hearing 'third' means 37 and 38 are behind you and cannot be recovered.
teaching.strategy: She tells you outright that there are four findings and that they are on your sheet as sentences. That is the strongest recovery anchor in the whole talk: each ordinal she says puts your pen on the right line.
teaching.preview_focus: Underline the ordinal-free part of each sentence, then decide the slot. Three of the four gaps want a plural noun, so the -s is decided before she speaks.
teaching.watch_out: Two words maximum. Her natural phrases are longer than the limit, so trim to the head noun and its one necessary modifier.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
RETURNED GOODS
Definitions
- Moving goods back up the supply chain is known as ______ logistics.
questions.explanation: A printed noun follows the gap, so predict the word in front of it. 'The term you want is' is as explicit a definition marker as a lecturer gives. She then repeats the single word on its own, which is your confirmation. Write it without the noun.

prediction.note: The noun is printed, so only its modifier is wanted. One word, and it will mean backwards.

teaching.answer_quote: the term you want is reverse logistics. Reverse, because the goods are going backwards

paraphrase_link.printed: Moving goods back up the supply chain
paraphrase_link.audio: the goods are going backwards up a chain

form.note: One word. Writing 'reverse logistics' repeats the printed noun and scores zero on a one-word limit.

teaching.recovery: She says the word twice in one breath. If you missed the first, the second is two seconds later and stands alone.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Scale
- On last year's figures, about ______ per cent of clothing orders are returned.
questions.explanation: The printed frame says last year's figures, which warns you an older number is coming first. She gives a quarter with a rising tone, then corrects herself: a quarter was two seasons ago. The current figure is thirty. Write the digits only.

prediction.note: A percentage, so two digits. 'Last year's figures' tells you an out-of-date one arrives first.

teaching.answer_quote: On last year's numbers it's closer to thirty per cent

distraction.signal: Sorry — a quarter was two seasons ago
distraction.note: Her voice rises on 'about a quarter'. In this variety a rise means 'still with me?', not a question, and never a signal to write.

form.note: 30 or thirty. 'A quarter' is a fraction, not the keyed figure, and the per cent sign is already printed.

teaching.recovery: If the two figures blurred, take thirty: she attaches 'two seasons ago' to the other one, and old numbers are never the key.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Customer behaviour
- Ordering one item in several sizes and keeping one is called ______.
questions.explanation: 'Is called' promises a term you may never have met, so predict a single noun and wait for the naming verb. 'That practice has a name in the trade' announces it a clause early. The word is bracketing, and the -ing is part of it.

prediction.note: A trade term. Expect an -ing form, because it names a habit rather than a thing.

signpost.phrase: That practice has a name in the trade

teaching.answer_quote: It's called bracketing, and on some product lines it's now the majority of orders

paraphrase_link.printed: Ordering one item in several sizes
paraphrase_link.audio: order the same shirt in three sizes

form.note: 'Bracketing', not 'bracket'. The frame prints 'is called', so the box wants the whole name.

teaching.recovery: If you lost it, she opens the next stretch with a question: 'So why do people send things back?' That is question 34 starting.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: - The reason given on about two-thirds of clothing returns is ______.
questions.explanation: 'The reason given' wants a single noun, and the printed fraction tells you to wait for a large figure. Quality is named first and is a genuine category, which is exactly why it is dangerous. She calls it a distant second and then names fit.

prediction.note: One noun naming a reason. The printed fraction means you want the largest category, not the first named.

signpost.phrase: The reason given on about two-thirds of clothing returns is

teaching.answer_quote: The reason given on about two-thirds of clothing returns is fit. Just fit

distraction.signal: The survey answer everybody quotes is quality
distraction.note: She confirms quality is real before demoting it. A category that is admitted and then ranked second is not the answer.

form.note: The noun 'fit', not the verb 'fitted'. Her last three words hand it to you in noun position.

teaching.recovery: Lost it? The Halstow warehouse digression follows and carries nothing. Use those twenty seconds to finish writing and rejoin at 'Back to the money'.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt:
Money
- Processing one garment can cost more than the item's ______.
questions.explanation: A possessive before the gap forces a singular noun. 'Here's the thing that decides everything downstream' is her loudest emphasis marker in the talk. She prices the handling, then says it exceeds the margin. One word.

prediction.note: Singular after a possessive. A money word, and not the price, because the frame compares it to a cost.

signpost.phrase: Here's the thing that decides everything downstream

teaching.answer_quote: that is more than the margin on the item was in the first place

form.note: Singular: the frame prints 'the item's'. 'Margins' scores zero even though she is talking about a whole product line.

teaching.recovery: If the dollar figures pulled you off, her next sentence opens 'Which is why so much of it never goes back on a shelf'.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
questions.prompt: - Where checking costs more than the garment earns, the firm's rational choice is ______.
questions.explanation: The frame wants a destination, and 'rational choice is' means a single noun. She rules freight out with a flat 'no, it isn't', names inspection labour as the real driver, and only then gives the destination. Uncountable, so no -s.

prediction.note: A destination for goods, stated as one noun. No article is printed, so no article in the box.

signpost.phrase: Which is why so much of it never goes back on a shelf

teaching.answer_quote: the rational move for the firm is landfill

paraphrase_link.audio: the rational move for the firm is

distraction.signal: it isn't the freight that decides that
distraction.note: One 'isn't' at normal speed cancels the noun that follows it. Mark every negative on the page during the preview.

form.note: Uncountable. 'Landfills' is a US plural for the sites themselves and does not fit this frame.

teaching.recovery: If you lost this one, she announces the next section aloud: 'Right, the trial.' Move your eyes to the sentences and let 36 go.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: Charging a return fee cut the return rate, but total customer ______ fell by as much.
questions.explanation: 'Total customer' before the gap forces an uncountable noun about money. She flags the finding as the one everybody expects, then flips it with 'But'. The mark is on the second clause, and the last line explains it: they ordered less.

prediction.note: Uncountable and about money. Never add an -s after 'total'.

signpost.phrase: The first one is the one everybody expects

teaching.answer_quote: But total customer spending fell as well, and it fell by enough to wipe out the saving

paraphrase_link.audio: fell by enough to wipe out the saving

distraction.signal: Yes, the return rate dropped
distraction.note: 'Yes, X. But Y.' The concession is already printed in your sentence, so the gap must be on the far side of the but.

form.note: 'Spending', not 'spend' or 'spent'. The gap sits between an adjective and a verb, so it must be a noun.

teaching.recovery: If you missed it, she opens the next line with the word 'Second'. That single word puts your pen on the right sentence.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: Garments that cannot be sold as new are now sent to ______ rather than destroyed.
questions.explanation: 'Sent to' plus 'rather than destroyed' wants a place, and places in this trade are plural. 'Second finding' tells you the sentence has started. She says clearance outlets, so take the two-word chunk and stop before 'which'.

prediction.note: A destination, and it contrasts with destruction, so somewhere goods are still sold.

teaching.answer_quote: they go to clearance outlets, which are a genuinely profitable business now

form.note: Exactly two words, and the -s is on the second one. 'To clearance outlets' is three and scores zero.

teaching.recovery: Missed it? She says 'Third, and this is the one I'd put in an exam answer', which is her loudest cue of the afternoon.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: The largest fall in returns followed the publishing of accurate ______ for each garment.
questions.explanation: 'Accurate' before the gap wants a plural noun for data. She marks this one as exam-worthy, names it, and then rules out size labels in the following clause. Write the plural: the -s is fixed by 'accurate' and by the sense.

prediction.note: Plural data of some kind. One garment has many of them, so the -s is decided before she speaks.

signpost.phrase: this is the one I'd put in an exam answer

teaching.answer_quote: They published accurate measurements on every product page

distraction.signal: Not size labels, which are meaningless across brands
distraction.note: The wrong answer arrives after the right one here. A 'not X' clause following the key is still a rejection, not a revision.

form.note: Plural. 'Measurement' loses the mark even though you heard the word, because 'accurate' and 'each garment' both demand several.

teaching.recovery: If you were still writing, her word 'fourth' opens the last sentence. There is exactly one answer left, so use the ordinal.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
questions.prompt: Nothing changed at Kellwood until returns were shown as a separate line in the ______.
questions.explanation: 'A separate line in the' points at a document, and this one is plural in English. 'And fourth, the structural one' announces the last finding. She says the accounts, then explains it: once it had a line, it had an owner.

prediction.note: A financial document. In this sense the English word is always plural, so write the -s.

teaching.answer_quote: nothing changed until returns appeared as a separate line in the accounts

paraphrase_link.printed: were shown as a separate line

distraction.signal: buried inside general operating costs
distraction.note: The first accounting phrase in the sentence is where returns are hidden, not where they need to be. Wait for 'until'.

form.note: Plural. 'Account' is a bank account and means something else entirely in this sentence.

teaching.recovery: Last mark on the page. If it went, put a plural financial noun in the box during the check; a blank scores nothing.

what_makes_this_hard.note: Six of the ten answers are preceded by a plausible wrong candidate that she names, discusses and then drops. The vocabulary is easy; the discipline of waiting is not.
what_makes_this_hard.why_hardest: The rejected candidate comes after the key rather than before it, which reverses the habit the rest of the talk builds.

title: Lecture: why reinforced concrete fails

script_json.title: Lecture: why reinforced concrete fails
script_json.scenario: A civil-engineering lecturer explains how steel is protected inside concrete, the two processes that break that protection, what a bridge inspection survey found, and why he blames maintenance rather than materials.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about the failure of reinforced concrete structures. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, settle down. Today, reinforced concrete, and specifically why so much of it built in the last century is now coming apart. I'll set up the chemistry, then take you through the two attack mechanisms, then a survey of road bridges, and I'll finish with an argument you may not agree with.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Start with why we reinforce at all. Concrete is superb in compression. Squash it and it just gets on with it. But pull it apart and it's hopeless, because concrete is weak in tension, so we cast steel bars into the parts of a beam that are being stretched.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, steel in the open air rusts. Steel inside concrete does not, and the reason is chemical rather than physical. Fresh concrete is strongly alkaline, and that alkalinity grows a microscopically thin oxide film on the surface of every bar. We call that film the passive layer, and while it holds, nothing happens at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So the whole subject reduces to one question: what destroys the passive layer? And there are two answers, and only two that matter.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first is slow and it is universal. Carbon dioxide from the air works its way in through the pores and reacts with the alkali, and the concrete gradually stops being alkaline from the outside inwards. That process is carbonation, and you can watch its front advance with a spray bottle of indicator.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The second is faster and it is local. People assume this one is coastal — the sea, the spray, the marine structures. It is far more often the road. What breaks the film here is chlorides, and inland they arrive by the lorryload every winter as de-icing salt.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings me to the single most important number on any drawing, and the one that gets cut first when a job is running late. It isn't the strength of the mix. It's how far the bar sits back from the surface, and the word for that is cover.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick aside, because it makes the point better than I can. There's a footbridge at Merridge where the drawings specified forty millimetres and the site poured it at twelve, and you can read the whole story off the underside without any instruments at all. Anyway, back to the mechanism.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Once the film is gone, the bar corrodes, and rust takes up several times the volume of the steel it came from. So the bar swells, the concrete around it cracks along the line of the bar, and eventually a slab of the surface detaches. The word you want for that detaching is spalling.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — the survey. Eleven hundred road bridges, inspected on a common protocol over four years, which is the largest consistent data set anybody in this country has.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the finding that surprised people was where the damage starts. Everybody expected the deck surface, because that's where the salt lands. Sorry — expected is wrong, everybody assumed it, which is different. In practice the damage starts at the expansion joints, because that is where the salty water gets underneath.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: On repair, the survey is blunter still. The only intervention that stopped corrosion outright, rather than slowing it, was cathodic protection, which works by making the whole reinforcement cage electrically negative so the steel simply cannot give up ions.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Patching, by contrast, has a failure mode that nobody expects. You cut out the damaged concrete, you put new alkaline material back, and the repaired area is now healthier than everything around it. Which drives the corrosion straight to the boundary. New damage appears within about two years, and not where you would look for it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh — hang on. I said the damage appears at the patch. Let me be precise, because it matters for your coursework: it appears just outside it, at the patch edges. The patch itself is fine. It's the ring around the patch that goes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the argument, and then I'll let you go. Everyone in this field talks about better materials, and the materials are not the problem. Self-healing mixes, stainless reinforcement, coatings — all real, all expensive, none of them fitted to the structures we already own. What actually decides the life of a bridge is maintenance.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which is a budgeting argument dressed up as an engineering one, and that is exactly why nobody wins it. Next week, timber, which fails honestly and in public.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Lecture: how a new word gets into a dictionary

script_json.title: Lecture: how a new word gets into a dictionary
script_json.scenario: A lexicography lecturer describes the evidence editors collect, the three tests a candidate word must pass, and why he says a dictionary records usage instead of authorising it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about how new words are added to dictionaries. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: All right. Everybody asks the same question about this job, which is: who decides? So today I want to take that apart. First the evidence editors actually work from, then the tests a candidate word has to pass, and then, at the end, an argument about what a dictionary is for. That last part is where we'll disagree.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The evidence first. Nobody sits in a room deciding what English ought to contain. Editors work from an enormous searchable body of real language, gathered from print, broadcast, transcribed talk, and now the web. The technical name for that body of material is a corpus, and the good ones run to billions of words.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Inside that corpus, the unit that matters is the individual recorded use. One sentence, dated, with its source attached. Those are citations, and the whole trade runs on them. An editor doesn't argue about a word. An editor counts them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How many do you need? The old working rule was ten independent citations. Sorry, ten is what I was taught, and it's out of date. Most houses now want twenty before they'll even open a file, and they want them from unrelated writers.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, where do candidate words come from? Several routes, and one of them fills more slots than the rest. You take two existing words and fuse them, keeping the front of one and the back of the other. We used to call those portmanteau words, after a Victorian joke, and some of my colleagues still do. The current term is a blend.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A digression, because somebody always raises it. There is no committee. There's no vote, no ceremony, no letter of admission. It's a spreadsheet and an editor with a deadline, and if that disappoints you, I'd say it should reassure you instead. Nobody has ever received a letter about it. Anyway, back to the tests.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Three tests, and a word has to pass all three. Frequency, which is just how often. Spread, which is how many different kinds of writer use it. And the third one, which is the one that kills most candidates, is durability. Is it still there in five years?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And a point people find genuinely surprising: nothing is ever taken out. A big historical dictionary doesn't delete. It isn't a question of space, and it isn't squeamishness. The word simply gets tagged obsolete and stays on the page, because somebody reading an old book still needs it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. Four observations about the practice, and these are the sentences on your sheet. I'll number them as I go, so if you lose your place, count along with me instead of reading ahead. Each one surprises students, and each one has a practical consequence for anybody who works with text for a living.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First. The words that give editors the most trouble are the ones born in conversation, because talk leaves no dated record. A word can be in every playground in the country for a decade before anybody writes it down, and the first citation is then wrong by ten years.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second. The volunteer reading programs that built the great dictionaries still exist, and I'm fond of them, but they're no longer where the material comes from. Most of what lands on an editor's desk this morning was pulled out of digital archives overnight by software.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, and this is the commonest reason for a rejection. A word gets turned down when everybody using it works in the same place. If the citations all come from one industry, it fails the spread test, however frequent it is inside that world.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the argument I promised. A dictionary does tell you which spelling is commoner, and people take that as a ruling. It isn't. The entry records use. It doesn't grant permission, and it never has. Nobody at any dictionary has the standing to permit or forbid a word.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So: evidence, three tests, and a book that describes rather than instructs. Next week we'll look at what happens to a word after it's in, which is where the real fights are. Bring the two entries I posted, and read the short piece on labelling as well, because that argument is this one in miniature.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Lecture: how the railways gave us the clock

script_json.title: Lecture: how the railways gave us the clock
script_json.scenario: A history lecturer describes how local solar time was replaced by a single railway-set standard, how the change was distributed and resisted, and who actually had the authority to make it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about the history of standard time. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Morning, everyone. Today's one of those topics that looks like it's about technology and turns out to be about authority. The clock on your mobile is set from a national standard, and nobody thinks that's remarkable. Two centuries ago it would have looked like an outrage. I'll do the before, then the imposition, then the resistance.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the before. Every town kept its own time, and that wasn't sloppiness on anybody's part. It was astronomy. You set the town clock at the moment the sun stood highest over your own church tower, and that gives you local solar time. Perfectly accurate, and slightly different in every valley.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the gaps were wider than students expect. Kellwood, which is only a couple of hundred kilometres inland, ran about eleven minutes behind the capital. Sorry — eleven is Merridge. Kellwood is further west again. Kellwood ran sixteen minutes behind, and a traveller crossing both lost a quarter of an hour without doing anything.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: All of which was perfectly liveable while the fastest thing on the road was a horse. It stopped being liveable the moment somebody tried to print a timetable. A timetable has to make one statement about when a train departs, and you cannot do that in a country with four hundred separate noons.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So the companies imposed one. And the reason they could impose it is that the wire ran beside the track. A signal went out from the observatory every morning down the telegraph, and each station pulled its clock into agreement as the signal arrived. It's the wire that made this possible, not the railway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: On the trains themselves the arrangement was cruder. Each service carried one watch, in a locked case, and it wasn't the driver who held it, because drivers had rather a lot on. It was the guard. That watch was legally the train's time, and if it drifted, the guard paid the fine.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick digression, because it's my favourite document in the whole subject. There's a diary from a stationmaster at Halstow who spent four years writing to head office about a clock that was, by his own account, forty seconds out. Four years of letters. They never once replied. Anyway, back to the argument.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Here's what I want you to notice. By the time anybody legislated, the thing was already done. Railway time crossed the country in about a decade, and for most of that decade it had no legal standing whatsoever. It was a private arrangement that the whole population had simply started obeying.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Four consequences now, and they're printed as sentences on your sheet. This is where the resistance comes in, and the resistance is the part worth your attention. I'll say the number before each one, so keep your pen level with my voice; each one lands in a single clause.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First. Towns fought it, and they weren't being sentimental about the sun, whatever the newspapers said at the time. What they objected to was who was doing the setting. A private company was now telling a borough council what hour it was, and nobody had voted on that anywhere.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second, and this is my favourite object in the story. During the changeover, public clocks in a good many towns were fitted with two minute hands? One showed the town's own time and the other showed the railway's, and you read whichever one applied to you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third. Parliament was, as usual, last. The question was actually settled in the courts, in a dispute about when a public holiday began, because it started at midnight local in one town and midnight railway in the next. After that judgement the legislation was a formality.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the one I'd like you to sit with. We did not adopt a national clock because it suited human beings. It doesn't, particularly. We adopted it because it suited trains, and everything since — the shift, the school bell, the tram — has been organised around a standard built for rolling stock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things to take away. The problem was the timetable, the mechanism was the wire, and the authority belonged to nobody in particular. Next week, the working day, which is the same story with the clock pointed at people instead of engines.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Lecture: why streets sort themselves

script_json.title: Lecture: why streets sort themselves
script_json.scenario: A social-science lecturer sets up a simple grid model of household preference, gives the result it produces, compares it with survey evidence, and warns what the model can and cannot be used for.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about why residential streets become divided. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, good afternoon. Today, why streets sort themselves, and I'll warn you at the start that this one has a twist in it that most people find uncomfortable. I'll set up a very simple model, then give you the result it produces, then what real survey evidence says, and finally what any of it is actually good for.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The model, then. Put two kinds of household on a grid, at random. Give every household one rule, and only one: it will stay put as long as some fixed share of its immediate neighbours resemble it. That share is what we call its tolerance, and in the first version everybody has the same one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the number people expect to matter turns out not to. Run it at a half and you get near-total separation, which surprises nobody. The interesting behaviour starts much lower, at about twenty-five per cent. Sorry, no — twenty-five is the earlier version. On the version in your reading it's thirty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What the runs show is that the sorting isn't gradual. A street stays mixed, stays mixed, stays mixed, and then over a handful of moves it goes. The moment when the movement starts feeding itself has a name, and the name is the tipping point.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But there's a precondition the diagrams never show, and it is the thing my students always miss. Nothing sorts unless somewhere is empty. A household can only act on its rule if there is a house to move into, so the whole process is rate-limited by vacancies. A completely full street cannot divide at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A digression, and it does become relevant. The first version of this was worked out on a chessboard with two sets of coins, by somebody sitting on a train, who did not own a computer and never used one for it. Worth remembering the next time you are told a result requires a supercomputer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Anyway, back to the substance. Because the model contains no motives whatsoever, and real households have a great many.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Ask people why they chose an area and the answer that comes top of almost every survey I have read is schools. Price appears too, of course. It comes second, and it comes second by a distance, which unsettles economists rather more than it ought to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And here is the consequence planners care about. The model is not symmetrical. Getting a street to sort takes a handful of moves. Getting it back takes decades, because the households who would remix it are precisely the ones the current mix repels. Once a street has tipped, it is very hard to reverse.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Four things to finish on, and you'll find them written out at the foot of your handout. I'll take them strictly in the order they're printed, and I shan't be going back over any of them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First, the result itself, which is the uncomfortable bit. Mild preferences are enough. Nobody in the model wants to live apart from anybody. Every household in it is perfectly content to be in a minority. And you still get almost complete segregation inside a few dozen moves.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second, and do follow this carefully, because it is the sentence people misquote at me. The model does not show that prejudice is absent from the world. It shows that the pattern does not require prejudice. Those are two different claims and only the second one is demonstrated here.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, the lever. If you want a street to hold, what works is not exhortation, and it certainly isn't policing who moves in. It's building a wider mix of housing types along a single street, so that the range of households arriving is broad by construction rather than by anybody's choice.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the warning I give every year. A model of this kind is an explanation. It is not a forecast, and anybody who reads a particular street's future out of it has misunderstood what they are holding. It tells you what is sufficient to produce a pattern. It never tells you what caused this one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So: one rule, a threshold around thirty, a tipping point, and a result that requires nobody at all to be unpleasant. Next week we put prices into it, and the picture gets considerably worse. Read the two short papers, please, and not the long one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Lecture: coverage and what people are afraid of

script_json.title: Lecture: coverage and what people are afraid of
script_json.scenario: A psychology lecturer explains the mental shortcut behind risk judgement, the two dimensions that inflate perceived danger, and which communication techniques actually move a decision.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about how news coverage affects the risks people worry about. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK, let's start. People are extremely bad at ranking dangers, and they are bad at it in a patterned way, which is what makes it studyable. I'll give you the mechanism first, then the two dimensions that distort it, then a study, and then four techniques and which of them actually work. The last part is the useful part.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The mechanism is a shortcut, and it's a sensible one most of the time. When you're asked how likely something is, you don't run a calculation. You try to think of an instance, and you judge the risk by how quickly one comes to mind. The name for that shortcut is availability, and it works beautifully until somebody controls what comes to mind.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which is exactly what a news cycle does. And this leads to the thing missing from almost every risk story you will ever read. You're told how many people were affected. You are almost never told how many were exposed. That second figure, the one underneath, is the denominator, and without it a number means nothing at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, two dimensions. Take two hazards that kill identical numbers of people. One of them will still feel far worse, and the research is consistent about why. The first dimension is whether the death is ordinary or horrifying, and the technical word for that in this literature is dread.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The second dimension is about choice. A hazard you take on deliberately, a sport, a diet, a drive, feels smaller than one imposed on you, even at identical rates. So the question isn't how dangerous it is. The question is whether the exposure was voluntary.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A digression, and I promise it's short. Somebody asks me every year whether journalists do this deliberately. In my experience they don't. They're selecting for what's new, and what's new is by construction what's uncommon, and that is enough to produce the whole effect without anybody intending anything. Anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Back to the evidence. There's a study I want you to know, because it puts a figure on the asymmetry. The team counted broadcast minutes given to two causes of death over four years, adjusted for how many people each one actually killed, and the ratio came out at about twelve to one. Sorry — twelve is the print figure. On broadcast it was eight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the last finding from that team is the encouraging one. Perceived risk does fall over time, but not because people learn the numbers. It falls with exposure. A hazard you have lived beside for ten years stops feeling like a hazard, and the psychological driver there is plain familiarity.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Four techniques, and they're the table on your handout. One column for what each one does and one for where it breaks. I'll number them as I go, so count along with me instead of reading down the page, because these four rows come at you without a break.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First technique, comparison. You set the hazard beside a familiar one and say, look, this is about the same as driving to work. And it fails, reliably, for a reason that has nothing to do with arithmetic. Audiences find it insulting. They hear it as being told their fear is silly, and they stop listening.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second, frequencies. Say three in a thousand rather than nought point three per cent, and comprehension improves measurably. But it isn't free, because it only works if the person presenting it has been shown how, and in most newsrooms nobody has. What that technique needs is training.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, the single case. Tell one named person's story and people remember it for years. Recall goes up enormously. What does not go up, and this is the awkward part, is accuracy. You've made the hazard vivid, which is precisely the distortion you were trying to correct.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, delay. Simply postpone the decision by two days, and the over-reaction drops off sharply. It's the cheapest of the four and the least popular, because two days is exactly what nobody has when the story is running.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So: a shortcut, two dimensions, and four techniques of which one and a half work. Next week, the same problem in medicine, where the numbers are better and the outcome is very nearly the same.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

title: Lecture: reading a diet out of a rubbish heap

script_json.title: Lecture: reading a diet out of a rubbish heap
script_json.scenario: An archaeology lecturer explains what survives in a domestic waste deposit, how it is recovered, what the bone chemistry adds, and why a midden is a record of disposal rather than of diet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about what archaeologists learn from domestic waste deposits. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Morning. Today we're on rubbish, which is, I'd argue, the most honest thing a settlement leaves behind. Nobody arranges their waste for posterity. I'll do what survives, then how we get it out of the ground, then what the chemistry adds, and then a warning about what none of it actually tells you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the deposit itself. A settlement that stays put for a few generations builds up a mound of shell, bone, ash and broken pot, usually just outside the door. There's an old word for that heap and we still use it. It's a midden, and a good one can be two metres deep.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, what survives in it? Bone survives. Shell survives beautifully, especially in the alkaline conditions shell itself creates. Plant food, on the whole, does not — with one exception, and the exception is the whole of archaeobotany. A seed survives if it has been charred. Burnt, and then dropped.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings me to recovery, and this is where the discipline changed. You cannot see a charred seed in a trench. It is the size of a full stop and it is the colour of the soil. So you take the soil away and you put it in water, and the light material rises and is skimmed off. That technique is flotation.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And for everything heavier, what governs your results, more than any other decision on the site, is the size of the mesh. Everything smaller than the holes goes out with the water and you will never know it was there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Standard practice on a domestic site used to be four millimetres. Sorry, no, four is coarse — four is what you use for building rubble. On a midden the standard is one millimetre, and the difference between the two is roughly every fish bone on the site.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick digression. The first person to argue this properly was a research student whose supervisor told her the extra sieving was a waste of a field season. Her thesis is still cited and his is not. I mention it because your own instincts about what is worth recording are probably better than mine. Anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Back to the science. The chemistry arrived in the eighties and changed the questions. You take a fragment of human bone and look at the ratios of two elements in the protein. Carbon tells you about the plants at the base of the food chain. But for how much animal protein somebody was actually eating, it isn't the carbon, it's the nitrogen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Four cautions to end on, printed as sentences at the bottom of your page. I'll take them one at a time, in the order they're written, and nothing separates them, so don't go hunting backwards for one you have already let go.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First, and this is the one I would put on the wall. A midden is a record of what a household discarded. It is not a record of what a household ate. Those two sets overlap, obviously, but they are not the same set, and everything else follows from that gap.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second, the survival problem. Bone lasts and plants mostly don't, so if you simply count what comes out of the sieve you will produce a picture of a population living on meat. That is a bias in the evidence, not a finding about the diet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, and this is the one students resist. We talk about the diet of a period, but almost every deposit anybody has published belongs to one household. It is one family's rubbish, from one yard, and you cannot get a region out of it however good the sieving was.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the positive one, because I don't want to send you away with nothing. There is one thing a midden gives you that almost no other source does, and that is seasonality. Shell growth rings, fish bones, the age of the animals killed — all of it dates to a time of year.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So: charred seeds, a fine mesh, two elements and four warnings. And if you take one thing out of this room, take the first of those cautions, because it is the difference between a careful piece of work and a confident piece of nonsense. Next week, cooking vessels, where the residue is on the inside and nobody threw it away at all.
