title: Lecture: how animals find their way

script_json.title: Lecture: how animals find their way
script_json.scenario: A biology lecturer separates the compass problem from the map problem in animal navigation, reviews the evidence for a magnetic sense and an odour map, and argues that the real finding is redundancy.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about how animals navigate over long distances. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, morning. This is the lecture where I have to tell you that the honest answer to the title is that we don't entirely know. Which is a good thing, not a bad one. I'll separate the two problems first, then go through the candidate mechanisms and the evidence for each, and then tell you what I think the real finding is.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Start with the simplest case, which is an animal that has not been anywhere unfamiliar. An ant leaves the nest, wanders about for twenty minutes, and then runs home in a straight line. It hasn't followed its own trail back. It has kept a running total of every step and turn, and the term for that is path integration.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But that only works from a track you have actually walked. Take the animal somewhere it has never been and it needs two quite different things, and undergraduates run them together every year. It needs to know which way is north, and it needs to know where on the earth it currently is. The first of those is a compass. The second is a map.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the way you tell them apart in the field is by moving the animal yourself. You take it a long way from home in a covered box, you let it go, and you watch the direction it picks in the first thirty seconds. That whole class of work is called a displacement experiment, and everything I'm about to describe rests on it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, mechanisms. The compass first, and there are three known ones: the sun, the stars, and the earth's magnetic field. The magnetic one is the interesting one, because we still cannot say with confidence what the receptor is.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The proposal everybody's heard of involves tiny crystals of an iron mineral in the tissue, and the mineral is magnetite. It's an elegant idea, and an old one. But I have to be straight with you: the anatomical evidence for it is thinner now than it was twenty years ago, and two of the best-known sites turned out to be contamination.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick digression, and it's a warning about method. Half the studies in this area were done on birds that had been in captivity for years. Take an animal that hasn't flown since it was a chick and you are measuring the aviary, not the species. That criticism has done more to clean up this field than any single result. Anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Back to displacement. The homing pigeon work is where the map argument actually lives. A bird taken four hundred kilometres from its loft still comes home. Sorry, four hundred is the old training figure. The published displacements go out to six hundred kilometres, and they still come home.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what supplies the map is not what people expect. Landmarks are the obvious candidate and they clearly matter close to home. Vision is the other obvious one. But block a pigeon's nose and its homing collapses at range, while the same bird with covered eyes does fine. The map, at distance, seems to be built out of smell.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Four conclusions, and you have them as sentences at the end of your handout. I'll count them off out loud, so stay with my voice rather than working down the page on your own; they run straight on from one another.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First. A sun compass is not a compass on its own. The sun moves across the sky all day, so knowing where it is tells you nothing about direction unless you also know the time of day. That is why every sun-compass animal we have tested turns out to carry an accurate internal clock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second, on the magnetic evidence. Almost all of the good behavioural work comes from birds released when the sun and stars were unavailable, which in practice means under heavy cloud cover. That is a real constraint on the literature and you should say so in an essay.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, and this is the finding I would build an answer around. No animal we know of relies on a single system. They carry three or four and they cross-check, and my word for that, the word I want back in your essays, is redundancy.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, which follows from it. When you disable one sense in an experiment, the animal usually still gets home. So what a clean experimental result normally measures is not the sense you removed. It's the animal's switching between systems, and that is a much harder thing to design a study around.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So: two problems, three compasses, one contested receptor, and an animal that is better engineered than our experiments are. Next week, the same question in insects, where the brains are small enough that we can be specific. Read the review, not the news coverage of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The British version of the accent drill. You will hear a student services officer at a college leaving a voice message for a new student, the day before term starts. The same message is recorded in three varieties of English. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.

lines.speaker: s1

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Ground floor, first door past the lifts. There'll be a queue at nine, I won't pretend there won't be.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Bring some photo ID with you, and something that's got your postcode on it. A bank letter, a tenancy agreement, that sort of thing.

lines.speaker: s1

lines.speaker: s1

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, that's everything. My surname's Ashby — A. S. H. B. Y. And your reference number starts with a Z. Z, then double four. See you tomorrow.
